speechtext:
Before the orders of the day are called, I would like to read the following newspaper item :-
Washington, D.C., April 13.-President Roosevelt to-day transmitted to the Senate Mr. A. LAVERGNE.
treaties with Great Britain in relation to the fisheries on the great lakes as between the United States and Canada.
And I would ask, in view of these treaties having been presented to the United States whether the Prime Minister is prepared to bring down information to the parliament of Canada the representatives of the other side interested, which. I should think, would be the natural and constitutional course.

speechtext: We have not yet received the ratification. As soon as we receive them, they will be communicated to the House. I should think that, as they have been communicated to the United States Senate, we ought to have them here.

I wish to direct your attention to something that I have noticed several times of late and that, it seems to me, ought to be made right. Comparing the English version of the orders of the day with the French version, I find that the items are not the same on the two papers. For instance, take the items under the headings * Public Bills, and Orders ' in the Order Paper of to-day, I find, in the English version,' item 21 as follows :-
No. 21.
February 12-House again in Committee on Bill No. 2, An Act to amend the Canada Shipping Act.-Mr. Lancaster.
But, in the French version, item 21 is Bill (No. 18). But Bill (No. 18) is item No. 22 in the English Order Paper, being the second item under the heading ' Public Bills and Orders.' Then in the French version, I find that the fourth order under ' Public Bills and Orders,' being item No. 24. is Bill (No. 43). But. in the English version, this is the third order under this head or item 23. I find that Item No. 30 of the English orders appears as item No. 22 in the French orders. It seems to me, as well as I can judge, that the French version is correct. Rule 28 provides :-
Rills reported after second reading from any standing or select committee, shall be placed on the orders of the day following the reception of the report, for reference to a Committee of the Whole House, in their proper order next after Bills reported from Committees of the Whole House.
According to that the second order under ' Public Bills and Orders ' in the English Order Pancr ought to he the first, for it is ' House in committee on Bill (No. 18) to amend the Railway Act (reported as amended).' As I understand it. Bills reported from committee as amended must

come first on tlie Order Paper and the Bills reported without amendment second. But they are reversed here. I have noticed these differences several times and have wondered how they arise. It seems to me that both versions ought to be the same, for, in that way, you avoid any danger of doing injustice.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The matter will be looked into.
The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) was to lay two documents on the table today. Might I ask if they are ready ?

speechtext: I thought it better to have copies made. Of course, I will produce the originals if the hon. gentleman desires it, but if copies are presented they can be used-
Well, may I have one now ?

I have given directions to have the copies made. But there are quite a number of dredging contracts in the order in council and a separate report of the chief engineer as to each one. They are being copied, but P cannot promise them before to-morrow. I would ask 1he hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) if it would not be convenient for him to discuss the matter in committee, as each item will be in the estimates. I will have the copies desired by to-morrow.

Mr. Speaker, I move for leave to discuss a question of urgent importance, the question of dredging contracts at Midland, Tiffin and Victoria harbour.
Leave being granted.

The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) stated yesterday, in answer to a question from myself that he was proceeding, during the coming season, to expend moneys for dredging at Midland. Tiffin-which is a point adjoining Midland -and Victoria harbour, without asking for tenders for the work for which the money is to be expended; but proceeding upon the prices that prevailed last year. Therefore I know, having seen the tenders of last year, what prices are to be paid for that work, without the report of the minister being brought down, which I expected to see .to-day. Now, Mr. Speaker, in that somewhat well known document called the report of the Civil Service Commission, upon page 42, will be found a very pertinent and *very strong reference to the millions upon millions of dollars that are being expended in different parts of the Dominion on dredging ; and I will call the attention of the House to the reference in that respect.
In certain cases there may be over-payments of wages such as the notorious instance which was brought to light about a year ago, when a clerk of works appointed hy political influence was found to have sublet his work to another person at a much lower rate. Your commissioners consider that some steps should be taken to organize the large army of employees in connection with this department, many of whom have served their entire lifetime in its employ, and bring them under definite regulations so that their employment mav be considered fixed and stable.
And furthermore, in volume II of the evidence of the Civil Service Commission, the following appears upon page 1100 :

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Q. You have a chief superintendent at St. John?-A. Yes, for the maritime provinces.
Q. And you have also dredging done by contract?-A. Yes.	_
Q. In connection with the dredging done by contract you have inspectors?-A. Yes.
Q. There was a statement made in the House of Commons during the last session, I think, by Mr. Bennett, that one of these inspectors of dredging to whom you paid so much a day, farmed it out to another man at half price?- A. Less than half. He was getting $3 a day, and he paid out $1.25.
Q. How are these inspectors of dredging appointed?-A. This year, when we ask for a recommendation for local men we state that they must be men of good standing and reputation, and furthermore they are invited to>
make a declaration to the effect that they are not in any way connected with companies or individuals who are performing dredging. We are trying to avoid the fact of relatives of contractors being employed to superintend them, and we are going to exercise the closest possible supervision so as to see that every inspector is on his work all the time that the work lasts.
By Mr. Fyshe :
Q. Why not hold the local government engineers responsible for that?-A. The local government engineer has perhaps forty works to look after. He cannot be at one work the whole time.	_
Q. He can get one of his subordinates to be there?-A. He cannot do it for all the works; he would require an immense staff. One man has to have charge of half a dozen works. The Toronto engineer, for instance, runs as far as Manitoulin islands, and he has to go around the shores of Lake Ontario, and he has perforce to trust somebody for some of the works.
Q. Could not the government so manage that a government official connected with the department could exercise an oversight?-A. We do. Our engineer or the superintendent of dredging visits the places at times, but they are not there all the time, and while they are not there, it is like when the cat is away.
By the Chairman:
Q. It would be in the interest of the contractor to connive at irregularities in inspection?-A. Very few would do anything of that kind, according to my experience, but it

could be done. The remedy I have always favoured for a state of things of that kind is a permanent staff of inspectors, appointed by the government as the engineers are appointed. I would have the inspectors entirely under the control of the department and with no local interests. They would act without fear or favour, while the local man who owes his position to local influence, is more or less influenced by that local power.
Now, Mr. Speaker, consider that within the past few years the firm of Bowman & Company have been paid the enormous sum of $2,000,000 in round figures for dredging -$2,000,000, let there he no mistake in the figures, because they are according to the returns brought down in this House ; and that the firm known as the Great Lakes Dredging Company, which is composed of Mr. .Tames Bowman, member of provincial parliament for North Bruce in the Ontario Legislature, A. F. Bowman, his brother, and Mr. James Whelan, of Port Arthur, son-inlaw of the hon. member for Rainy River (Mr. Conmee), have been paid $1,350,000 within a few years ; that a concern known as the Owen Sound Dredging Company, which is composed of the Hon. A. G. Mac-kay, leader of the Liberal opposition in the Ontario legislature, who is half owner of the whole concern, the other half being owned by a Mrs. E. H. Horsey, have been paid upwards of $350,000 to $400,000. Now I will confine my remarks to these three firms, because these three particular firms have had their dealings exposed before the Public Accounts Committee of this Dominion-and there will be more of that in the future. Now what is the position of affairs with regard to these dredging companies ? We are blandly told to-day by the Minister of Public Works that despite the fact that there are appropriations which will run, I assume, over half a million dollars, that the Minister of Public Works has gone to his colleagues and his colleagues have said : There is no necessity for calling for tenders for this large amount of work, whatever it may amount to ; and I think the figures will show that at the points indicated by the hon. gentleman, the dredging will cost half a million dollars. The hon. gentleman told the House yesterday that with the consent and concurrence of his colleagues he had obtained an order in council by which no tenders are to be called for this year for the expenditure of that vast sum of money, that very considerable sum of money, at all events. Now we have to-day lying in this House, in the custody of the proper officer in that behalf, the chairman of the Public Accounts Committee, the original tenders which the hon. gentleman is going to accept, the figures that have not been discussed yet before the Public Accounts Committee, but will be discussed in the next few months. And what do those figures show ? I would ask, and I think it is with-Mr. BENNETT.
in the rights of this House, that these contracts should now be laid on the table, because they particularly refer to this work where the large amount of from $100,000 to $150,000 will be spent the coming season. Those are tenders for the work to be done at Midland and at Tiffin, and the production of those documents will show this fact, , that there are, or supposed to be, two rival companies competing for the work. Two tenders have been put in, one by what is known as the Midland Dredging Company, of which Mr. If. W. Grant is the secretary treasurer, and the other by what is known as tne Penetanguishene Company, of which Dr. Spohn is the secretary treasurer. Now, both these tenders are in the handwriting of F. W. Grant; and I challenge the Minister of Public Works now to send to the office of the clerk of the Public Accounts Committee and produce those tenders and lay them on the table, because they will prove to the hilt, what X have stated. Is not this an odd state of affairs ? The criminal law of this country says that yon can send to the penitentiary a man who interferes and causes the withdrawal of a tender ; yet though I brought this matter specially to the notice of the Prime Minister ten days ago in the House, and made the same allegation, I have never yet heard the matter mooted by the department. On the contrary, I have heard the Minister of Public Works stand up here yesterday and say that an order in council has been passed (o give these very people who have been tendering and have defrauded the people of Canada, a contract without a tender being called for. Now I think it is high time that these tenders should be brought down, and I will ask the Premier if he will have a messenger sent for those tenders so that they may be laid on the table and may be inspected by members. I do not think I am asking any thing beyond what is in the interest of the government of this country, when exposure has been made along those lines. Now, what did these tenders show ? These tenders showed that the Midland Company, called the Great Lakes Construction Company-that is the corporate name-tendered on the Midland work at 53 cents a yard and that the Penetanguishene Company tendered on the Midland work at 57 cents a yard, that on another work at Waubaushene, the Midland Company tendered at 18 cents a yard and the Spohn Company, or the Penetanguishene Company, tendered at 16 cents a yard.
What kind of material?

All kinds of material except rock which is especially provided for. tinder these figures the Penetanguishene Company would have received the Waubaushene work and the Midland company would have received the Midland work. But, these gentlemen evidently were not

For the work at Midland. The hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) was acting at that time as Minister of Public Works. I would ask the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugs-ley) to direct that these tenders be brought down from the committee room. It only requires a direction on the part of any Minister to have them brought here so that lion, gentlemen may pass them from hand to hand to see them in all their nakedness and their fraud because there is fraud on the face of them.
Oh, oh.
Yes, there is fraud on the face of them.
On whose face ?

If I said on the face of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Johnston) I think every one would assent to it. I say it is a serious matter and, what is more, these tenders have been seen by many hon. gentlemen on this side of the House.
Mr. PUGSLEY'. There has never been any attempt to keep them secret at all They were produced openly before the Committee on Public Accounts.

However, they are there now and if they were to be removed a number of gentlemen have seen them as a matter of proof and if it were not so it would be a most unfortunate thing perhaps for all parties concerned. But, they are there now and I challenge any minister to lay these papers on the table because they will prove that the tenders of the two companies are written in one and the same handwriting, that of F. W. Grant.
Who is Mr. Grant ?

Brother of the hon. member for North Ontario. What next happened ? There were tenders called for at a number of different points and this so-called Dominion Dredging Company of which Mr. Gordon Stewart is the secretary treasurer, put in a tender for a number of works. Some hon. gentleman asks : Who is Mr. Stewart 1 He is the son of the hon. the senior member for Ottawa. The Stewart Company tendered for a large number of works and the Stewart Company, not having the plant to nerform the work did. as I am informed and believe, go to other dredging concerns and offer to sublet. But, there was so much clamour made over the matter that the Minister of Justice, then acting as Minister of Public Works, did what ?-did not, as I am informed, call for public tenders and ask publicly for competition, but permitted these tenderers to put in new tenders among themselves. If there was no fraud in the case of these two companies that I have mentioned there is proof positive and conclusive that the so-called Grant Company tendered on the Midland work, that their tender was 53 cents per yard for all material outside of rock and that when the second arrangement was made, they only got 26 cents a yard for that work.
Do you blame the department for that ? Do you find fault with the minister for letting it at 26 cents ?

No, but what I do find fault with the minister for is dealing with people who are attempting to put up a fraud on the government. That is the reason that my complaint is made now. I say that the minister should go into the open market and ask for tenders. When the Spohn Company and the Grant Company thought there were no other parties who would intervene their tenders were respectively : Grant, 53 cents, and the Penetan-guishene Company, 57 cents, but when the Stewart Company could not undertake the work by reason of the insufficiency of their plant, the acting minister made a new arrangement, not by calling for public tenders. I regret that the Minister of Justice cannot hear what I am saying in this respect so that he might be in a position to acquiesce in my statement or deny it. When the matter came up again the Grant Company got the contract at 26 cents a yard. There was some work to be done at a point called Tiffin below Midland and that work, without any competition at all, as I am informed, was handed over to the McKay Company at 27 cents a yard. Now, I am going to ask the hon. gentleman what can be thought of this transaction in the face of the statement that one of these supposedly rival companies, through its secretary, writes out the tenders of both companies ?
AVould the hon. gentleman excuse me for a moment ? Did I understand him to say that there were no tenders called for the work at Tiffin and that the work was let without any call for public tenders ?
That is what I am informed.
By whom ?

Well, I have private information on that score. In support of that I will prove something by the records which lie up in the office of the Public Ac-

counts Committee and which the minister, so far, has not brought down. I am surprised that the right hon. First Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) does not ask that these records should be brought down here in the face of an accusation of this kind. It can be rebutted if it is not true.

ill-. PUGSLEY. Any member of this House would have just as much authority to order them from the custody of the Public Accounts Committee as I would have or as the Prime Minister would have.

If the Prime Minister wishes it. I will ask if I have the concurrence of the House in sending a page to the clerk of the committee to bring them down and lay them on the table and if there will be any objection to that being done.
It is a matter for the Public Accounts Committee entirely.

What position' is this matter in? There was a tenderer bold enough to write not only the tender of his own company but the tender of a supposedly rival company. There is no question about it. The handwriting is as a like as two peas, and to showr there was connivance and fraud between these two tenderers w7hen the so-

called Grant Company tendered In supposed competition their figure on the work is 53 cents a yard, but when the government found that Stewart could not take the work at 30 cents they were afraid to give the contract to the Grant Company at 53 cents, and for some reason or other the work is allotted to them at 20 cents a yard. The Minister of Public Works asked me where I got my information and I will tell him where I got part of my information. Attached to these tenders and in the committee room at this moment is to be found a schedule showing the names of the different contractors with the figures at which they had tendered opposite their names and a circle is placed around the name of the lowest tenderer. Underwritten on that schedule is, the McKay Company for the work at Tiffin, and no tenders are asked for the work at Tiffin at ail, and the minister cannot find in all that file a single tender for the work at Tiffin, and there under the signature of Mr. Aylesworth, the acting minister, not in his handwriting but in the writing of some person, on that file appears ' Tiffin, OwTen Sound Dredging Company, at 27 cents a yard.' Will the Minister of Public Works say there were tenders called ?

I would say to the hon. gentleman that the report of the chief engineer in my department is, that in respect to ail the works with regard to which he has recommended the fixing of the time during the present season for the completion of the work, in every one of these he reports to me that public tenders were called by public advertisement. And I may say further that I would not think of extending the time except in cases where tenders have been publicly called for.

Let the general public understand what this dredging operation is. Everything hinges on the one question whether or not these scows are filled, and I say that the country is paying for scows which are presumably filled and which are never filled. I say that the country is paying inspectors to inspect the work who are never there. The evidence of Mr. Gobeil which I have quoted proves conclusively that the inspector on the Spohn dredge was not there at all. Has that man been prosecuted for the fraud he practised on the government ? Not at all. Has the other inspector who connived at the theft been prosecuted ? Not at all. What do these dredging operations [DOT]mean to the people of this country ? Let me take the case of the Grant Company. You can see from the papers before the Public Accounts Committee that in one mouth alone that dredge was paid over $11,000, and when it is considered that these dredges work over eight months in the year that means that the dredges would aggregate about $90,000 in the season. And it was sworn in the committee the other day by the owner and the representative of the McKay dredge that

tlie Inspector was not there to inspect the work.
I thought you were speaking of the Grant Company. You go from one to the other. Which are you speaking of: the Grant Company or the McKay Company ?
' I should have said that the McKay Company had the Grant dredge under lease last year.

It is certainly very inconvenient, and if I know anything about the rules of parliament it is very objectionable for a member from his place in the House to refer to what is occurring before a committee of the House.
There is no inquiry at all about it.

The House cannot know what is taking place before a committee until that committee reports to the House. This matter is still under investigation before the Public Accounts Committee, and I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) wTill see that it would be very much better that these matters should be threshed out in the Public Accounts Committee, and then when the committee reports to the House it will be properly before the House for discussion. I take that point, Mr. Speaker.
You cannot get a report from this committee.

The Minister of Public Works is mistaken. The inquiry in the Public Accounts Committee is about dredging at Fesserton in connection with the Spohn Company, and there is no question at all about the McKay Company, at Midland. The papers have been moved for and brought down and in due course it will be investigated, but so far I am simply speaking from documents that have been laid on the table.
Is it not a fact that Mr. Wilkinson was here but a very little while ago in connection with the McKay Company dredging and that the matter was gone into by the Public Accounts Committee ?
Since my bon. friend does not recollect the circumstances I do not want to detail them all.
I ask your ruling, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the matter is before the committee under investigation and has not been reported upon to the House, the rule is explicit and plain that no reference to it can be made in the House until the report is received by the House.
But there is a denial that the matter is before the committee.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is another point.
It is the question of the Fesserton, dredging which is before the committee.
What are the papers before the committee for?
To be dealt with in due course of time.
Then it is before the committee.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The question is: Has this matter been before the Public Accounts Committee under investigation and has a report been made to the House ? If it has been before the committee for investigation and if no report has yet been made the rule is plain that no reference can be made to it in the House until there is a report from the committee.

My information is that the matter is before the committee. All these documents are still before the committee, the tenders, the contracts and all the papers, and no report has yet been made to the House.

I have in my desk a copy of the evidence as printed so far, and that document states that the inquiry before the committee is in reference to the dredging at Matchedash bay. There is no reference in the printed evidence to the dredging at Midland and there is no inquiry into it.

Will the hon. gentleman deny that at the request of the Public Accounts Committee these papers have been produced from my department and submitted to the committee and are now in the custody of the committee and have been there for weeks, and that the matter has not yet been disposed of ?
It is quite right to say that the papers have been brought to the committee and they will be dealt with in due course, but there has as yet been no inquiry at all into the Midland business.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Of course, that is a point to be cleared up. I have not been in the committee and I have not had an opportunity of ascertaining what the committee has been doing. The whole question is: Has this matter been before the committee under investigation, and if so, and if it has not been reported upon of course it is improper to discuss it in the House. I would like to be clear on that point before making a definite ruling.

Your ruling is quite clear, Sir, that if there is an inquiry in the committee, until the report is made a discussion cannot take place in this House. But, I presume, that the information which an hon. gentleman gets otherwise than from what has taken place in the committee he can use. What I understand the hon. mem-br to state is that he has obtained this information from the examination of docu-

merits which lie in the Public Accounts Committee, but that no investigation has been had as to the matter to which he refers. Surely .Mr. Speaker, in that case any hon. member can use the recoi'ds of parliament or the records of the department for the purpose of obtaining information and can bring that information before this House. You have said, Mr. Speaker, that there has been some discussion as to what the facts are on which this matter is based, but in that regard we have the statement of the hon. member, who is the only person who actually knows the facts in that regard, and surely we may take his statement that he is not stating what has been elicited by any examination before the Public Accounts Committee, but what he has obtained from records which are accessible not only to the members of the Public Accounts Committee, but to every hon. member of this House who likes to go and examine them. If the investigation had commenced, then I think it would be clear that the hon. member could not discuss it; but no investigation, as the hon. member has said, has taken place, and, therefore, he having ascertained the facts which he proposes to deal with by an investigation of his own and from public documents which are of record, I submit that he has a right to discuss them.

In confirmation, let me give what is stated in the printed proof which I hold in my hand. After stating that the committee met on February 28, it says ' further consideration of the payment to the Penetanguishene Dredging Company. That is a matter that is not under discussion.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: There seems to be a difference of opinion as to what has taken place before the committee. I think I must assume that the documents which are before the Public Accounts Committee have been taken there for some purpose. They are now in the possession of the committee, and the proper and usual course if an investigation as to same is pending would be to have them transferred here for the purposes of discussion otherwise as they have not been reported to the House. I shall have to rule that the discussion is out of order.

I moved for some papers early in the session. The papers were brought down ; I got the information I required from those papers and sent them back to the Auditor General's Department. Do you rule that I cannot make use of the information I got from those papers because they are before the Public Accounts Committee?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Not at all. In that case the documents were sent back to the department, and no further action would be taken on those documents until thev were Mr. LENNOX.
returned to the Public Accounts Committee.
I assume that if the documents are in the possession of the Public Accounts Committee they are there for some purpose of the committee. Where an investigation allowed them is pending until the committee disposes of them by returning them to the place from which they came or by reporting them to the House, I do not see how I can rule otherwise than I have ruled, that the discussion upon them is out of order.

Mr. Speaker, I would ask whether your ruling means that no member can discuss any payment made bv the Auditor General because the papers regarding it are before the Public Accounts Committee, because in that case all inquiry on any subject could be blocked by members on the government side of the House having the papers brought before that committee.

Weil, Mr. Speaker, I will attempt to avoid any matter of a controversial nature by simply referring to what is to be seen in the papers and not at all to the question of what the evidence lias been. The very certificates that give this company this colossal sum in one month, or thousands and thousands of dollars in a season

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think I should do the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Lake) the courtesy of answering his question. I would not at all press the ruling so far as the hon. member suggests. This matter comes before the House in this shape. An hon. member rises to discuss it and states that the documents show that so-and-so has occurred. After some discussion another hon. member rises and takes the point that this matter is still before the Committee on Public Accounts under investigation and that the documents are still before that commute. On that state of facts I am bound to assume, and I do assume, that the committee is still seized of the documents, and until the committee reports either in the shape of forwarding the documents or reporting to the House with reference to the investigation that has been made, discussion is out of order. That is as far as I go as to the proceedings before the committee.

The reference to the Public Accounts Committee is the reference of all the public accounts of the year and of the Auditor General's Report. Do you rule, Mr. Speaker, that we cannot discuss any account that is in the public accounts or in the Auditor General's Report because they have been referred to the Public Accounts Committee? Our argument is that an order from the Public Accounts Committee to produce the documents before that committee or a reference to the House does not in the slightest degree preclude any hon. member of this House from discussing any I paper on any item that has been discussed

before the committee. The Public Accounts Committee is not a special committee to which this House has referred any particular item on which to report. It is one of the ordinary committees of the House, and the fact that it takes cognizance of a matter does not remove it from the jurisdiction of the House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am in this position, that on the one side reference is made to documents which are before the Public Accounts Committee, and on the other side the point is taken that the matter is still pending before the committee. It is quite impossible for the Speaker to decide as between two adverse views based upon two different statements of the facts, and under these circumstances the only position and the proper position for the Speaker to take, it seems to me, is the well known one, both in England and here, that ' until a committee report it is irregular to refer to its proceedings in debate in the House.' In view of the assertion that these documents are still before the Public Accounts Committee and under investigation, I cannot decide otherwise than I am doing.

Do you hold, Mr. Speaker, that the Public Accounts Committee is a special committee, or a committee of the House that comes under the rule to which a matter has been referred for the purpose of reporting?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The statement is made that the Public Accounts Committee is seized of the documents for investigation, and that the investigation is pending. Then the term ' proceeding ' which is laid down in the practice applies, and until a report upon the matter has been made to the House or the documents have been ordered to be laid before the House, it will be impossible to have a discussion upon them here.
I think on the question of order

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am quite prepared now to allow discussion on that question and after that discussion I shall rule one way or the other ; but I cannot make a ruling and have discussion later on about it. The point of order is now open for discussion and after it has been discussed I shall rule finally on the question.

Would not a consideration of the actual practice in the Public Accounts Committee enable us to determine whether or not certain documents are under consideration in that committee ? At the beginning of the session and throughout the session the members of the opposition find in the Auditor General'^ Report items such as in their opinion call for inquiry. Very seldom does the opposition member when moving for papers, know that the papers will produce tangible result; but from information that he may
have received from private sources he moves for papers that he may investigate them and, as a matter of fact, no one but himself investigates them. In fact the papers are not laid before the committee ; they are brought over from the department to the clerk of the committee and are by him put in the proper pigeon holes and are never seen, in all probability, except by the member who moved for them. When papers are brought down there are probably a hundred different matters on which the papers are before the committee.
Are not the papers brought before the committee by order of the committee ?

The papers are brought from the department by the order of the committee, there is no question of that ; but as a matter of fact they are not laid before the committee until some one moves to examine witnesses and when he examines the witnesses the papers are brought before the committee. Let me show to my hon. friend the absurdity of his position. Of the papers brought before the committee probably not one-twentieth are investigated by the hearing of evidence. If the rule is to be that the moment papers are brought down before the Public Accounts Committee, then the subjects with which they are concerned are excluded from discussion in this House until the committee reports, there will be on an average eighty cases each session that never come before the committee, and the committee cannot make a report because there is no subject before them.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think it is quite unnecessary to discuss a ruling which has not been made or suggested, that is that every paper before the committee is to be ruled out of discussion here.
The Minister of Public Works takes that view.
I beg your pardon, I said nothing of the kind.

Then what does it come to ? It has been contended that the moment papers are brought down to the Public Accounts Committee the House is debarred from discussion upon them until the committee reports. I point out that there cannot be a report until something further has been done in the committee than the mere examination of papers by a member. The hon. member for Simcoe says that this matter was never before the committee. His word must be sufficient for the committee in that respect.
The printed records show that.

Apart from the proof lie brings, the hon. member's wmrd is sufficient for this House, but when he brings the

record and shows that it is another dredging matter altogether, it practically comes to (his that the Minister of Public Works wishes to prevent discussion on dredging contract ' A ' because dredging contract ' B ' is being investigated before the committee.

In so far as the dredging goes, the question of dredging stands by itself. Ever since the Public Accounts Committee commenced the hon. member for Simcoe has been examining witnesses in regard to dredging. His first motion was in regard to one certain payment and several times, whilst the committee lias been in session, he has branched oft from that payment altogether and gone on to other matters not pertinent to it at all. His attention was called to it

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: That will be entering upon a discussion of what occurred before the committee, which I could not permit.

This has gone on and I wish to say further that I asked the hon. gentleman only on Friday last, to close the inquiry and bring a report to the House regarding dredging. He refused saying that he had other witnesses to examine.
Certainly, and I am going to examine witnesses about this matter. Do not go away with the idea that this will not be' further investigated before the committee.

If the *ruling just given is correct it is a rule that has been more honoured in the breach than in the observance, because every session there are questions before the Public Accounts Committee, some of which will be investigated and some will not; during the time these papers are before the Public Accounts Committee, we go into a Committee of Supply here and we proceed to vote money for similar items, we take up the Auditor General's Report with these items that are before the Public Accounts Committee for consideration and we ask all kinds of questions about them. I think, if my memory is correct, we have sometimes brought down the original papers from that committee for the convenience of the House when we were inquiring into the expenditure of public money in connection with some of these items. At the present time there are several items regarding timber limits that are before the committee. I moved for some papers there as well in reference to some timber limits. I looked into those papers, I got all the information I required, and therefore it was unnecessary either to call witnesses or to bring the departmental officers before the committee. I obtained the information and I left the papers there. Would it be said that I had no right to use the information or to discuss those items in this House because the papers were before the Public Accounts Commit-Mr. NOETHRUP.
tee, when the Public Accounts Committee will not deal with them during the whole session, will make no report whatever ? If I understand, it is only questions with which the Puplic Accounts Committee deal and upon which they report, according to the terms of the order of reference, ' their findings, suggestions or observations,' that we may not discuss. Take the case with which the hon. member has dealt. It is true that one item of dredging that lias been before the Public Accounts Committee has been inquired into.
What is that ?
The Fesserton case.
That cannot be so because the hon. member said that the Pene-tanguishene matter is before the committee.

It is the Fesserton case of the Penetanguishene Dredging Company.
Mr. PUGSLEY'. And Owen Sound ?
Nothing about Owen Sound.

I think the minister confuses the two names, the dredging company in Penetanguishene and the dredging company at Fesserton. The hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) is discussing an item that the Public Accounts Committee have not considered at all and that item may not be considered by the Public Accounts Committee. Would it be held that because these papers are before the committee for examination by any private member of this House, but have never been brought up and examined and investigated by calling ns witnesses under oath, we had no right to speak of them in this House ? We have always dealt with these questions when in Committee of Supply, we would discuss items belonging to the same locality or to the same public work, for which we were voting money. We discussed them ad libitum, and there is no objection notwithstanding that they are before the Public Accounts Committee. I hold, if I understand the rule, that we have a perfect right to discuss any matter unless it is a question being examined by the Public Accounts Committee as a Public Accounts Committee and not by a private member, a matter on which evidence is being taken either from the departmental officers or some one interested in the contract or some one who can give additional information that the committee desires to have before making its report, with its observations, conclusions or suggestions to this House. It is only with regard to these things, I think, that we are debarred from speaking in this House, and not the others.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The ruling which the Chair makes in the matter is this : If the

matter is really before the Public Accounts Committee, after the papers have been sent from one of the departments, and has not been dealt with by the committee, reference can be made to it in this House. The question comes down to one of fact-whether there are proceedings in connection with this matter pending befoye the committee or not. The statement is made on one side that there are such proceedings; the statement is made on the other side that there are no such proceedings. The hon. member (Mr. Bennett) who initiated the discussion was certainly quoting from proceedings before the Public Accounts Committee which had not been reported to the House, and so was clearly out of order. Of course, I did not wish to interfere unnecessarily. but when the jioint was taken, it was clear to my mind that the hon. gentleman was quoting proceedings before the Public Accounts Committee not yet reported to the House. So, my ruling would be, if there are proceedings pending before the Public Accounts Committee on this matter, until the matter is reported to the House, it would be out of order to discuss those here. If the hon. member will conduct his discussion on the line of not referring to or quoting proceedings that are still before the committee, he will have a perfect right to proceed.

I take it, Mr. Speaker, that your ruling is that I must not make a reference to any evidence that has been given before the committee.
iMr. SPEAKER. Or to any documents which are the subject of a pending reference.
I do not wish to transgress your ruling. Then, I understand that, having moved for certain documents

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the documents are there and are not being investigated, you have a perfect right to discuss them.

Very well. Now, early in the session I moved that certain documents should be laid before the Public Accounts Committee referring to the dredging at Midland. I have seen those documents, together with the tenders for the work, and I will quote from these. I repeat that the tenders for the work at Midland are of the Penetanguishene Company and the Grant Coni)>any and both are written in the handwriting of Mr. F. W. Grant, the brother of the hon. member for North Ontario-there is not the slightest doubt about that.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member says he is referring to documents before the committee. The whole point is, have these documents been before the committee for investigation.
Yes, certainly.
Yes.
No evidence was taken.
I am astounded that

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) has announced within the last twenty minutes that lie intends to do so and so before the committee proceeds ' further ' with the investigation : and he says that he intends to call ' other ' witnesses.

I intend to bring these matters up before the committee at some future day. Surely no hon. gentleman on the other side who is a member of the committee will make the statement that the authenticity of these two tenders has been brought up or evidence adduced. Mr. Grant has not been a witness before the committee. Hon. gentlemen opposite are mistaken. Now, in the first instance, the Grant tender for the work at Midland was for 53 cents a yard. I believe I am right in the assertion that tenders were not publicly advertised for, but the work was subsequently given to that company at 26 cents a yard. That is surely an astounding thing-that a company, within a short space of time, probably a few weeks, would offer to do work at 26 cents which so short a time before they had asked 53 cents for. But that is on the record. I said there were no tenders for the work at Tiffin. There can be no question that, in the original asking for tenders, none were asked for the work at that point, -or, if they were, they are not filed on record in the department.
Of course, I will look into it. Tiffin is part of Midland, is it not?
It adjoins.
Are not they the same ?

Yes.
Sir. PUGSLEY'. It may be there were no separate tenders for Tiffin as distinguished from Midland.

The hon. minister (Mr. Pugsley) cannot understand this matter thoroughly because he was not in (.'barge of the department at the time, and, as he has not recently looked at the schedule, it will not be fresh in his memory. There is a schedule prepared by the department showing where all these different works have been performed, with figures placed opposite the name of the respective tenderers, and by the acting Minister of Public Works-the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth)-a circle around the name of the contractor who has secured the job. There is also a lead pencil memo, which shows that the Tiffin work goes to the Owen Sound Dredging Company at 27 cents a yard.
Now, let us take these records and see what they mean to the country. In one mouth tills company draws $11,089. It must be remembered that this work is certified to in these returns as paid for at the rate of $2 a yard. The scows are large scows carrying perhaps not 200 yards at a load

but certainly over 100 yards. Therefore, if this material is not rock but clay, though paid for at the rate of rock, it means that they receive at least $200 for a load instead of $34, the amount they ought to receive. Another question that presents itself is whether or not the inspector inspects in this case. There are certificates lying there- more than one and more than several- on which this company has been paid large amounts which bear no signature to show that the inspector had anything to do with it. That is a serious statement, but the minister can verify it by bringing down the documents from the Public Accounts Committee.
Now, let us follow these figures a little, This company is paid $11,089 for one month. Working eight months, they would receive about $90,000 for the season. Now, these dredges are not expensive concerns to work; -probably $25 to $40 would pay for the wages of the men and the coal. That being so, you can see that there is colossal profit. It is no wonder that the stockholders in these dredging companies-there are scores of such stockholders-make their boast in the streets of Midland that they are receiving from 75 per cent to 100 per cent dividend. Why, it is the easiest thing in the world to do this when you have an inspector who cheerfully certifies that these dredges are working fifteen hours a day even on into the month of December when it is utterly impossible for them to work for that length of time, and when you have a manager of a dredge, who, with equal cheerfulness, will certify to the same thing.
Let us take another case, the case of the MacKay Company, the owners of dredge No. 9. I asked a question as to the amount per day this dredge was making and I find that it is earning $210 a day, if she is working twelve hours a day. Now, contrast that with the figure at which this same dredge was previously hired by the department, which was $S0 per day. Is that not enough to put the government and the Minister of Public Works on his guard with the people he is dealing with? Look at the Auditor General's Report of a few years ago, and you will find this dredge of MacKay, Horsey & Company, working at $8 an hour, and there are figures that prove conclusively that she is earning $200 a day-not earning it but she is paid that much.
Does the hon. gentleman know whether the company that got paid for the dredging, paid for the coal and all that?
In both cases the company paid for operating.
Paid the coal bills themselves ?

No question about that. There are facilities afforded for fraud in Mr. BENNETT
these matters, owing to the fact pointed out by the commissioners, the appointment of these local inspectors. Take the case dealt with a year or two ago in the committee. A man named Eastwood was appointed, and he cherfully tells the committee that he drew $3 a day and never went, near the work ; as Mr. Gobeil says, he retained $1.75 a day out of the season's wages, and gave the other man $1.25. But the dishonesty of that man was nothing compared to the dishonesty of other government inspectors, because the other government inspectors had been in the employ of the country for some years. Now the figures prove what I have stated, that these dredges which cost about $100,000, or are given out to cost that much, are paid $80,000 to $100,000 in a season, less the wages, which are not a large item. Is it not a suspicious circumstance that the secretary treasurer of one company is actually writing out tenders for both companies ? And yet the minister says that these are the people to deal with. How ? By not allowing them to be subjected to competition. Why ? Because he thinks the prices are fair and reasonable. The minister in that respect is going directly contrary to law. What right has the government to spend an amount running in all probability -I cannot tell the amount, because the minister promised to bring down that schedule to show where the work is to be done. May I ask the minister now : Is the large work at Port Arthur to be done under a similar arrangement, and that at Fort William ?
No, that does not come under this, that is a different contract.
Is that a contract that lias been let by tender this year ?

No. The hon. gentleman must be aware that the contract for the work at Port Arthur, upon the Mission and Kamanistiqua rivers, was let some time ago, and this work, extending over several years, was provided for in the original contract.
Then may I ask the minister this question : Will the Collingwood work come under this order in council ?
I am not sure whether the Collingwood work is included in this order.
And Little Current ?
No, Little Current is not in this order.
' Well, Mr. Speaker, I think I have shown the government that this is a case where they should be on suspicion.
I may say that we are always on suspicion, and always watchful.

Well, I compliment the Minister of Public Works on this fact, that he has done for the first time during the past ten or twelve years, what must be done for the future, and what the public will insist upon, namely, that every one of these inspectors shall make himself amenable to the criminal law by making sworn declarations as to the returns. These matters attract public attention, as they must necessarily do. Take the case of MacKay & Company. It is only a few years ago since Dr. Walsh and Mr. MacKay started in this dredging business, with an old dredge named No. 9 that they were anxious to rent to the government at $8 an hour. To-day they are owners of two dredges that are openly discussed by people who know their cost, and are stated by these gentlemen themselves, to have cost with their scows, over 8100,000 each. Talk about where the money comes from !
Dredges cost $100,000 to $200,000. Dredging plants are very expensive.
I have been informed by the manager of this concern that these dredges cost over $100,000 a piece, with the scows. These gentlemen had no extrinsic business.
You can hardly be sure of that. I know many a dredge that is not paid for yet.

These gentlemen had no extrinsic business out of which they could make money to become the owners of these dredges. I say now that as these facts are disclosed in the Public Accounts Committee by documents that are lying there, the fraud perpetrated by the Grant and Spohn companies, or by Spohn's company, in the face of the fact that their original tender was for 53 cents a yard, and that afterwards they accepted the work at 26 cents a yard, in the face of the fact that the certificates of the inspector up there show that he has not in certain cases certified to them
In how many cases ?

I did not charge my memory with them, but I think, in looking them over, I say more than three. In face of the evidence, which the hon. gentleman can read when it is printed, given by the man representing these dredges, as to whether or not the inspector was there when the work was done, and having regard to the enormous amount of money that is being expended
If it would be right to refer to the evidence, I might ask the hon. gentleman if the inspector was not dismissed the moment it came to the knowledge of the department ?

The hon. gentleman is confounding this case with another. This is a case where a huge expenditure is to be made. The minister cannot tell me what works will come under the purview of this order in council, but the Victoria harbour work, the Tiffin work, the Midland work, and perhaps the Collingwood work will come within it, and I assume the expenditure will be upwards of half a million dollars. The government knows all this, the government knows what this dredging is costing. I say the public will not be satisfied, and is not satisfied. Irrespective of politics, the public do not believe, from Owen Sound to Collingwood and Midland, that the government has ever got value for the money that is being disbursed. I submit that instead of allowing this order in council to be acted on, tenders should be called forthwith for this work. Let it be put up to public competition, and let there be no more of these suspicious circumtauces allowed to exist.

I am not at all sorry that the hon. gentleman has brought this question before the House. I recognize that the matter of dredging, and the question of having the work honestly, efficiently and satisfactorily done, is one of great importance. It is becoming yearly of more importance, because there is a rapidly increasing demand in all sections of the country, both upon the Atlantic and the Pacific, upon the rivers and the great lakes, for dredging to be performed for the purpose of giving accommodation to steamships which are every year becoming larger, therefore, the cost of dredging must increase year after year. I am sorry to have to say that the Dominion is not properly equipped, in my judgment, with dredging plant. We have no adequate dredging plant upon the great lakes. We have, in the maritime provinces, for use there and in the Baie des Chaleurs, only a comparatively few dredges-I think some nine or ten altogether. The dredging plant owned by the government is not at all in my judgment, what it ought to be for a maritime country such as Canada is. There is an enormous demand for dredging on the Pacific coast, on the Atlantic coast, on the St. Lawrence, and other rivers, the Baie des Chaleurs and the great lakes. Therefore, the department has felt obliged to ask for tenders for a great deal of the dredging work in the past and has necessarily done that work by contract.
Now, I quite agree that one of the most important things to be attended to is tlie matter of inspection. Of course, there are some cases where the engineers of the department can measure up the work in situ and determine with a considerable degree of accuracy the quality of material to be dredged, but in. a great many cases-I think 11 am safe in saying in the majority of cases

-this work cannot be accurately performed without very great expense, without having a large staff of engineers going to an expense which probably the department would not be justified in incurring. Therefore, it has been found in most cases that the department Were only able to let contracts and to pay for the dredging work on the basis of scow measurement. In order that the government may be properly protected it is necesary to have inspectors examine each scow load as it is taken away from the dredge with the view of making a proper report to the department. Therefore, a great deal depends upon the honesty of the inspectors and upon the faithfulness with which they do the work. I recognize that. The Minister of Public Works, the chief engineer of the department and even the resident engineer, who has a considerable territory to look after, cannot guard the public with respect to the quanity of material which is taken out of the scows and therefore, as I have already said, we must depend to a very large degree upon the honesty and upon the faithfulness of the inspectors who are appointed for that purpose.
But the department has imposed the further check that the owner or manager of the dredge also certifies as to the number of yards in these scows.

Yes. that is true. There have been some cases that have come to the notice of the department in which inspectors have not done their duty. There has been one case which probably was the case that the hon. gentleman bad in mind where a man who was entrusted with the duty of inspecting scow loads had farmed the work out to another party. He was getting. I think, $3 a day and he employed another person at $1.50 a day to do his work. That was a most improper thing to do. The department did not engage or rely upon the man whom he appointed, but the department relied upon himself and the department had a right to expect him to perform his duty.
But both of those men were appointees of the government.

That may be, but still the man who was appointed as inspector was the man to whom the department had a right to look, and he was the man that the department appointed to perform this duty. When the matter came to the notice of the department that officer was dismissed. There was another case that occurred upon the great lakes.

Did you make him pay back the money ?
Mr. PUGSLEY'. There was no evidence that there was any intention to commit a Mr. PUGSLEY.
a fraud. It was simply, on the part of this man# a misconception as to his duty.
That man actually got $30 for the use of the boat under his wifes maiden name, which boat was never used.
I am not aware of that case.
That is the same case.
He charged and was paid overtime.

There was another case that occurred in connection with dredging at one of the ports of the great lakes, where a man who was appointed inspector was employing another party who was ins)) ector upon a dredge which was working in the same locality to do bis work. That was an improper thing to do, and when this matter came to the notice of the department the services of both of them were dispensed with.
I have a good deal of faith in human honesty, and I believe that the great majority of the people who are appointed to-attend to these public duties do endeavour to perform their duties honestly, and I have no reason to suppose but what the great majority, if not all of the inspectors who are in the employ of the department, are men who can be relied upon. The minister and his officials are not accustomed to take the recommendation of local people as the hon. gentlemen suggests, but they make inquiry in regard to a man's character, in regard to his antecedents, in regard to his efficiency as an inspector of dredging and they appoint him after all these inquiries are made, believing that he will do his duty faithfully. I thought it desirable-perhaps I am taking undue precautions-to avoid in so far as could possibly be done any opportunity for fraud occurring as far ns the inspectors are concerned. I have adopted a rule which has met with the hearty approval of the officers of the department, that the inspector must, with his returns, send in a statutory declaration to the effect not onlv that the quantity as certified by him is correct but, that he has personally seen and has had an opportunity of determining as to the measurement of every scow load of material to which lie certifies. That is, I think, a pretty good check put upon the inspectors, because, when an inspectors knows that he has to make a statutory declaration which has all the force of an oath as to his personal supervision of the work and as to his personal knowledge of every scow load. I do not think that he will neglect his duties or certify with respect to scow loads he has not seen and as to which he has no personal knowledge. I have also caused a circular to be sent out to all the inspectors in the employ of the department calling

their attention to this important duty which rests upon them, and informing them that any omission to perform their duty will be a ground for instant dismissal. No excuse will be taken for failure to perform their duty in this regard. Therefore, it seems to me that in so far as the department or the minister could reasonably do so we have taken every precaution to guard against any difficulties of this kind as far as future work is concerned. I may say to my hon. friend who is not disposed to be over-warm in his praise, either of the Department of Public Works or any other department and who, I am almost inclined to think, may fairly be subject to the criticism of being unduly harsh in his judgments and making statements very often which have no foundation in fact but which really rest very largely upon his own imagination and upon his desire to make a point against the government
Will the hon. gentleman allow me ?
If the hon. gentleman will pardon me I am going to pay him a compliment.
The hon. minister cannot mention one statement I have made for which I have not given the proof.

I am glad that my hon. friend has shown that spirit which only can animate the members of this House in that he has given me, as the present minister, credit for having framed regulations which are of a most reasonable character and which are well calculated to protect the public in so far as dredging is concerned. The hon. gentleman has attempted to convince the House that it is wrong to fix the time during the present season for the completion of the work of Tiffin, Midland and Victoria harbours, and he says-if I understand his criticism, that is the only ground upon which he bases it-that the two companies who tendered for this work put in tenders which were written by the same person and which were for a larger amount than the contract was ultimately let for. I think I am stating the matter as the hon. gentleman put it to the House. Now, I am not aware that it is a ground for charging two men with fraud that they should be aware of the tenders which each respectively put in for a public work. If as a private individual I were to invite tenders for a dwelling house and there were a dozen tenders put in, and the tenderers got together and Mr. Brown said to Mr. Jones :	You
tender at $20,000 and I will tender at $25,000 knowing that a good many other tenders would be put in. I am not quite prepared to say that these two men could be charged with fraud or conspiracy because they did that.
