The case is very different where there are two different works one of which would fall to each of the different tenderers.

Until the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) spoke in the House I never heard the point raised that tenderers could be charged with fraud simply because they had done what I have described. It would be a very different matter if there were any collusion between them and the minister or an official of the department with regard to these tenders. If the hon. gentleman had been able to show that one of these tenderers had information from the minister or the chief engineer or the deputy minister so that the lowest tenderer might have been allowed to withdraw his tender, then he would have made an exceedingly strong point against the department because that would show collusion and conspiracy. But that is not the case at all here. Tenders were put in for different works and I suppose they were hoping that among them all both companies might be awarded contracts for certain dredging, but I am not aware that that constituted any fraudulent act upon their part.
Does the minister approve of that in connection with public works 1

I am not called upon to express my approval or disapproval. As minister I would much prefer, even where a large number of tenders for different works are called for, that one tenderer should not know the figure which the other tenderer is putting in. But where tenders are called for half a dozen different buildings and the contractors arrange to put in different figures in the hope that Mr. A. may get the contract for two or three different buildings and that Mr. B. may get the contract for two or three more, I am not aware that it is a fradulent act on their part unless it can be shown that a trusted employee of the man who is giving the contracts was a party to some conspiracy or collusion with the contractors. However, nothing of that kind has been Suggested in this case. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) insinuates that there must be something wrong because the company which tendered to do a part of this work at 57 cents a yard ultimately took the contract at 27 cents. But if I were to express any opinion on that I would say that it shows that these tenderers found they could not get the work at a higher figure than the officers of the department said that work was reasonably worth, and that the Minister of Justice who was then acting Minister of Public Works insisted in the public interest that the work should be taken at the smaller figure which the chief engineer reported was reasonable. If that shows anything at all it shows that the acting minister was safeguarding the interests of the people.
Is it not fair to assume that the acting minister consulted the chief engineer on the matter ?
I should think he did.
When I tell the minister that dredging had been done in Midland previously at 15 cents and 16 cents a yard, it is no wonder he looked surprised when they asked 56 cents.

There is a very great difference in the cost of dredging. It all depends upon the material to be dredged. In the city of St. John there are places where dredging can he done at 50 cents a yard at a profit, but there are other places where the contractors claim there is no profit in it at 90 cents a yard, and one of them insisted not long ago that he should be' paid $1.25 a yard. Everything depends upon the nature of the material to be dredged.
What explanation can the minister give of their dropping from 57 cents to 27 cents ?

It may very well be that upon further enquiry they found the work could be done for less ; or, that they found they could not get contracts in other directions where they might profitably employ their dredges, or; that on account of excessive competition they were willing to take the smaller profit and come down to the figure which the acting minister insisted on ; there may be very many reasons. Or, the work may have been of a different character, as my hon. friend behind me suggests.
The minister knows that the work was identically the same work and he cannot get away from the question in that manner.

The other day the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) professed to have a knowledge of carpentry work beyond that which an ordinary man of his profession and mine enjoys, but let me tell him that it often happens that the most reputable and experienced builders differ to an extraordinary degree in the tenders which they put in for a particular work. Not long ago it came under my own observation that in respect to buildings to be erected in one of the western provinces there was over $100*000 difference between the various tenderers.
What was the size of the contract ?
And there was a difference of $100,0Ov.

Yes. That variation in tenders comes within my knowledge almost every day. It is remarkable how widely Mr. PUGSLEY.
contractors of experience and good judgment will differ as to the probable cost of a work. When the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) was criticisms' the action of the government in allowing me to exercise my judgment in fixing the time during the present season for the completion of the work, he did not call attention to the fact that this same Owen Sound Company is only getting 8 cents per cubic yard for the dredging which it has at Victoria, so that although they are getting 27 cents per cubic yard at Tiffin they are only receiving 8 cents at Victoria.
If the minister is fair he will explain to the House what the nature of the work at each place is.

That just illustrates what I said a m'ornent ago, that everything depends upon the quality of the material to be dredged. When the Owen Sound Dredging Company proposed to do the work at Tiffin at the same price as was provided by the contract, which was awarded to them after public competition, for dredging work at Midland, of which Tiffin forms a part, I said that I would not extend the time for the dredging work at Tiffin unless they would also agree to do the work at Victoria Harbour at the rate of 8 cents per cubic yard, and it was only when the company agreed to do the work at 27 cents and 8 cents per cubic yard respectively that I agreed to recommend the extension of time to my colleagues. The hon. gentleman apparently could not forbear to make reference to the fact that Mr. Stewart happens to be a son of the member for Ottawa. Hs says that his company tendered at 30 cents per cubic yard. Well, there could not surely be any objection to that, as it was the lowest tender obtained, after public tenders were called for. See, Mr. Speaker, how careful the department was in regard to that contract. When the Dominion Dredging Company declined to go on with the work, while the acting minister might have been justified in letting the contract to another party at the same price, he declined to do so, but only gave it to them on their consenting to reduce the price to 26 cents per cubic yard. So we have the work at Midland at 26 cents per cubic yard, the work at Tiffin, which is a part of Midland, at 27 cents per cubic yard, and the work at Victoria Harbour at only 8 cents per cubic yard. The hon. gentleman has a further criticism: He says that this work being an important work, I ought not to extend the time for its completion without again asking for public tenders. Now, there are reasons which I think are cogent reasons, and which might very well operate upon the mind of the minister in inducing him to extend the time for the completion of this work. I may say that these are not the only dredging contracts in respect to which a recommendation was made to council. To begin with, I had to consider the

character of the work that was going on at Midland and at Victoria harbour. The Grand Trunk Pacific are creating a new port at Tiffin, and are laying out their plans upon a most comprehensive scale, with a view to conveying across the great lakes from Fort William the vast traffic which is to be developed in the Northwest in the next few years. They are immediately planning for elevator accommodation there to the extent of 2,000,000 bushels, and their plans include accommodation for 10,000,000 bushels of grain at Tiffin. They are working with all possible rapidity. They are pushing their road through the western country at such a rate that they expect by this fall to be hauling grain from Edmonton to the great lakes, and they expect by the 1st of October to have their elevator at Tiffin completed and to have their rail connections there, so as to be in a position this fall to handle the grain traffic which they expect from the lakes; and they have strongly urged me in the public interest, in the interest of transportation, to have this work so far completed by the 1st of October of the present year that large lake vessels will be able to steam up to their elevator and unload the grain into it and so they may transport it eastward.
What is the date of the order in council?

A week or ten days ago. This company, it is reported to me, have performed their work in a most satisfactory manner. They have a thoroughly up-to-date dredging plant; they know the ground; they have been working there during the past season, and they are prepared to do this work in time for the Grand Trunk Pacific so that the dredging and the elevator will both be completed by the 1st of October. Now, Sir, I thought that it would be wise in the public interest to do everything that was reasonable to have this dredging work done by next fall, so that steamers might use the elevator of the Grand Trunk Pacific. My chief engineer reports that the price is fair and reasonable. I do not believe, if we asked for new tenders, that we would gel the work done for less than 26 cents per cubic yard in one case, and 27 cents in the other case, considering the nature of the material. So far as Victoria Harbour is concerned, the Canadian Pacific Railway are pressing the matter in the same way. They too are adopting a new policy of transportation. They have made up their minds that the wheat of the Northwest, instead of going to Buffalo and seeking an outlet by American ports on the Atlantic ocean should pass through Canadian channels, and they are spending an enormous sum of money improving their line of railway. They are building a new line to Victoria harbour, and are spending, I believe, about $60,000 a mile to obtain a grade of three-tenths of one per cent, practically a level line, over which their large locomotives will be able to haul a 215J
train of sixty cars at a time, thus greatly reducing the cost of transporting the grain. They too have urged me to push on this dredging work and have it completed if possible this season, so that they can bring the grain over the lakes to Victoria harbour, and then transport It eastward. Seeing that this company were equipped with a magnificent plant, one of the best in Canada, knowing the satisfactory work they performed during the past season, and having the certificate of my chief engineer that these prices were reasonable, and getting the work done at Victoria harbour at the ridiculously low price of 8 cents per yard-
Does the minister say that the same company is doing the work at Tiffin and Victoria harbour?
I think so-the Owen Sound Company.
That 'is not my information.
What is the hon. gentleman's information?
The information I have from Midland is that the Owen Sound Company have the Tiffin work and the Grant Company, the Victoria harbour work.
The Owen Sound Company, I am sure, have the dredging both at Tiffin and at Victoria harbour.
Has the Grand Trunk any work?
Not to my knowledge.
That is the company that is called the Canadian Construction Company.

I do not know as to that. I may be wrong, but I am quite sure that the Owen Sound Dredging Company have the contract both at Tiffin and at Victoria harbour. Being able to get the work done at Victoria harbour at the ridiculously low price of 8 cents per cubic yard and at Tiffin at what my engineer informs me is a low price considering the nature of the material, 26 cents per cubic yard, was it unreasonable that I should say to this company : If you are willing to do both of these pieces of work at the figures of last year, I shall extend the time for you for the purpose of providing the necessary accommodation for these great railway companies, so that they may be able to handle the grain traffic during the coming season ?

Section 36 of the Public Works Act says :
Whenever any works are to be executed under the direction of any department of the government, the minister having charge of such department shall invite tenders by public advertisement for the execution of such works, except in cases:

(a)	of pressing emergency in which delay would be injurious to the public interest; or
(b)	in which from the nature of the work it can be more expeditiously and economically executed by the officers and servants of the department; or
(c)	where the estimated cost of the work is less than five thousand dollars and it appears to the minister, in view of the nature of the work, that it is not advisable to invite tenders.
That is exactly what I have done. We have complied with the law in every particular.
What item of the estimates is to pay for this when it is done ?
In the main estimates of the current year there is an amount for improvements at Midland and also at Victoria harbour.
Which are not voted yet ?

Which are not voted yet. A sum was voted last year also but of course under the contract the department will not be obliged to pay if there is no appropriation or when the appropriation is exhausted and the contractor takes that risk.
At the end of the year the appropriation lapses ?
Yes, and the moment the appropriation lapses the payments to the contractor must stop.
Was there some dredging at Victoria last year ?
Yes.
At the same place ?

At the same place and the same price. Public tenders were called for both at Victoria harbour and at Midland. My hon. friend must not get into his head the idea as the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) has, even although he lives at Midland, that Tiffin is a different place from Midland. Tiffin is a part of Midland harbour. Last year public tenders were invited for dredging at Victoria and Midland and after public competition-
Is the minister sure tenders were called for in Victoria harbour 1

There is no question about it. I told the chief engineer of my department I would not extend the, time except where public tenders were called for and the contract let to the lowest tenderer. The contract is for dredging works required at Victoria and at Midland and in it it is provided that the contractor shall finish the work at the close of the season of 1907 or at such further date as the minister may fix and determine. The contract therefore gives to the minister the power to fix a time later than the close of last season for Mr. SPROULE.
the completion of this work. Therefore I am not letting a contract without tender,
I am simply exercising the power with the approval of the Governor General in Council, given me by the contract, of fixing the close of the present season as the time when the work should be completed. As the Grand Trunk Railway and Canadian Pacific Railway required the work it could not be wholly completed last season. The hon. gentleman speaks of the money these dredging companies have made. He speaks of one dredge earning $200 a day. Let me tell him that not many years ago the.city of St. John had occasion to hire a dredge. The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Daniel), who I think was then mayor of the city, will remember that they hired a dredge from Portland, Maine, and paid a rental of either $350 or $400 per day for it.
I made the statement that this same dredge that earns $210 a day had been hired by the department for $8 an hour.

That might very well be, but does not the hon. gentleman know that in that case the government would have to pay for her whether she broke down or not ? If she broke down during dredging we would have to pay the $8 an hour.
Nonsense.
Clearly we would, because she was there at the disposal of the government.
They were only paid when they worked.

Some dredging companies make money and others do not. Not many years ago, a prominent contractor had some dredging work in St. John. I suppose he thought he was getting a fair price but he did not continue in the business, he sold out when he got through with the work, and went out of the dredging business. He is a man of large experience and I presume that if there was a certainty of earning great money in that business he would have continued in it. Dredging, as I understand, is a risky business. To begin with the plant is very expensive ; it soon wears out, after a very few years a dredging plant becomes old and worn out so that if the man continues in his business he has to renew his machinery. That matter would have to be taken into consideration by the contractor. Dredging machinery is very apt to break down. Not long ago in connection with one of the dredges working upon the Atlantic coast one of the spuds broke and they had to send to British Columbia to get a large spud to take its place. Very often dredges will be under repairs perhaps for weeks at a time. There are all these risks to be taken. I recognize that if a man is lucky to have skilled foremen in charge of his plant he

may make money ; if on tlie other hand he has not a proper man handling this expensive machinery he may very soon lose a vast deal of money and therefore I would advise my hon. friend not to take too much stock in those rumors which he hears from time to time of the enormous dividends which these dredging companies are making, because there are losses which have to be sustained also.
We see the results. When gentlemen build $20,000 houses who formerly lived in tenements, it is pretty plain what is going on.

I wish simply to refer to one matter to prevent any misapprehension on the part of the hon. gentleman as to the position in which I, as minister, stand witli reference to extending the time for the completion of this contract. I said that the matter was under consideration and also that an order in council had been passed authorizing me to extend the time That order of course necessarily would be passed upon my recommendation and ordinarily I would be supposed to follow it up and fix the time for the completion of the work.
I may say, however, that for some little time past I have been urged by quite large transportation interests and also by the Boards of Trade of Winnipeg and Port Arthur to consider the question of dredging the harbours upon the Great lakes to a greater depth than 22 feet. These contracts provide for 22 feet but my attention had been called to the fact that the new lock which is to be built by the American government at the Sault is to have a depth of water over the mitre sill of 24 feet and it has been urged upon me to dredge the harbours both on the western and eastern shores of the great lakes to 25 feet. During the last few days, since this order in council was passed, this view has been very strongly urged upon my consideration.
X am now making inquiries in the matter, consulting with the chief engineer. I am not sure whether or not I will recommend to my colleagues that authority be given me to make a change in the contract so as to go to a greater depth. Hon. gentlemen can see that the question is a very important one and one which will involve some considerable additional expense. At the same time, I realize that in dredging these great harbours, both upon the eastern shores of Georgian bay and Lake Huron and also at Port Arthur and Fort William, we ought to look to the future. The lake steamers are becoming larger and are requiring a greater depth of water, and we ought to do what we can to keep the grain traffic of the west in Canadian channels and prevent it going to American ports. The chief engineer of the department tells me that, even taking the depth of water which the new American lock will have, 24 feet, and comparing it with the data of our work both at Victoria
and Tiffin and at Port Arthur and Fort William, it is not unlikely that, owing to the difference between the two data, the 22 feet depth proposed under the contracts will be sufficient. The matter is under consideration, and that is why I have not acted on the order in council and actually given the extension. For, if it is decided to dredge to a depth of 25 feet, it will require some arrangement to be made with the contractors that the work may go on and that we may not be compelled, having dredged 22 feet, to dredge to a depth of 25 feet. I am a thorough believer in the idea that, if it can be avoided, we must not allow these big ships which now transport the grain to Buffalo and other American ports to have an advantage in going to those ports, but we must make our harbours of sufficient depth to accommodate the largest vessel which in the future will navigate the great lakes. And, of course, the depth of the harbours on the western shore of Lake Superior must be the measure of the depth of the harbours on the eastern shore of Lake Huron and Georgian bay. Because if the big ships can enter Port Arthur and Fort William drawing 24 feet of water and cannot enter the harbours on Georgian bay or Lake Huron, they must of necessity take the traffic down to Buffalo and other American ports. This, of course, is a very important question as connected with our transportation problem, and I am sure the House will say that I am only exercising reasonable prudence in not acting immediately upon the authority of the order in council, .and in taking a short time to consider the matter with the officers of my department, getting all the information possible before deciding what is the best course to pursue. I make this explanation because otherwise my hon. friend might feel that I had not been entirely frank in saying that the order in council was passed, but the matter was under consideration.

Just a few words in reference to the question of how dredging contracts should be let. I think the first thing is to have a proper staff of engineers and to make a profile of the locality to be dredged. That, the hon. minister says, is rather difficult engineering work. It is no more difficult than any other engineering work on a railway or anything else. The proper plan is to have a profile, and to know the quantities and the material to be dredged before you put a dredge in at all. Then when you let the contract and the parties are at work it may be inconvenient to measure prism quantities and pay on prism quantities. It may be necessary to pay on monthly estimates, these, perhaps, to be founded on scow quantities or measurements of the material taken out. But in every case these estimates should be corrected at the end of two or three

months, or, at the very least, at the end of the season. In no case should the party dredging have any other payment than for the actual prism quantities he takes out. That is the practice in England and in most of the states of the American union and in practically every other country where the dredging is done. But what are the facts here? A couple of parties collude together to get a contract, and, according to the new morals brought up from St. John, N.B., that is all right. They have influence enough with this government to get their nominee appointed to measure the work. He even farms it out in some cases. And on this party's certificate the contractors are paid. And that is the only certificate-* no prism quantities, no profile, no correction of the work. In no other country in the world is such a thing permitted as is permitted by our Public Works Department. And why? It is no harm, according to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) where there are practically only two parties competing for a contract, for these parties to sit down and arrange prices for which they will bid. Why, that is nothing
Will my hon. friend (Mr. Haggart) pardon me ; I was speaking in reference to this particular work. In this case there were a large number of tenderers besides these companies.
Only one other.
I paid particular attention to the statement of my hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) and that statement was that the two parties who colluded were two-thirds of those who tendered.
No doubt about that.

And there is nothing wrong in that according to the Minister of Public Works-nothing immoral, nothing illegal. Why, in my reading of the statutes lately I have fouud that if a couple of parties attending a sale collude together, one saying to the other : ' You bid only so much for this and I will bid only so much for that,' and if that transaction comes before the court it is set aside on the ground of fraud and collusion. Why, there can be no greater collusion than for two to get together to arrange for high prices for such a contract as this. But, according to the new code of morals, this is all right-and, at least we can say that it is comparatively venial when we consider some of the other things done by those now in power. The Minister of Public Works seems not to take into account at all the statute quoted by my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) which provides that every work involving an expenditure of $5,000 or over must be let by contract. And the hon. gentleman ignores this statute notwithstanding the report of the Royal Commission to investigate the civil service and its recommedation on this subject.	1
How did I ignore it?

By letting a contract, or extending a contract which already existed, without tender, for works which may amount to $150,000 or $200,000 during the current year. There are estimates of $75,000 for one of the works and $75,000 for the other. And the hon. minister recommends to the Governor in Council to give him power to extend a contract for these works which contract was obtained by collusion.
But it was not obtained by collusion.

It is a fraud, it is a violation of the law which the Royal Commission appointed by the hon. gentleman himself, has drawn attention to. There is a similar Act in England. How do they do there ? As I have stated before in this House, they do not buy even a paint brush or a pound of nails without tender and contract. They do not do any piece of work, unless in the government workshops or navy yards, except by contract. The attention of the minister was forcibly drawn to it by the commission. They say to him : Look to England, there was a case in England where it was thought that for the purpose of keeping secret the construction of a gun of a particular pattern, it was in the public interest that the work should be done in secret; but the Public Accounts Committee in England said: That is not a sufficient reason to set aside the statute, that is not a sufficient reason to set aside the well known principle which has been adopted in reference to public works in England. No, they say, let every foreign government in the world know what the secret is, rather than that we should set aside the well known principle of letting public works by tender. But these gentlemen here in Canada-laws do not bind them, morals do not bind them. We had a set of morals brought up here the other day in reference to collusion. No effect at all upon hon. gentlemen. Statutory enactments are not of the least use. Wherever they think it is in the interest of their friends to let them a contract without tender, no statute, no law binds them. One would think that with the report of the Royal Commission before them showing violations of the law and making a comparison with the British system, they would at least have a little care. But the minister gets up boldly in the House and justifies the course he is pursuing. He says he thinks it is rather to be commended. Commended for what ? Getting an order in council passed and not putting it into effect. For what reason? Because the amount to be excavated by the dredges may be largely in excess of the present estimate. He says that he has in contemplation the deepening of the harbour at Port Arthur and Victoria, and Midland to the depth of the new lock which is to be constructed at Sault Ste. Marie by

the Americans. It is true that the Americans contemplate a depth of 24 feet on the mitre sill of the new lock. But the new lake dredging will not be done, it will not be in use for seven or eight years more. It will take that time at least to complete the dredging, and they will have to build a new lock I suppose in order to give the same facilities as at present, and when they do that we will have to export by Midland and other harbours, because we must be able to use vessels of the largest draft that navigate Sault Ste. Marie.
I only rose for the purpose of showing how the chance of committing fraud with reference to dredging could be removed, if these gentlemen who have the administration of public affairs in charge adopted ordinary reasonable means for the purpose of doing it, and had a proper system of estimating the work that is to be done, and would follow the law in reference to the construction of public works. Never mind about morals, never mind about collusion; although the most damaging thing that could ever happen to a minister or a government is the exercise of nepotism, appointing their friends or relatives to public positions and helping them to secure contracts. No government can last long which does that. The strongest man that ever occupied the woolsack in England, on account of the appointment of a few relatives of his to positions under the government, was driven into private life. What has become of the public sentiment of this country if the statements of my hon. friend from East Simcoe are correct, that friends of members of the government, sons and relatives of members of parliament, are receiving large contracts from the government ? It would be better that the commerce of the country should be stopped than that such things should be allowed to occur. Honour and integrity among public men are far above any wealth that can be acquired by such means, and hon. gentlemen will find out that the people of this country are awakening at last to these methods. I only rose for the purpose of making a few remarks with reference to what I considered the proper way of letting these contracts. It is simple, it is legal, there is no collusion about it. Above all things, let us keep the government and the people's representatives free from suspicion. For goodness sake, let us adopt the practice that, even when you wish to buy a pound of nails or a box of matches, you do it by open and public tender, by competition, and thus remove entirely temptation from the government.

I wish to express my disapproval of the policy laid down by the Minister of Public Works in respect to letting contracts without public competition. If any member of this House will take the trouble to look over the ' Hansard ' of the last three or four years and read the discussions that have taken place in connection
with tenders for dredging, they will arrive at the conclusion that something is wrong. For example here are two companies. My hon. friend from East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) has from time to time been pointing out that some men were shareholders in both, that relatives were in both of them, and that in some cases there was collusion, there was a joining of hands in order to deceive the government in the tenders they put in for dredging. For instance, when these two companies, the Great Lakes Dredging Company and Mr. A. F. Bowman, were tendering for work to be done in Port Arthur, one of them, the Great Lakes Dredging Company, put in a tender for 9 cents a yard and A. F. Bowman put in a tender for 18 cents a yard, and A. F. Bowman is a member of the Great Lakes. Dredging Company. If there had been uo other tenders between the two everybody knows what would have happened. The one for 9 cents would have been withdrawn, and the government would have been compelled to give the tender for 18 cents per yard.
Can the hon. gentleman point out any case in which a Minister of Public Works has allowed such a thing to be done ?
I do not propose to enter into a detailed discussion of all these matters.
Then why does the hon. gentleman assume that it would have been done when it never has been done ?

I am expressing my condemnation of the policy. I would like the minister to understand that when he comes forward, as he does this afternoon, and states that there shall be no public competition for the dredging that is to take place at these two points for the coming year, then I say the people of this country will not approve of such a policy. Speaking for myself, I wish to express my condemnation of the new policy laid down by the minister. Not only is the minister guilty himself but he has, in the order in council, received the endorsation of the cabinet and we have therefore every member of the government setting aside a statute of this country as read by my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) and as cited by my hon. friend from Lanark (Mr. Haggart). In reference to this statute we have a government, whose duty it is to carry out the statutes, coming forward his afternoon, and, through one of its representatives, saying that they will set aside this statute and that during this season dredging work shall be done without public competition at the prices they paid last year whether those prices were just or unjust. I see that the Auditor General has expressed himself upon this subject. Here is a letter :
Several eases came up during the season of 1906, where no public competition was in-

vited, but where a price for 1906 dredging was agreed upon between some official of your department and the contractor who had been dredging at the same place in the season of 1905.
In each of these instances the application for payment was accompanied by a typewritten slip-form, stating that ' as the case was one of pressing emergency, in which delay would have been injurious to the public interest, the minister directed that the work should be executed without a call for tenders/
It would generally be feasible for the engineering staff of one season to calculate what work remains to be done for the next year; and for the department to arrange its future policy in the early part of the winter. There would then be ample time to allow for public advertisement and tender, before dredging becomes possible in April or May.
Whatever difficulties have been caused in the past, by the late dates at which the votes of parliament were determined, will disappear under the new arrangement by which the fiscal year begins on April 1.
The money will now be voted several weeks or months before the opening of navigation; and there will always be sufficient time to invite tenders and award contracts, with the deliberation which is essential to such an important subject.
Here, the Auditor General, over his own signature, in the last Auditor General's Report (V-300) points out to the minister that this policy is a very bad one and he says that it ought to be discontinued. May I direct for a moment the attention of the right lion. First Minister (Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier) to a statement that he made some years ago with respect to the way in which public works should be carried on under his government when it came into power ?
It is an honest minister who makes a competent engineer. Sir, when we have a Liberal party administration at Ottawa, we shall not have such a system as that, we shall not have these errors which have been occurring, because the minister will then say to the engineer ;
' My government wants a plan of a bridge, or a plan of a block of buildings, prepare your plans, but mind, if the contract which is given is not filled exactly as it is wanted or one cent has to be paid, off goes your head at once/
From such men, to-day in the ranks of the Liberal party, can be produced such a Minister of Railways, Minister of Public Works, that there will he no disgrace upon the brow of any Canadian.
This was the policy laid down by the right hon. gentleman before he came into power in 1896. Now, we have ministers of the Crown setting aside the statutes. Now, after we have adopted a policy approved by the people of Canada which declares that there shall be public competition, we have that policy set aside and the right hon. gentleman and the members of his government adopt an order in council endorsing a brand new policy brought up from eastern Canada Mr. BLAIN.
by the Minister of Public Works. I want to call the attention of the hon. Minister of Public Works to something that took place at a meeting of the board of trade at Col-iingwood
The regular Board of Trade meeting was held in the court room on Tuesday night last, and it was largely attended.
The principal question was the harbour. The president wanted to get at the actual condition of affairs. It was generally understood that we had a depth of twenty feet of water in the channel at low water, but facts did not hear out this supposition. He wanted to know who was responsible for the incomplete and unsatisfactory condition of the channel.
Mr. Hughes, the inspector, produced a chart of the soundings showing bumps and lumps dotted all over the channel, which was explanation enough of the trouble.
The hoard will take energetic steps to have the channel cleared up as the contractors are evidently digging out the soft spots where it pays the best, and the engineer is either indifferent or ignorant of what is going on. Mr. Hughes only does as he is told, and has no discretionary powers on the work.
That is the condition up at Coilingwood, as presented to this House in 1907. Here was a contractor dredging, out the soft spots in order to make money. There are other instances if I were to take up the time of the House but I want to direct the minister's attention to the fact that if any department in this government requires to ask for public tenders surely it is the department of my hon. friend. The amounts involved are large. There may be a difference of opinion as to whether an item of $2,000 or $3,000 should be made the subject of competition and tender but there surely can be no question that the competitive system is advisable when such large amounts are involved as are expended for dredging. I read from the last report of the Minister of Public Works that at Port Arthur :
The total amount dredged from July 1 to end of the season of 1906, was 443,175 cubio yards, scow measurements, and the expenditure for the nine months ending March 31 last was $67,990.91.
My hon. friend from East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) has pointed out that the dredging companies that are under discussion have received more than $1,000,000

Two million.
Mr. BLAIN-two. million during the last few years for dredging. The newspapers have been pointing out that there is something wrong. My hon. friend from East Simcoe, in particular, has been directing the attention of the House to this condition of things. Here are two dredging companies, one assisting the other and both making an effort, of course, to make ail the money possible. We find that tenders are ranging between these companies and other companies

from 57 cents to 27 cents, to 9 cents and to 18 cents. Surely that fact is sufficient to warn the hon. gentleman who is the controller of this department against allowing any man or any company to come to him and say : X wiil do this work at the same price as that which was paid last year. That is not the policy that the people of Canada want to pursue in the year 1908. That is a policy that was discarded years ago. That is a policy that no municipal council in any province of Canada would permit for a moment and yet my hon. friend who is supposed to lead in this respect, to point out how the public works of the country should he constructed and to see that every care is taken to protect the public interest, has assented to a proposal of this ikind and has introduced a brand new policy with regard to this dredging work. What will these dredging companies think about it ? They wiil say: We have a friendly minister. Two tenders may go in for the one work and the same two contractors may tender for another work and they can decide with the approval of the minister which of them shall take one contract and which shall take the other. That is the condition of things in the Department of Public Works now. Are we to understand from the minister that these contracts are let for a term of years and that the government has no power to cancel them ?	[DOT]
Which contracts ?	.
The contracts for dredging in different parts of Canada.

I thought I had explained to my hon. friend that these contracts at Midland, Tiffin and Victoria harbours were let to the lowest tenderers after public competition of the widest character, and in the contract it is provided that they shall do this work during the season of 1907 or by such further later date as the Minister of Public Works may determine. Therefore, this is not letting work without competition at all. This is the case with regard to quite a number of contracts. This is nothing new with regard to contracts in tile Public Works Department, and it is not at all a new thing for the minister to have to fix a later date for the completion of a work. It has been done ever since confederation I suppose ; done by the late government as well as by this government. The hon. gentleman is entirely wrong in suggesting that I am letting this work be done without public competition. I am simply doing what the contract provides may be done. With regard to the dredging at Fort William and Port Arthur which the hon. gentleman included in his figures, in that case I am informed that in the call for tenders for the work at Fort William it whs expressly stated that the work was to extend over a number of years.
May I ask whether the government lias the power to cancel a contract which extends over a number of years ?
I have not the contract with me, but if the hon. gentleman moves for it it will be brought down.
The hon. gentleman corrects me when I say that this dredging is to be done without tender?
Certainly.

I made no such statement in the sense that the Blinister of Public Works seems to take out of it. I know full well that last year or the previous year tenders were invited, and I suppose the lowest tenderer was granted the work, but that is not the point under discussion. What I am calling attention to is the work to be done this year, and I state now in the presence of the minister that he has continued this work for 1908 without public competition. That is my statement. Is it correct or is it not?

It does seem to me that it is entirely wrong, because the contract was let by public competition. The prices were obtained by public competition and the contract itself specifies that the work is to be completed either at the close of 1907 or at such later date as the minister may determine. Therefore, the hon. gentleman is entirely wrong in saying that the work is being let without competition. All I am doing is exercising the power which the contract confers upon me to fix a date for the termination of the work.
What is the need of an order in council ?
I felt that I could do it without an order in council, but I also felt that in important matters like this it is desirable that I should go to my colleagues for their approval.
At page 5985 'Hansard/ 1907, there is a discussion on the question of dredging which I quote :

Bo I understand that contracts have been entered into with Weddell at one place and the Great Lakes Company at another that will run for six years or about $190,000 a year for the two?
Blr. 11SHER (Acting Blinister). The contract is terminable at any time at the wish of the government. The plan was made for the whole work and the contracts were let for the whole, expecting to occupy about seven years.
The contract was let on estimated quantities?
Yes.
How could the government let a contract covering work for six or seven years when the money has not been voted?
The contract can he terminated at any time. .

But if the contract is let 1 and the money is not voted I take it the con-

tractor would have reasonable ground for claiming damages._
The contract is let subject to the voting of the money in parliament.

In the session of 1904 a Bill was introduced by the then Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Prefontaine) relating to these two harbours, and I desired information on that subject and the minister at that time is reported in ' Hansard ' as follows:
We are therefore to understand from this citation that the government has power to cancel this contract at any time and the very fact that the minister now asks for an order in council to continue the work for next year is the proof. I say it is wrong for the minister to do any such thing. I believe it will not receive the endorsation of the hon. gentleman's own supporters in the House. The people of Canada will not approve of it, and particularly where the dredging in this department is surrounded by suspicion on every hand. Suspicion is created, for instance, by the fact stated by my hon. friend from East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) that one of the inspectors on one of these dredges never went near the dredge at all.
He swore to that himself.

The inspector swore to that himself in the Public Accounts Committee ; he swore that he had let the work to another and that he stood in the position of a middleman and took the profits and put them in his pockets. Then we have other suspicious things about the dredging, and I therefore repeat that the policy the minister has adopted in allowing the dredging at these points to go on for the summer of 1908 without public competition is a policy that the people of Canada will not endorse. In the face of all these scandals in connection with the expenditure of public money, the people of Canada will be surprised that the Minister of Public Works should say that hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of work should be done without public competition.

I wish to say a few words on this question, because I think we have embarked on a very dangerous principle. I remember some years ago bringing up the question in this House in connection with the expenditure of public money under the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. I drew attention to what I regarded as an innovation that would lead to very great abuses and probably great dishonesty if it were continued. The answer I received was that we had a new minister who was adopting a new and up-to-date method. I will ask any one who has given attention to the history of that department and to the report of the commissioners who were appointed to inquire into the civil service if I was not justified in the position I then took. For many years abuses were constantly creeping in, in connection with Mr. BLAIN.
the expenditure of public money, and parliament in its wisdom thought well to embody what it regarded as the correct principle in a statute, with the view of controlling every minister in the expenditure of public moneys. What does that statute say?
Whenever any works are to,_be executed under the direction of any department of the government, the minister having charge of such department shall invite tenders by public advertisement for the execution of such works.
That was the correct principle. That was crystallized in a statute for the purpose of controlling ministers of the Crown as well as their subordinates. There were some exceptions provided for ; what were they ? The first was : ' pressing emergency in which delay would be injurious to the public interest. Has the minister shown us that in these particular cases there was any presing emergency ? Why, the very order in council was passed before navigation was opened. Had he not time to call for tenders for these works ? What kind of cases were intended to be provided for by that exception ? Perhaps the breaking of a lock of a canal or the breaking down of some bridge, when there was not time to call for public tenders, and when it would be justifiable to do the work otherwise. Does the minister pretend that there was any pressing emergency in these cases ? He tells us what the Grand Trunk is going to do in hauling grain, and what the boats are prepared to do when the locks at Sault Ste. Marie will be deepened. But the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) tells us that these locks could not be deepened for six or seven years. Then what is the great emergency for dredging at Tiffin or Midland or Victoria harbour for the purpose of allowing large vessels drawing 24 or 25 feet of water to come down through the canal ? Is there any necessity ? Not at all.
If you build your wharfs and your revetment walls upon land which is dredged to a depth of 22 feet, how can you afterwards dredge to a depth of 25 feet without undermining your works ?

The hon. gentleman is not so young or so innocent as to think he can put that theory before this House. He knows that he does not require to do that. He presumes on the gullibility of this House to an extent for which I would not give him credit.
Not at all.
Now one of the dredgers is to the fore.

The very thing the minister mentions occurred at the wharf of the Canadian Pacific Railway at Fort William, and they had to rip-rap it to strengthen it according to the increased depth of the

channel. The same thing has to be done to the elevator at Victoria harbour constructed only two years ago.
The hon. gentleman is confounding two things-dredging and the building of wharfs.
Not at all. The wharfs at Fort William were built some years ago, the river was afterwards deepened to twenty-two feet, and on account of the extra depth the reinforcement had to take place.
The work was done before it was contemplated that they would require a greater depth. Dredging is not to build a foundation for a wharf or an elevator.
Must you not dredge for your foundation ?	.

The minister has the knowledge in his possession, and if he has to dredge the channel deeper he will have to put the public work to that depth, but in doing that he does not require to do the dredging this year. There is no urgency in that, so that this work does not come under that first exception. What is the next ? ' A work which, from the nature of the work, can be more expeditiously and economically executed by the officers and servants of the department.' In this case, are the officers and servants of the department doing the work ? Not at all. So it does not come under that. What is the last exception ?	' When the established cost of the
work is less than $5,000.' These are the three exceptions, and I draw attention to them, because this case does not come under any one of the three. The minister chooses to ignore that statement. He is a new minister, and he is adopting new methods like the late Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and if he continues them, we shall find in a short time that they will lead to abuses which will be among the greatest scandals ever brought to light, and I am satisfied that the hon. minister knows it. He is not doing this innocently ; he is too old at the business. His history in the province which he has left is the strongest reason we have for reaching the conclusion that he knows what he is doing, and what it is likely to lead to. When the hon. minister is asked, what do you depend on for the faithfulness of your inspectors, he says, we depend on the government making inquiry in regard to their character and capability. But it was said in the House last session that when the government were told by one of their own supporters that a certain individual was satisfactory with regard to character, capability or anything else the minister is bound to accept it. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) shakes his head, I will show him from 1 Hansard ' that that was the reply. What did that lead to ? The inspector is appointed and
we are told that he goes to the works about eight or nine o'clock in the morning. But the dredge commences work at five o'clock and the inspector, according to the sworn testimony, reported so many cubic yards of stuff dredged out of the harbour, and that i3 all the government had to depend on. He said that the engineer of the dredge told him the quantity. I drew attention to the fact that they had an inspector going around the hotels, puffing away at twenty-five cent cigars, hour after hour, while the dredge was working, but the certificates came in and the dredge was paid on the strength of this man's certificates. The money of the government has been dishonestly spent in that way without the department having any proper or intelligent knowledge of the work done.
Who told the hon. gentleman that ?
I have it from a man living right in the locality. Some one raises an ironical laugh.
You do not blame them.

This man is just as honest and just as truthful, and I think a little more so, than the man who raised that laugh. He stands as well in the locality where he has resided for thirty years as the hon. member does in his locality.
Is he dead ?

More than that it can be verified by not one but many people. I brought it to the notice of the government some years ago and they paid no attention to it.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

When you left the chair at six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I was dealing with a phase of this question which I had about concluded. I have a question to ask the minister, how many contracts that were let last year or the year before are to be extended under the principle that he has explained ?

I am sorry that I have not a copy of the order ready to-night. As I said to the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) I will lay it on the table tomorrow. But I should say, speaking from memory, some ten or twelve, possibly more.

All in Ontario ?
* Mr. PUGSLEY. No. They are all cases in which public tenders were called for and the prices fixed by competition.
Last year ?	[DOT]
Yes.

If each of these represents any considerable sum, the aggregate must be a large amount of money. In view of the facts brought out with regard to these tenders-presents to' my mind perfectly conclusive-that there was collusion between the tenderers, the attitude which the minister

Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) permit me ? I do not admit that there was collusion between all the tenderers or any of them. There is no evidence of anything of this kind. It is not contended that there was any collusion with the Dominion Dredging Company which was the lowest tenderer at 30 cents. Another fact which I should mention, but which was not brought out this afternoon is that when the Dominion Dredging Company informed the minister that they could not take the contract at the price of 30 cents the tenderers were invited again to tender on the work and it was reduced to 27 cents.
Were there public calls for tenders in the newspapers ?
No, the tenderers were invited to tender again.
Did it look as if there was something wrong when one tenderer put in a bid at 56 cents and another at 27 cents and then would not take the contract?
It was one tendering at 30 cents who could not take it.
I suppose, in the meantime he had been interviewed by the others and he had come to the conclusion that they could get a good thing if they had an understanding.
I think that is a very unworthy suspicion.
No tenders were called for.
Unworthy of what ? Of a public man ?
Yes.
Did not the circumstances justify suspicion ?

There was not a fact to justify suspicion. There is not a tittle of evidence on which any suggestion could be based that the Dominion Dredging Company did not make their tender bona fide. But, in consequence of having other work they could not take this contract. It has not even been suggested that they were in collusion with the others.
Did they make their deposit when putting in their tender ?
I cannot say at the moment.

The minister knows that that is one of the conditions of tendering, Mr. PUGSLEY,
that with a tender there must go the deposit. The minister, therefore, had them under his control and could have compelled them to carry out the contract. But he allows them to throw it up for some reason best known to himself, and divide it up with
And we get it done at 3 cents a yard less.

I want to tell the minister that I have been too long in this House not to know something about how contracts are given in many lines. I remember a case, some years ago, when three corporations tendered for something in connection with the work of the Department of Justice. The tenders were collusive, but they were all different, and each was accompanied with the required deposit. But when the tender was to be awarded, the lowest tenderer, to whom the contract was to be given, represented that he had made a mistake in his calculations and that he stood to lose a great deal of money if he were compelled to carry out the contract. That is one of the common ways of getting out of these things. The result was that when they came to sign the contract the successful tenderer was in London and the unsuccessful tenderer in Ottawa. When the man in London was notified to sign the contract, he wired back to let so and so sign it-his supposed competitor-that all three were in it together and it did not matter who got it. I had this statement of the facts from the Minister of Justice of that time. He was confronted with this evidence of collusion. And I believe that this had been carried on for two or three times in succession in the same way. It has been shown over and over again in this House that there is collusion amongst tenderers in connection withjpublic works. In the face of that fact I think there is not only suspicion but more than suspicion in this case. It is not enough to say that, because the contract was given at 3 cents a yard less than the original lowest tender, that we are justified in running on that line for several years.

Before the hon. gentleman passes away from that point, will he allow me to ask:	Does he suggest that
these prices are not as the chief engineer certifies, fair and reasonable ?

That is a question that the minister could not reasonably expect me to answer. But I may tell him, from what I know about the business that it would depend upon the material to be taken out. If' it were ordinary sand, gravel or clay, the prices are very big prices. I speak from the knowledge of a man in the business for years, who told me over and over again that in any moderately well-sheltered place, he could take out clay, gravel or sand at 10 cents a yard and make big profits. And the price in this case is 26 cents. I know of offers over and over again to do

this work for less than ten cents, for less than 9 cents, even as low as 8 cents, if the government would give the work.
They always have a chance to tender.

If the stuff is ordinary clay, gravel or sand, as I assume it to "be, these parties have a cinch in a contract at 26 cents a yard. It is not enough to say that the engineer certified the price as fair and just. We who have been in the House for any length of time have found, over and over again, that prices which were really two or three prices were certified as fair and just. For instance, we know that teacups were bought for the icebreaker ' Montcalm ' at $1.94 apiece, and this price was certified as just and reasonable. Then in the case of the contract of M. P. Davis, on the Cornwall canal, the same certificate was given concerning prices. The Auditor General refused to pay and held up the accounts for over six months. And they took off the difference between $52,000 and $29,000 for the work of that year, and with this reduction the contractor was satisfied to accept payment. The government's own engineer was satisfied that $52,000 for what was done that year was a fair and just price, when the contractor himself accepted $29,000 and was satisfied. So it is not enough to say that because a price is recommended as fair and just, you ought to be satisfied with it. There are other ways of ascertaining what is fair and just. The minister says the contract is a continuous one, and they have a right to expect it to continue. How does he make that out ? Let him bring down the contract.
The copy will be down at the next sitting of the House.
After this debate is over ?

I regret I could not get the copy in time for this afternoons debate. I will say to my hon. friend that the items in regard to this very work will all appear, in fact are already in the main estimates, and the matter can be discussed in Committee of Supply.
That does not make any difference, it is a question of fact. Is it or is it not a continuous contract?

I will tell the hon. gentleman what the words of the contract are, as near as I can remember. They are that the contractor shall do the dredging work required at such a place, say at Victoria harbour, and shall complete the work by the close of the season of 1907, or at such later date as. may be fixed by the minister.
Which is at the end of the fiscal year ?
No, at the close of the season of 1907, or at such later date as may be fixed by the minister.
Then it lies with the minister to decide whether the contract ends at the end of the fiscal year or not. Does the minister contend that the contract would not end with the end of the fiscal year ?
You have to take it as it is
I say that the contract closes with the end of the fiscal year. When the fiscal year expires and the money voted has lapsed, that contract closes.

The hon. gentleman does not seem to understand me. I did not say that the contract closed with the fiscal year, it is the close of the season of 1907 or at such later date as may be fixed by the minister. Those are the words.
Practically it means the close of the fiscal year, because after winter sets in they cannot do any dredging. Is the minister aware of this fact ?
What does the hon. gentleman say is meant by the words ' or at such later date as may be fixed by the minister ' ?

That is a sliding clause the minister has put in, I do not think it binds any one. But I will tell him that I have an indistinct remembrance of some such contract let years ago, and because the government saw fit to take that work from the party and put it up for tender again, the contractor held that he had a right to collect damages because the government refused to continue the contract. The contractor asked permission to go into the Exchequer Court to establish the fact that he had a right to have his contract renewed. The government granted him permission, and the Exchequer Court decided that he had not the right, that the contract closed with the close of the fiscal year, and when the money that was voted for the year had lapsed, he had no right to a continuance of that contract. What does Abe minister say about that ?
Will the hon. gentleman tell me what were the words of the contract upon which the contractor relied as entitling him to a continuance ? Those words would be extremely important.

My remembrance is that it was a contract on schedule prices until the work was done. Now they could ndf do the work all in one year, and he claimed they could not do it in two years, I think he claimed it would take two years to do it, and he was entitled to continue that work until it was done. Therefore I hold his case

was quite as strong as the case under consideration at the present time.

Any lawyer knows that everything depends, as to the rights of the contractor, upon the words of the contract; and if the contract was just as the hon. gentleman seems to put it, that the contractor was to do the whole of this work at schedule prices, then I would say as a lawyer without hesitation that he would have a right to do the whole work and be paid for it. But there must have been something in the contract which has escaped the attention of my hon. friend. Perhaps it was provided in the contract that if the appropriation became exhausted the contract might be put an end to. But that would be a very different ease from the one we are now discussing.

I claim that when the appropriation is exhausted this contract ends. Parliament might change its mind, parliament might take up some other work, parliament might change the -work altogether, and parliament has a right to end the contracts at the end of the fiscal year, whether the contractor likes it or dislikes it. Therefore the case is on all fours with this one. Now let me draw attention to another feature. Some think we are on the verge of hard times. The price of labour may go down, the price of everything may go down. Suppose that this contract continues. I saw a statement in one of the papers that it would take about six years to finish the work at Port Arthur and the work is being done there on schedule prices. If I understand the Minister of Public Works correctly, it was to the effect that this work -would continue under the same contractors from year to year until it was done, at the prices at which they have taken the contract for the last year.

The hon. gentleman entirely misunderstood me. I cannot see how I could have been so unintelligible. I stated this afternoon that in so far as this work at Fort William is concerned it is not a contract from year to year, but it is a contract for the whole work extending over a number of years.
For the whole work extending over a number of years ?
Yes, expressly mentioned in the contract.
Was there any time mentioned during which it was supposed the work was to continue ?
Yes, it was supposed that it would continue for six years and that was the statement made by the acting Minister of Public Works, the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher).
In what year was that statement made?
I think it was the year before last; it was either last year or the year before.
I suppose the hon. gentleman does not know the price at which the contract was let.
Yes, the price is quite low.
How much?
The price at Fort William is 9 cents per cubic yard with an additional allowance of 2 cents per cubic yard based upon the distance at which the mud is carried out beyond a certain limit.
That contract was made at 9 cents per cubic yard and this one is 26 cents per cubic yard.
That is very low.
I think it is reasonable.
The one at Victoria harbour i's 8 cents.
Victoria harbour is 8 cents and the other is 26 cents for the same kind of work.
Not for the same kind of work.

I take the Port Arthur contract to be on all fours with the case in which it was held by the Exchequer Court that a contract ended at the end of the fiscal year and that the contract could be abandoned by the government at that time. Let us look at the unwisdom and improvidence of entering into such a contract as this one. This contract is taken at 26 cents a yard. The minister was asked if there was any estimate made as to how much work was to be done there and his reply was that he thought not. Therefore, we do not know how long this work is likely to last. But, suppose it lasts for four, five, six or seven years
It will not last that long.

Well, it will last a few years. Suppose that it was taken at a time when wages were very high, suppose that we were right on the verge of hard times when wages would drop 15, 20 or 30 per cent when the cost of supplies and everything else would drop and when work of this kind could be done for perhaps 75 or 80 per cent less than the price which would yield a good profit when the contract was made, in what position would the government find themselves with a contract of this kind on their hands? I will wait until I can get the minister's attention. I want to ask him whether, if I treated him in that way, he would regard it as an act of courtesy? I say that if he had the instincts of a gentleman he would not treat me in this way.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman must withdraw that remark.
Well, I will withdraw those words but I wish that I had some other words that would convey my meaning.
I trust that the hon. gentleman will not again make an exhibition of himself in the manner that he has done this evening.

I will make such an exhibition as in my judgment seems proper until the hon. gentleman sees fit to treat me with that courtesy which is due from a minister of the Crown to any member of this House who is exercising the right which he has of dealing with these public accounts of a minister.

Mr. Speaker, I would like your ruling upon the question as to whether, if a member does not choose all the time to look at the hon. gentleman who is addressing the House, he may be characterized as wanting in courtesy. I heard what the hon. gentleman said although for a moment I turned to speak to my hon. friend on my right (Mr. Carvell). But, that should not justify the hon. gentleman in saying what he did say to me.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think it is hardly a point of order. It is a question of taste, I suppose.

I was saying that provided prices and wages fell the government would find themselves with a contract on their hands that represented hundreds of thousands and even millions of dollars, whereas, had they an opportunity of calling for tenders, they could save a lot of money to the country. I say it is an improvident and unwise contract, and that it will just as surely as we are here to-night lead to improper conduct on the part of somebody. This is one of the devices that the minister has in his own hands which enable him to improperly use public money, and to pay it out to his own favourites in such a way that the government does not get full return for it. The minister is a new man, he has adopted this new system, and I predict that we will live to remind him of what it has led to. The system, in my judgment, is a very bad one. The money which has been spent in a few years with three of these firms reaches the total of $3,700,000. That is a large amount of money.
What is this new system that the hon. gentleman speaks about as having been inaugurated by me? It is not a new system. This has been done before in the case of contracts like the present.
I have not knowledge of it being done since the Act was passed to compel the government to do these works by tender and contract.
Yes, this was put up for tender.

This was a departure from the statutory law. This sum of $3,-
700,000	has been paid out to these three firms one of which is doing dredging at 8 cents a yard.
They are now being paid 9 cents and the contract has been varied from 20, 30 and 40 cents a cubic yard.

Yes, they were getting 30 and 40 cents for the same work that they are doing now for 9 cents. On account of the constant attention that has been given to this question in this House, especially by my hon. friend from East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) for sheer shame they were obliged to put this work up to public competition and the contract was given and they are now doing the work for 9 cents a yard for which thef were previously getting 23 cents. I will say that the work for which they are getting 26 cents a yard would have been done this year, if tenders had been invited, for 8 cents a yard the same as they are doing it for Victoria harbour.
It is not the same kind of work.

And yet the government have denied themselves the opportunity of saving the money of the country. They have paid $3,700,000 in a few years for one class of work and they would go on and pay out that money. Noth withstanding the fact that many of these contracts may be let at a price three times as great as they should be let at they will allow them to go on from year to year and pay the price regardless of whether the country is getting any return for the outlay or not so long as it happens to suit their convenience. It is wrong, it is improper, it should not be continued and if the minister continues it, just as sure as he is here to-night, we will have an opportunity of reminding him in the future of the abuses that have developed under his administration, we will bring to light transactions similar to those which have been disclosed to-day, we will meet the minister with the argument that is presented to him to-night, and we will show him how improper and illegal is his conduct in making contracts and carrying on public work in this manner.

I want to ask the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) to take a few notes as he has promised us that when his estimates come down he will be able to give us all the information that we want in respect to these contracts. I am informed that last year the department called for tenders for dredging in the province of Quebec. Tenders were invited for dredging at Blanche Shoals and the Stewart Company were the lowest, but they were full of work and could not take the job and it was handed over to Messrs.

T. F. Moore and Company of Montreal, who are a sort of manufacturers agents, something like Merwin and are dealing very largely with the government. The contract was awarded to Moore and Company.
At what price ?

It is for you to get me that information when the estimates are up.
Mr. PUGSLEY'. Were they the lowest tenderers ?
Stewart and Company were the lowest but they did not take the job and it was given to Moore and Company.
What became of their deposits.	,

The Stewart Company were the lowest tenderers for the dredging at Dorion but they had to throw up the job and it was given to L. Cohen & Sons. L. Cohen & Sons are a firm of Jews in Montreal who run the jew vote in the interest of the friends of the government.
I am not aware that that is any disgrace.

It is not, but they are not dredging men.
Mr. PUGSLEY7. Were they the lowest tenderers ?
Stewart and Company were the lowest in every case but they were so full of other jobs that they could not take these.
What price did Cohen get.
It will be for the minister to get that information. At Maskiuonge Stewart and Company were the lowest but they were unable to carry out the contract and it was handed over to L. Cohen & Son.
Was it at the same price?
I know nothing about the price, I want the minister to get that information.
I will be very glad to.

At Point Cavagnole the Stewart Company was the lowest but it was handed over to Cohen & Sons. At Racquette river the Stewart Company was the lowest tenderer but having, their hands full of other jobs the work was handed over to Cohen & Sons.
If there was so much money in it one would suppose they would try to carry out the contract.
I think there was something in it for somebody but we will deal with that later.
Who got that contract ?
Cohen & Sons, this Arm of Jews at Montreal.
Why do you call them a firm of Jews. Can't Jews do dredging work ?
Certainly they can, but they are in a mercantile business and they are not the kind of men that should be given dredging contracts.
I am told they have done the dredging work very satisfactorily indeed.

At St. Placide, Stewart and Company tendered lowest but the work was handed over to Cohen & Sons. I want to know from the minister what he did with all these deposits of Stewart and Company and why the contracts were allowed to be handed over to other parties. Another j)iece of information I want from the minister is : Has the contract for the Quebec harbour improvements to Messrs. Dus-sault & Lemieux been renewed for this year. Has a new contract been entered into with this firm at the same prices as last year's work ?
Perhaps the hon. gentleman would put that in the form of a question and I will get the answer in the ordinary way.
I thought you could answer that now.
I cannot keep all these things in my head.

If the minister has not extended the contract this year I ask him in the interest of the country not to do so and for this reason. Some of his predecessors in office entered into a contract with Hussault & Lemieux in 1903 or 1904 for harbour improvements at Quebec. The contract given them was number 4163. They did that year $183,000 worth of work. That is what they charged for it, and I want to refer the minister for a moment to some of the charges that were made and will be made this year if this contract is extended. That contract was extended by order in council for 1904-1905 and no new tenders were called for and the government paid that year $224,000. The next contract was 5011 and that was extended by order in council for another year and at the same prices and they earned that year $107,609. Another contract was entered into with them, for the next year (1906-1907) by order in council, and they earned $98,937.40.

Mr. Speaker, I must confess I am somewhat unfamiliar with the rules of this House, but I would ask you, whether, when a gentleman asks permission to move the adjournment for the purpose of discussing a particular matter, is it

open to another hon. member to discuss something entirely foreign to the question. The permission to move the adjournment was given simply to discuss the question of dredging.
This is dredging.

Pardon me it is not. This is wharf building. I addressed myself to the question raised by the hon. member (Sir. Bennett) as to the dredging contracts at Victoria and at Tiffin and now the hon. member (Sir. Taylor) is dealing with wharf building at Quebec.

I wish to say, Sir. Speaker, that the motion of my hon. friend (Sir. Bennett) was as to renewing contracts without tender. Because the minister had informed him yesterday that several contracts were to be renewed. I see in the Dussault contract an item of 18,000 yards of dredging at 75 cents a yard. That contract has been renewed year after year at 75 cents a yard and the person that the contract was given to had no dredge, and he farmed it out at 15 cents a yard and this government is paying year after year 75 cents a yard for it.

I am not aware of it, and I presume the department is not.
The hon. minister is paying 75 cents a yard for mud dredging at Quebec when he is getting it done at other places for 15 cents. The thing on its face shows that there is something wrong.
Does my hon. friend know that there is a vast difference between dredging in the St. Lawrence, where the tides rise and fall, and dredging on the lakes?

Yes, there is some difference, but as the motion for adjournment is made simply to discuss dredging, I will take another opportunity to discuss the prices the government have been paying for supplies.
