speakeroldname: Mr. F. B. CARVELL (Oarleton, N. B.).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when this matter came up I was somewhat at a loss to understand the object the hon. member for East Simcoe had, and I am not entirely clear about it yet. I may say that there have been a number of dredging contracts discussed in the Public Accounts Committee and evidence has been given in some of these cases, but, as I am not allowed under the rules of the House to discuss them, I will not transgress by attempting to state what the evidence shows. Suffice it to say, that in my humble opinion the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) has gained very little satisfaction from the evidence that has been adduced in that committee, and it seems to me that he is now attempting to get before the country certain matters before they are brought out under oath in the Public Accounts Committee. If we can believe the statements we have heard this afternoon on both sides



of the House, we must come to the conclusion that had the hon. member for East Simcoe had his way, and stated everything he wanted to state, his story would have been very different from what the story actually is. We were led this afternoon to believe that a new contract had been entered into by the Minister of Public Works for dredging at Midland, Tiffin and Victoria harbour. Now, the facts are, that something like a year ago tenders were called by the then acting Minister of Public Works for dredging at these three places. The hon. member for East Simcoe has attempted to show that a great wrong has been done to the country because two of the tenders put in by presumably rival firms where in the handwriting of a gentleman who has the misfortune to be a relative of a member of parliament on this side of the House, and the hon. member for East Simcoe, with characteristic audacity, draws the inference that there must be something crooked in the transaction, but my hon. friend did not tell the House what he might have known from an examination of the documents-what he did know. My hon. friend, in the first place, went through a lot of cheap g5rmnastics in daring the government to bring down the papers and lay them on the table of the House in order that the members might have a chance to examine them. Does he not know that he and every member of the Public Accounts Committee and every member of this House has had a chance to examine those papers during the last two months? I think I am not trespassing on the rules of debate when I say that the hon. gentleman made that statement with the deliberate intention of making the people of this country believe that this government were trying to conceal from the public something which they had a right to see, although he knew that there was no attempt to conceal anything. He was asking the government to do something which they could not do. He knows that these papers are in the custody of the Public Accounts Committee. This House, which places those papers in the custody of the Public Accounts Committee, has the power to take them from the custody of that committee, if a motion is made to that effect, but what right has the Minister of Public Works any more than the hon. member for East Simcoe to say to the clerk of the committee, you will bring these papers down herg and hand them over to a messenger and have them laid on the table of this House? It is simply a cheap way of insinuating that the government has been trying to keep from the House and the country certain papers which they were entitled to have. If those papers had been examined by the Public Accounts Committee and evidence had been adduced, then I am forced to the conclusion from what I have learned here this afternoon that the hon. member for East Simcoe himself knows Mr. CARVELL.
that he would not have got from them anything like the evidence that he has attempted to place on the records of the House this afternoon. What would those papers show? I gather, from the statements made by the minister, who has not had an opportunity of examining the papers, and from the admissions of the hon. member for East Simcoe and other members on the other side of the House, that they would show that about a year ago tenders were called for this work; and I hope hon. members of this House and the people of this country will not forget that those tenders were open to the whole world. They were not confined to two or three dredging firms that happened to be in Owen Sound, and I have a very shrewd suspicion that perhaps one of the objects of the hon. member for East Simcoe is to get a rap at a gentleman who lives in Owen Sound and is a member of one of those dredging companies. There is an election coming an in the province of Ontario before very long, and a certain gentleman who lives near Owen Sound may play a prominent part in those elections, and I think the hon. member for East Simcoe had that fact in mind. However, tenders were put in by two rival companies at 53 cents and 57 cents respectively, and my hon. friend wants the people of this country to believe that because those tenders were in the same handwriting there was collusion. He says, what greater evidence of fraud do you want than that? Now, I am willing to admit that if those tenders were not open to the public, and those two firms alone had been invited to tender and had put their heads together to keep up the price, that would be evidence of fraud. But when the work is open to the whole world. I fail to see evidence of an offence against either moral law or the legal rights of any one in the fact that those two firms put their heads together to get as good a price as possible. The best proof of that statement is what took place in this very case. These two companies put in their tenders, and they were pretty high tenders, I should imagine. At the same time a third man came in and tendered at a little more than one half the price, 30 cents. The very fact that the third man came in and cut the price down shows that there is no harm in the action of the other two, because they were liable to have another tenderer come in. The Dominion Dredging Company received the contract at 30 cents, but found that they were not able to do the work. It was hinted this afternoon by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) that there must have been a nigger in the wood pile somewhere. Why these hon. gentlemen can see graft in everything that takes place.

Hear, hear, that is about right.
(Mr. CARVELL. I sometimes wonder if they are going back in their minds to what

took place-when they were in power. I cannot imagine people seeing something crooked in everything that takes place unless they were of a crooked mind. They must have been used to crooked transactions when they were running the government and therefore think that every one else does the same. I am afraid that this will be the case if ever this country should be so unfortunate as to again have them in control of the government. The hon. member for Bast Grey (Mr. gproule) says : I have been at this business so long that I know how these things are being done. Yes, he does, there is not a man on the front bench of the opposition who does not know how such things are done, they can go back in their minds to the old Connolly and MCGreevy transactions. They are postmasters in the art of manipulating tenders and contracts. There is nothing they cannot tell about in that line, and they have an idea that no matter what takes place on a government contract, whether by private contract or by public tender, there must be something crooked about it. The insinuation was thrown out this afternoon that because the Dominion Dredging Company were unable to carry out their contract at 30 cents and tkrew_it up, there was graft in that somewhere and a scheme put up between these people by which the country was to lose money. What are tl;e facts? The government did not go to the next lowest tenderer and offer the work at 53 cents but according to the statement of the minister this afternoon they sent out telegrams to every one who had tendered: these people came in and the country gets the work done at 27 cents instead of 30 cents. Is there anything wrong in that ?
It is worth 9 cents.

My hon. friend says it is worth 9 cents. That is why I say it is absolutely unfair, worse than unfair to bring up a discussion of this kind under the present circumstances. The hon. member from Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) brings this up before we have had a chance to examine witnesses or to ascertain the character of the work, whether it is worth 8 cents as the work at Victoria Harbour, or 26 cents or 27 cents here. In view of that I am forced to the conclusion that the hon. member for East Simcoe brought this matter up in order to spread these statements broadcast over the country before witnesses could be examined on the case, and I believe if my hon. friend had been allowed to have these statements go to the country unanswered, you would never have heard of a witness being called before the Public Accounts Committee to get at the exact facts of the case. Now I presume they will have to go on with it.
These contracts were let at 26 and 27 cents instead of 30 cents, and in every move of the Public Works Department in this case the public interests were safeguarded and the price has been constantly lowered.
216J
My hon. friend, in the next place, raised the cry that the Minister of Public Works has let this contract without tender and that it is a new contract. The member for East Simcoe had no hesitation in saying that this is a new contract. The member for Peel (Mr. Blain) this afternoon would not take the word of the Minister of Public Works when he told him over and over again that it was not a new contract. I do not think the member for Peel (Mr. Blain) is so obtuse that he could not understand the Minister of Public Works. I give him credit for having ordinary abilities, his hearing is good so far as I know, and I am satisfied he must have understood the Minister of Public Works. Yet he would not take his statement and went on declaring it was a new contract. The member for Grey (Mr. [DOT]Sproule) this afternoon took the same course and when driven into a corner he dragged up from his memory some old contract when he and his friends were in power and tried to argue that it was a parallel case. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) has told this House repeatedly this afternoon that contracts were let last year for the work at Victoria harbour, at Midland and at Tiffin, and that there was a clause in these contracts providing that they were to be completed before the end of navigation in 1907 or at such later date as the minister should decide. All the minister has done in this case is to carry out the terms of this contract. All he has done is by an order in council to provide another date when this work shall be completed, and, Sir, I would like to ask the hon. gentleman who brought up this matter if they can see any reasons why the government should hope to get a lower tender for this particular class of work if they had put it up this year than they were able to secure last year.
There is another thing. When this work is well under way and the firm have their dredges and scows and plant at the location, surely they can go on and do the work cheaper than it could have been done if they were driven out, new tenders called for, and a new contract given to a new firm. I submit that under these conditions you would not get a new firm to go in there and do the work as cheaply as it is being done at the present time, certainly not cheaper. For these reasons it seems to me that the Minister of Public Works is amply justified in taking the course he has taken. I am satisfied the House and the country will justify the ministers in that course, and that the member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) will not be able to make the people of Canada believe that a new contract has been let by the Minister of Public Works without tender; they will realize that it was simply a continuation of the contract let last year and simply carrying out the terms of that contract, that under the conditions of the contract the public are getting this work done as cheaply as it could possibly be done

and that not only the terms but the letter of the law and the contract have been carried out to the full.

It will, I think, be generally admitted that it is quite the proper thing for the opposition to criticise public expenditures. I for one have never any objection to anything like a fair criticism, but I submit that such criticism as has been offered this afternoon, is entirely unfair and unjustified and I do not think that any good purpose can be served by gross misrepresentations-if I may use the word slander. I believe that a great deal of the discussion this afternoon is largely composed of misrepresentations and slander. As I understand the situation it is not a question of new contract, it is a question of properly dealing with a contract that had been let under special conditions. What were the conditions ? That a certain class of work should be done within a certain time and that it might be done within this time or at such later time as the minister would fix for the completion. I submit that any contractor taking the work would base his tender upon that clause of the contract and say: If it is not possible for me to do it with all reasonable effort within the time specified in the contract. I am in the hands of the minister of the Crown, and I expect such treatment as a subject ought to expect from the Crown, no undue advantage will be taken of me but I will be given a reasonable opportunity to carry that work to completion.
The hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) this afternoon stated that this work was done on a very different basis from dredging anywhere else in America, that scow measurement was something that ought not to be tolerated, and this work was being done without proper measurement and on the mere certificate of the inspector who watched the loading of the scow where the dredge was operated. I am surprised at the hon. member making that statement because he has been Minister of Railways. He made the further statement that the measurement of dredging excavation was a matter that could be measured just as a railway contract could be measured and that it was always measured in place in every other country but Canada. The hon. gentleman is entirely mistaken. I venture to say that, generally speaking, dredging in the United States is done by scow measurement, and done in that way after the government of that country had had experience in place measurement. And why ? Because a greater amount of mismeasurement-or, if you like a stronger word, of fraud,-existed under that system than under the present system. And that is why they adopted the scow measurement. All the dredging done in this country, so far as I know, is done upon plans and cross sections showing the Mr. CARVELL	.
depth of water, the area to be dredged, and the class of material, so far as the engineers can test it by borings and otherwise. And what does the contractor tender for ? He tenders to do a certain amount of dredging for a certain price within a limited time within the area shown by the plans. And usually, it is by scow measurement. Why ? A good deal of work can be done by place measurement, solid rock for instance, or excavation that is above or near the surface can be done by place measurement. But the case is altogether different if the work is at the bottom of a harbour. To get the measurements you have to send down divers, and the contractor has to send down divers to see that he gets fair play. And you cannot leave the work for more than two weeks or a month because there is a constant washing in of material. Prices would be one-half or one-third higher if the measurements were not taken as the excavation is made. I do not suppose there is a harbour being dredged in this country where there is not material of a more or less silty nature. In many places it partakes of the nature of quicksand or clay that will fill in in twenty-four hours and take away one quarter of the measurement that the contractor might fairly claim. I do not say that that appertains generally but it does appertain in some cases. Therefore, it is easy to see the enormous difficulty that surrounds this question of fair measurement and why frequent measurements would be necessary if full measurement is to be given for the actual quantity taken out. If you are measuring in place, everything depends on who holds the tape. And it is the diver who holds it. You cannot estimate the amount of dredging in any other way. That is the reason for favouring scow measurement both from the point of view of the government and from the point of view of the contractor. The best evidence of this is that if you take the work done by railway companies and harbour companies, where they pay not out of government funds but out of their own funds, they usually do it in that way. It is not a practical thing to do it otherwise. I need not dwell upon that feature of the case, because any one who will consider the difficulties of the case will see the reasonableness of scow measurement. Is there any great chance for fraud in scow measurement ? I am bound to say that there are cases where work is done by place measurement. I know of a case on the American side near the Soo, where a large quantity of dredging had to be done. But why was place measurement adopted ? Because it was a new channel, and nearly the whole area was through where the water was to run for the first time and the work was practically in plain sight. There is no contractor who would not prefer place measurement in excavating if he could get it. A contractor

never gets better fair play than when he has the work where he has an opportunity to see by his own assistants that he gets paid for what he does actually move. The hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) says this is a new policy which comes to us from the east. Well, the wise men are said to have come from the east. But I must say, at the same time, this is not a new policy. The same criticism was levelled by the hon. member for East Simcoe and some other hon. members on that side in 1904 against the Minister of Public Works of that time and on pretty much the same ground, concerning work at Port Arthur and Fort William what they alleged was let without tender upon much the same ground as in this case. The minister of that time decided that as the work had been let under terms of competition in the first instance, and as the work was in part for bringing the harbour down to a certain depth and making slips in new places to the harbour line where elevators and other constructions had gone up in the meantime, this was a class of work for which he could not well get a tender. The work was done, not at the price of 33 cents, as the hon. member said, nor at 23 cents. But the basis of the contract as a whole was 15 cents, not 33 cents. The hon. member for East Grey must have a very short memory, because within the last year I went over this whole matter in detail. I had before me the return brought down to this House and I gave the facts in the case, and they were these : that fully 75 per cent of the entire yardage was on the basis of the contract price, 15 cents, and that the only case in which higher prices were paid was in the case I referred to-where there was the removing of an old structure such as a dock, and the making of certain slips into the harbour line, in order to facilitate the transportation of grain from that particular harbour. Now it is not fair to revive these statements which are without foundation in fact, which have been over and over again contradicted. The hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) made these statements this afternoon. He has no facts, he never did have facts, and cannot produce a single fact to warrant that statement. I think perhaps the hon. gentleman should not have made that statement.
Now, let me say a word with regard to the question that has been raised this afternoon, that of deepening the harbour. The hon. member for Grey says that there is no emergency, no hurry, no occasion for the government to move to deepen the harbour. I would recommend the hon. member to inform himself. Eet him inquire from his own friends, I will give him the name of one of his own friends in the town of Port Arthur, a good Conservative, Mr. J. J. O'Connor. He is shipping agent for the elevators at that point, and he told me only
a short time ago that for many years they have been under a great disability in the harbours of Port Hope, Port Arthur and Fort William, for the reason that they could not get the same charter prices that the shipper from Duluth got, and that even last year they were at a disadvantage of from one-eighth to one-quarter of a cent per bushel ; they had to pay that much more than the man at Duluth would have to pay for shipping his grain to Buffalo or New York.

The hon. member entirely misunderstood me. X did not speak of Port Arthur at all, I was speaking of Victoria or Midland, and showing that there was no great urgency to give a contract now to provide for ships that would draw a mueh greater draught of water than they do now, because they could not get through the Sault Ste. Marie canal until it was deepened there, and that would take some years.

He did say that, and he said more. I.et me inform the hon. gentleman that I am advised on good authority that the Sault Ste. Marie canal will have a depth of 24) feet and will be completed inside of two years. It is only a few months ago that I was discussing that question with an engineer employed on that canal, and he told me that he had prepared plans and submitted them, to deepen the water to 25 feet, and he felt quite confident that the canal when it was completed would have a depth of 25 feet. But I am pointing out what our difficulty has been for the last four or five years. I am sure lie will find that all our Canadian shippers of grain find that all our Canadian shippers of grain through Canadian channels have been placed at a disadvantage of a quarter of a a cent a bushel up to last year. There was some slight decrease within the last few years because of the further improvement of the harbours of Port Arthur and Fort William. But we are still at a great disadvantage. You cannot charter a vessel and get the same prices as the American shipper. There is another disadvantage which militates against the Canadian shipper of grain which is mostly as bad, and it is this : If he wires for a charter for a cargo his offer will not be taken if the vessel owner can get a cargo from either Superior or Duluth. The American boat will go to the port where they have 25 feet of water today, and where they have had it for some time. The Americans have spent $5,000,000 on the harbour at Duluth. The minister has told us here to-day, and I am glad to hear it, that if Canadian shippers of grain are to be put upon equal footing with the American shippers of grain or other products they should have the same facilities, the same advantages in our harbour that the Americans have on their side of the line. Now I submit that we cannot have all these

things at once. Even if the hon. member's statement was true that the American canal would not be completed for four or five years, that would not diminish the urgency or change the responsibility of the government to relieve the Canadian shipper of the disadvantages under which he is placed today. There is a little more than the question of the depth of water in the new American lock. On our side to-day we have 21 feet of water on the mitre sill. Our harbours ought to be put in a state to enable us to enjoy the advantages of our own canal at the Soo, but they are not. Now. hon. gentleman will find when they discuss the subject with captains or gentlemen acquainted with navigation, that they cannot navigate a vessel drawing 21 feet of water in either one of those harbours. They can get her through with a tug, and that is a consideration. But she cannot go under her own steam into those harbours if she is drawing 21 feet of water, because that class of vessel must have more than one foot of water under her keel in order to steer her own machinery. She could not lay at anchor in our harbours, even if she did get into them as she would pound on the bottom. She cannot take part of her cargo at one elevator and the rest at another, as is often done, to take a certain grade of wheat. It has to be taken from a certain class of grain and from more than one elevator. They have frequently to go to more elevators to finish their load. Now in the harbour of Superior or Duluth they can go drawing two feet, perhaps more, of water, and they do not need to trim, and that makes a great difference in the cost. So all these things militate against the Canadian shipper and place him at a disadvantage from which this government should relieve him at the very earliest possible moment. It is important that the government should take the ground that all work from this date should be done on the new basis. The hon. gentleman knows that to cut out two or three feet from the bottom will be a very costly undertaking. The prices will be very much higher, and if we are to be ready within two, or three, or four years to meet the traffic up and down on the same footing as the American shipper, why. Sir, we ought to get to work at the earliest possible moment. There ought to be no hesitation in undertaking a work so meritorious m the public interest.
I am not going to discuss the resolution itself, that has been done by others. But I will point out that there are cases where it is in the public interest that contracts of this nature should be treated just as this contract has been treated. Let me say here that it is a mistaken policy to undertake to ask tenders for this class of work every year. It is a policy that entails largely increased cost. Let me give a case in point.

In 1904, the Minister of Railway and Canals asked for tenders, to be closed on April 15. The hon. member for East Simeoe (Mr. Bennett) raised some objection. He thought that it was going to be an advantage to some dredging company on account of navigation being closed and he asked that the time be extended. I have heard the statement and I have seen it in the Conservative press that the minister resisted the request for an extension of time. It is not true. The minister did not resist an extension of time. He said very plainly that no objection had been made, he consented at once to make a change and he did make the change. The hon. member for East Simeoe and, I think, the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) this evening said that the price of dredging had been brought down by reason of this action. I took occasion last year to make some remarks on this subject and these will be found in ' Hansard.' I went into the matter fully in detail and explained how this reduction in the cost of dredging occurred. Hon. gentlemen opposite have claimed that it was due to the extension of the time from April 15 to first of May. I want to ask if any hon. gentleman thinks than any condition of ice in the harbour of Fort William or Port Arthur between these dates would make any difference to a contractor. The contractor does not tender because there is ice in the horbour or because there is no ice in the harbour. He tenders upon the estimates, plans and representations as to the character of the work and specifications of the engineer, which he submitted to him in that regard. The hon. member for East Simeoe in a speech last year stated that the opposition kept hammering away at the minister and that the result was that the new companies came to the front and that the Weddell Dredging Company brought down the price. I heard the hon. gentleman make the assertion that he had never made a statement in connection with dredging that -was not founded on fact. That assertion is absolutely wrong. There was not a word of truth in his statement as to the cause that had brought down the price of dredging. The Weddell Dredging Company did not tender in that year in which the extension of time was asked for.
I could go on and show that of the statements which this hon. gentleman made 90 or 95 per cent were absolutely without any foundation whatever. To use the words of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) they were reeking with falsehood. But, I am not going to dwell upon this subject. If you strip it of the misrepresentation and slander which has been levelled at the government in connection with these contracts there will be nothing to find fault with. The work which was done in 1904 was open to public competition. The prices in 1904 were actually higher on the average than in 1903. What did bring down the

price? I have made that matter plain. I will make a statement again because I think it might very well be impressed upon the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite and I hope they will retain it in their memory this time. The work that was being done in 1903-4 was redredging, in a very large measure, a portion of the harbour that had been dredged years before, bringing it down to a uniform level, including some widening, which, of course, would be fairly good excavating. It involved a haul of over twelve miles in some cases and would any reasonable man say that class of work could be done for the same figure that you could do work in a heavy cutting where there was a face twenty or more feet or even twelve feet in extent and where there was not half the distance to haul ? That was the condition at Fort William. The work that is being done there now is being done altogether in another harbour, you may say. The river divides itself iuto three branches about two miles from the point where it empties into the bay. On the west branch is the Canadian Pacific Railway terminal, on the mission or southern branch is the Grand Trunk Pacific terminal. This is the harbour in which the work is being done for 9 cents a yard and it is a different class of work altogether. That is one of the cases that brought down the price. It is dredging largely in sand, silt, boulders and clay. I will give hon. gentlemen some further reasons for the reduction in the price.
Nine cents does not include boulders.

I think there is a higher price for boulders and solid rock. The contract provides that solid rock shall be paid for by measurement in situ. There is some solid rock in the harbour I do not know that any of it has been excavated. I will just refer for a moment to what really brought down this price, or influenced it very greatly. In 1904, tenders were asked for and the hon. member for East Simcoe claims that his objection and action caused the extension of time that resulted in bringing down the price and I am going to give a stronger reason. In discussing this question in 1904, the then Minister of Public Works said that :
The tenders that are invited are simply for the present season's work.
I (recognize that there is a very large amount of work to be done at Port Arthur. I hope that the officers of the department will be able to make a thorough survey of the whole work there, allowing time to advertise for tenders for work extending over two or three years, in which case there is no doubt that the cost of the work could be materially decreased for the reason that proper and up to date plant could then be supplied. At the present time the plants that are being used are not of the latest type of dredging plants. The dredging that has been called for is for the present season's work, but I understand that before we reach another season the department will ask for tenders for a more extensive work and giving sufficient length of time to enable those tendering for the work to provide plant to do it at the least possible cost.
That is the measure that brought down the price. Let me point out that to successfully compete for work of this kind involving many millions would necessitate the securing of a plant of very large dimensions costing in the neighbourhood of half a million dollars. Is it reasonable to suppose that auy contractor would undertake to make that expenditure for a single season's work of five and a half months and run the risk of being cut out at the end of the season. The present method of letting a contract for a period of years covering a certain area within this harbour is the reason that the price has been brought down, and the reason is not that which hon. gentlemen opposite have undertaken to assign to it. When I was listening this afternoon to the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Haggart) telling us that there should be no nepotism and no favouritism, and that public matters should be transacted above suspicion, I must say that I quite agree with him, but what surprised me was that such professions should come from a member of the late Conservative government which was not only corrupt speaking generally, and which not only had a number of grafters around it, but was rotten 'at the very head. We have the word of one of its own members that it was a nest of traitors, and the hon. member (Mr. Haggart) was one of the nest. I desire to say a word or two before this debate closes because of some statements which were made by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) and in the course of which I am sorry to say he endeavoured wilfully to mislead the House. The hon. gentleman held in his hand a statement from which he purported to read a list of tenders for dredging contracts during the last year and he repeatedly called out the name of the Stewart Company. There is no such company as the Stewart Company and nobody knows that better than the member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) and the member for Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) who also used the expression. But, it would appear that these hon. gentlemen wished to endeavour by insinuation or by any other means to cause it to be believed that supporters of the government are endeavouring to make money wrongfully. As the hon. member for East Simcoe has been good enough to use my name repeatedly in this connection, I want to say to the members of this House that I have no interest whatever in the Dominion Dredging Company, that I never had any interest in the Dominion Dredging Company to the extent of one farthing, that my influence as a member of parliament has never been used on behalf of the Dominion Dredging Company, that I have never spoken to the Minister of Public Works or to any other minister or to an official of the Public Works Department, or to any official of any other department regarding the business or the tenders of the Dominion Dredging Company. I want to make that statement clear so that hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House may have no wrong impression about the matter. I am afraid that some members on the opposite side are too apt to measure others by what they would likely do themselves if they were placed in similar circumstances, when no doubt their influence would be exercised on behalf of those in whom they might be interested. I do not know that I need say any more on this question. I do not know that it is any crime that the Dominion Dredging Company should tender in competition with other firms for work under this government or any other government. I happen to have a son who is a member of that company, and I do not know that that is any crime either. My son in that firm is only one of a number of honourable men in connection with it ; men just as honourable, if not more so than those gentlemen on the opposite side of the House who have thought fit to refer to this matter on several occasions. Further I have nothing to say.
But I would like to ask while on my feet why it is that when a number of companies containing some very active friends of the opposition in this House are tendering every year for similar work, only those composed of men who are suspected of being supporters of this government are singled out for. attack in this way. There are other dredging contractors, one of them a Conservative candidate for this House. Why is it that we never hear these men accused of doing anything dishonest in securing contracts, or attempting to secure them at higher prices than they should get ? It seems strange to me, sitting in this House and listening to the speeches of hon. gentlemen opposite, that two or three companies should be singled out and referred to as if they were dishonest. I want to ask these hon. gentlemen who have mentioned the name of the Dominion Dredging Company, to state where that company ever got a contract from this government or from any other government that was not put up to public competition. I know very little about the business of that company. I happened to be in England last year when they received their contract, so that it cannot be said that I used my influence in that case on their behalf. It cannot be said truthfully that I ever used my influence on behalf of that company. Is it fair for hon. gentlemen opposite to be continually attacking a company because a son of a member of this House happens to be a member of It ? I challenge hon. gentlemen opposite to point to any dishonest act ever committed by that company, or to any contract they ever received for which their price was not the lowest. That company have never received any favour at the hands of the Minister of

Public Works. I make this statement to show how little ground there is for the assertions continually made by hon. gentlemen opposite in this regard. Perhaps I should not be surprised at the statements of the hon. member for East Simcoe, because we all know his record ; but I remember several years ago, when I was a young member of this House, and questions of this kind were being discussed, the hon. member for East Simcoe contended very strongly that the policy of the Minister of Public Works in asking for tenders was wrong. That policy was that Canadians should do work for Canadians, and that no tender would be received from any tenderer who had not a dredge registered in this country previous to the calling for tenders. The idea expressed by the hon. member for East Simcoe at that time was that in order that there should be the fullest competition tenders should be invited from our neighbours to the south. I can imagine what an outcry would be made by the hon. member for Leeds and the hon. member for East Simcoe if any hon. gentleman on this side of the House made such a suggestion as that. If the hon. member for East Simcoe was correct on that occasion, it ill becomes him, in this House and on public platforms in this city, to make attacks upon myself and upon members of the Dominion Dredging Company. I iiave nothing further to say. I desired simply to put myself right before the members of this House. I have been slow to speak on this question. I am anxious to retain the good will and the good feeling of members of both sides of the House, but when I hear hon. gentlemen speaking as the hon. member for Leeds and the hon. member for East Simcoe both spoke this afternoon repeatedly about the Stewart Company when they knew perfectly well that there was no such company as the Stewart Company, I felt it my duty to make this explanation.

Mr. -Speaker, .1 expected to commence the discussion of this question at the opening of the sitting this afternoon and it seems to me that when a member intends to bring up any other matter than the subject before the House, as has been done to-day, common courtesy towards the other members would prompt him to notify those who

expect to participate in the discussion of the subject set down for debate. This was not done this afternoon, and after the hot air we have heard to-day I shall try to talk business. I wish to deal with this question of immigration not as a party question but as a business proposition and to show why I and those whom I represent are opposed to the bonus system. I do not blame the government for having granted bonuses at the outset, as it may have been necessary at the time the law came into force to induce immigrants of the farming class to go to the Northwest. I admit that something had to be done to encourage this class of immigration. But the bonuses have been diverted to other classes and I am sorry to say that the system has opened the door to speculation. It would seem that there is ground enough for speculating without speculating in human flesh as has been done in in any instances. During a previous discussion it was shown that misrepresentations have been made for the purpose of securing the bonuses on immigrants. The bonus system has opened the door and permitted the Canadian Manufacturers Association to flood the labour market. It has been the means of furnishing to unscrupulous agents the opportunity to take advantage of the laws and has brought to our cities more sufferers and more beggars. It has also enabled land speculators to realize large profits. It has even induced charitable institutions, church societies and the Salvation Army to step in and organize on a solid basis, all for one sole aim and object, the making of money no matter how. I am willing to grant the right to any one to make all he can but I do not grant the right to speculate on the good will of the poorer classes of people who are ready at the slightest suggestion to go anywhere in order to better their position, but who do not desire to replace their fellow workmen, so as to force them to starve or become undesirable citizens.
It would seem that the time has arrived when the flow of population to Canada is so numerous and Canada is so well known that bonuses are no longer necessary. While by that system we have induced a large number of farm hands to come to the western provinces, we have also succeeded in overflowing the labour market in all large cities of Canada. Has any one derived any benefit from this overflow? Some one will say yes, the merchants have, the industries as a whole. The manufacturers may have added for a time to their output and their profits, believing as usual that the temporary increase will be permanent and believing also that such an influx of population would be the means of crushing down labour as I have heard some eminent men say. Such men declare that they are friends of labour and of society. Are those who through the bonus system have thus brought these people to Canada ready to support the whole
or part of the army of men who are crying for bread throughout the country ? Of course not. Why ? Because it is' a business proposition for them, it is a money making affair and why should we any longer pay to induce men to come to our country? We may have to pay as much as we have paid in bonuses to return certain classes to the countries from which they came.
But it may be said, we have amended the law with respect to immigration. So we have, we have spread literature throughout England and the old country calculated to lirevent skilled labour and mechanics from coming to Canada. I acknowledge that the government have done this but other powerful bodies have taken upon themselves to do the unjustified work that some of the government agents were doing some time ago. It may be said that we have good booking agents and their instructions are to be very severe so as to prevent others than those specified in the law as being subjects for bonuses from coming to Canada. Under our present system it is impossible to prevent any one who chooses to bring out undesirable immigrants from doing so. We may have to pay $5 a head on classes of people whom we do not desire. Is it possible to prevent any one from saying : I am going to Canada to work on a farm or in such other work as would bring me under the bonus system ? It has been done, and is done every day, but it is wrong. They know that some men living on the other side-and we heard this last night- have only to say: I am going to Canada to work on a farm. I also asked some of these men who came there what they had to respond and they told me that they had been advised, that, if asked, all they had to do wras to reply that they were coming to work on a farm in Canada. Are we to believe the booking agents on the other side are not up to date ? Are we to believe that they are not looking for a dollar ? Do we not know that the institutions I have mentioned are open for business the same as anybody else ?
But we are asked : What about the construction of our great railways which must be built and for which we must have hands? I acknowledge that we must have men for these railways. But the work on railway construction generally lasts about seven to seven and a half months, as the work is paralyzed by the weather during the rest of the year. Well, are these men supposed to earn enough during the summer to keep them all winter ? Will any hon. gentleman who happens to be a railway contractor say that that is the case? Of course, there is always the same answer-they can find work in the cities. Well, have they found any this winter? Have not we seen in the newspapers that in all the large cities hundreds and thousands of men are walking the streets or waiting at the doors of the city halls begging for bread? Would it not be

lions of Britain's overflowing population.
It says :
Land settlement and cultivation is the way to prosperity in Canada. As the land is cultivated, so the demand for mechanics and skilled tradesmen of an active -and enterprising turn of mind will increase.
They are advising people to come and they are holding out inducements to mechanics and skilled tradesmen. It has been said that that is not the class of people that we are trying to induce to immigrate. I will acknowledge that the effort of the government is not directed to bringing about the immigration of skilled mechanics but still this organization holds out inducements to skilled mechanics in literature of this kind. I also have a little booklet entitled * Canada in a Nutshell.' This has been circulated all over Great Britain and on the back of it is pasted a little piece of paper on which is printed:
The Salvation Army emigration office in London is specially recognized by the government of the Dominion of Canada.
On the lower part of the title page it is stated that it is ' Issued by the authority of the Minister of the Interior, Ottawa, Canada.' That is a sample of the literature that is being circulated to induce people to come to Canada. It is impossible, whether it be the Salvation Army or anybody else, when it is made a matter of business, to entirely disassociate this movement from the monetary consideration. If I were in England and if I were placed in the same position I have not doubt that I would do the same thing. I would look upon every man who left for Canada in the light of the $5 that would go into my pocket and the Salvation Army and every other organization of this kind are doing the same thing.
There is also another feature of this question which I desire to bring before the House and which may have come to the notice of some hon. members. It will be remembered that there was a strike in the coal mines in the province of Nova Scotia. That has nothing to do with what I have just mentioned, but it emphasizes the claim which I make that misrepresentation is resorted to by people in Great Britain for the sake of the bonus. That shows that while the coal mines in Nova Scotia were far from wanting men, representations of this kind were made in order to obtain the bonus, and it also shows that the government, while paying this bonus, has no control over the class of immigrants which are induced to come to Canada through agencies of this kind. We may say, as it was said yesterday, that the policy of the government is not to grant aid to immigration, but if it does not do it directly it does it in an indirect way. It gives the money to one to give to another which is exactly the same thing in the end as far as I can see. It goes to a third party instead of going direct to the immigrant himself.' The immigrant does not get it but he is induced to come here by the money granted by way of bonus. I have some documents here that have a special bearing on the subject and which are of late date, but at this hour I shall not trouble the House by reading them all. I should like, however, while discussing this question of misrepresentation to direct the attention of the House to a resolution passed by the Montreal District Council of the United Brotherhood of Carpenters and Joiners of America. It is as follows:
Montreal, January 27, 1908. Resolution presented by Messrs. J. Hibbins and J. Gauthier, and adopted:
Whereas, the present condition of the labour market is most deplorable, owing to its being continually augmented by unscrupulous builders' exchanges, manufacturers' associations, private companies and individuals, or their agents, who take every means in their power to -obtain the country's money, and therewith negotiate with church homes, self-help societies, and more especially with the members of the Salvation Army to bring to- this country at so much per head, anybody without regard to their fitness or the country's good, the main object being of course, for the prow tit obtained, which quite often results in adding to the ranks of the incompetents, and also to the criminal classes, thereby lowering the standard of both living and the active population.	.	,
We note particularly that which is carried on under assumed religious auspices as being the most pernicious and misleading. And, furthermore, that not wdthin the writer's knowledge has there ever been a real scarcity of labour, but many depressions, especially during the winter months, which make the present conditions most reprehensible. And, while we do not propose to discuss who is the

most to blame, as the guilty parties everywhere are now doing, the results which must fall so heavy on all labour, make us resolve that we immediately withdraw both our support and influence from any and every member, of the federal or provincial parliament, or member of any municipal body, who does not immediately seek every means to stop one cent more of the country's money being subscribed in any form or manner for assisted immigration purposes, the whole of which is unnecessary and unwarranted.
Therefore, be it resolved, that the vote of this District Council of Carpenters be sent to our labour member, and also to the Minis-* ter of Labour, without delay, in order that a repetition of such a state of affairs will not be.
I will conclude by stating that instead of paying bonuses, instead of opening the door to speculation and encouraging the operations of unscrupulous agents, it would be of greater benefit to the country if we simply allowed our successful settlers in the west to act as our immigration agents. I claim that as long as we continue to pay these bonuses we will not achieve satisfactory results and we will not get the class of people in this country that we desire. I do not wish it to be understood that I am opposed to immigration, but I am opposed to the government offering inducements to bring to Canada an undesirable class. The country is well known, it is the promised land, everybody is looking to Canada and everybody will come. The 75,000, or 2,000,000 people who are walking the streets in England will be only too glad to come over to Canada without the payment of this $5 bonus. This is my position, and I may say that this is the expression of the views of organized labour not only in the city of Montreal but throughout Canada from Victoria to Halifax. I speak here to-night not merely as the member for my own riding, but I speak as representing the organized labour of Canada from ocean to ocean.

The hon. member (Mr. Monk) by whom this resolution was presented to the House, made many comparisons as between the present immigration policy of Canada and the present immigration policy of the United States. Lord Strathcona in a letter of date November 15, 1900. written to the Hon. Clifford Sifton, then Minister of the Interior, gave an illustration of the differences that exist between the conditions in the United States and the conditions in Canada, and he set forth many important reasons why it is necessary for us in Canada to make more strenuous efforts to obtain immigration than is the case with regard to the United States. Lord Strathcona wrote :
On the other hand the United States have been working for many years on the continent and had the advantage of direct steamship communication which we did not and do not now enjoy to any great extent, and in consequence they were able to attract a larger
population which yearly drew more and more people to it. There is no immigration agent so potent as the successful emigrant; besides they secured the great bulk of their people before we were in a position to offer prairie land to any extent to immigrants to Canada and in times that were less prosperous than those of recent years.
It seems to me that with hundreds of thousands of acres of fertile land in our Canadian west that are to-day unoccupied, untilled and unproductive, we do require a large number of immigrants. We require immigrants to till that soil and to make it produce so as to add to the wealth of this Canada of ours. And not only to add to the wealth of our country directly by making that fertile soil produce crops that will give us wealth, but indirectly that it may give to the manufacturers of eastern Canada, as immigration to the west has done in recent years, added markets for the output of their factories. I think, Sir, that in connection with our immigration we may direct our energy with great profit to bringing to this country desirable immigrants for the cultivation of that western land, and we cannot bring desirable immigrants for that purpose in any too great numbers. On the other hand I think we may direct our energy to keeping out of this country any immigrants who would not make good Canadian citizens. I do not think it is desirable to bring to Canada, at least at present, immigrants who shall enter into competition with the labouring men and mechanics of our cities and towns, and I am pleased to say that it has not been the policy of the present government to induce to come to this country such immigrants as will compete with Canadian workingmen and artisans. I quite realize too that in bringing to this country an immigrant who is physically diseased or who is mentally unsound or who is a moral pervert, we may do more harm than the good we will do by bringing here a dozen men who are physically, mentally and morally sound. I have risen tonight, however, not so much to dicuss the question of immigration in a general way as to direct the attention of the House and of the people of this country to the important part that has been played and is being played to-day in the development of Canada by the German-Canadian settler.
If I occupy a few7 moments of the time of the House in discussing the importance to Canada of the German-Canadian, I think I shall be occupying the time of parliament in a manner in which it has not been occupied before in the history of Canada. When I speak of the German settler in Canada, I speak of him as I have met him and known Jiim in my own province of Ontario. I know7 that the German settler in Canada has not played the very important part in the discovery of the country and in the laying of the foundations of the country that has been played by our French Cana-

dian friends ; yet I do contend that the German settler in Canada has taken, is taking and is likely to take a much greater part in the development and progress of Canada than most of our Canadian people who have not come into immediate contact with our German Canadian citizens have any idea of. The earliest settlement of German people in the province of Ontario was, I think, in the Niagara peninsula, and there are to-day considerable settlements of German people in the counties of Norfolk, Lincoln and Essex. But the German settlements that have thrived most and that seem to have taken the deepest root in Ontario are the settlements originally formed in the county of Waterloo ancl that have extended into the neighbouring counties. In the year 1800 two Germans named Joseph Sherk and Samuel Betzner, came to the present county of Waterloo and settled near the present village of Doon on the Grand river. They were the first German settlers, and the first prominent white settlers in the county of Waterloo. In the following year, 1801, they were followed by a number of other German families-Bechtels, Kinseys, Ros-enburgers, Biehns and other families of German names and German nationality. These people came from the State of Pennsylvania to what is now the township of Waterloo. The distance from that part of the State of Pennsylvania in which they had their homes to the county of Waterloo was about five hundred miles, which they travelled, not by railway train, for in those days there were no railways, but by horses and wagons, coming over the Alleghany mountains, through swamps and forests, over roads that were bad, and through much country where there were no roads at all. The ingenuity of the German, the manner in which he adapts himself to his circumstances, may be shown by one little instance, that of Joseph Sherk, to whom I have already referred. The first table used in tne county of Waterloo was in the house of Joseph Sherk. It consisted of a pine stump some five feet in diameter, around which this German pioneer built his first rude settler's cabin. The township of Wil-mot in the county cf Waterloo was settled by a society of non-conformists under the leadership of one Christian Naffsiger, who was a Hollander. He left his home in Amsterdam and went to New' Orleans. From New Orleans he journeyed northward to Lancaster County in the State of Pennsylvania. Acting on information and advice given by German friends in Pennsylvania he made his way northwestwardly to the township of Waterloo, to the little German settlement there. Looking about for a tract of land on which to settle German friends he intended to bring to the country, he arranged with the then local government to obtain on easy terms what is now the township of Wilmot. Having concluded his bar-Mr. MILLER.
gain with the local government, he proceeded to Britain where he interviewed George IV, and by the British government the bargain he made with the local government was confirmed. That was in 1822. The township of Woolwich, in the county of Waterloo, was settled in the first place by German people about the year 1810, and German pioneers settled in the township of Wellesley in Waterloo county in 1832. These fertile tracts in Waterloo county, in those early days settled by German people, are occupied by German people to-day, and there is no tract of agricultural land more productive, no matter where it is, within the bounds of Canada, than those German townships of Waterloo county, an no people engaged in agricultural pursuits in Canada that man for man are possessed of greater wealth or have met with greater success than the German people who occupy and cultivate them. The German settlements in Waterloo county extended in later years to the adjoining counties, so that we now have very considerable German settlements in thfe counties of Perth, Wellington, Huron, Oxford, Bruce and Grey, and there are no men in the Dominion of Canada who have made better settlers than these German people, whose names are rarely found on the lists of our courts and are seldom or never seen in any of our police records. The German as we find him in Canada is naturally a religious man, and the German citizens of Canada are probably the most faithful church attendants of any of our Canadian citizens. In Germany the people were for the most part members of either the Roman Catholic or the Lutheran Church ; but in Canada we have German people belonging to the Roman Catholic Church, the Lutheran Church, the Evangelical Association, whose people are commonly known as German Methodists, the Baptist Church, the Mennonite Church aud some to the Presbyterian Church. The German is a man of domestic habits, fond of his home and of his home life ; and while the German families are not usually so large as those of our French Canadian friends, yet the head of a German household usually rules over a nest in which there are many younglings to be clothed and fed. The German people whatever may be their position in life, whatever may be their possessions or their financial standing, teach their children that honest toil, whether of muscle or brain, is no disgrace. The German people are brought up to work, and they all work, and are characteristically industrious. It is supposed by a great many people who do not know them so well as i do that the German, as we have him in Canada, is addicted to the excessive use of strong drink. This is an erroneous idea ; in fact, the very reverse is the case. He is usually a sober man. Perhaps a very small percentage nf the German population would be in favour of a prohibitory liquor

law ; not a very large percentage of them may be classed as total abstainers ; many of them drink moderately of their liquors of lighter brew ; yet they are a sober people, and the German communities in Canada will be found to contain a much smaller number of men who are addicted to the the immoderate use of strong drink than will be found in a community of Irish Canadians or Scotch Canadians, or English Canadians.
I will not say that the German farmer is the best farmer we have in Canada. If I should say that my friend behind me (Mr. McKenzie) the chairman of the Agricultural Committee would perhaps call my attention to the Scotch farmers in this country and there are other members who would point out the excellencies of the English farmer and the Irish Canadian farmer. While it would not be correct to say that the German in Canada is the best farmer we have, I may correctly and truthfully say that we have no better farmers in Canada than the Germans. One characteristic of the German farmer is that he will not settle upon poor soil. He may settle upon a farm that is out of order, that will require a great deal of labour to make it a comfortable home, but he will see to it that he will settle on a soil that by his own hard work he can convert into a good, productive farm. The German will prefer to settle on a piece of good land and struggle to pay off a large mortgage to taking a piece of poor and unproductive land without the debt. As I have said, the German, whether upon a farm or wherever else he may be found, is industrious, thrifty and economical and usually succeeds.
But if our German Canadian succeeds as a farmer he succeeds in no less degree as a manufacturer. It seems to me that the German is naturally a man of mechanical ingenuity, that he is naturally a mechanic and, therefore, in that tract of Ontario through which more than a century ago the German pioneers either followed or created a blazed trail to guide them in their way through the Canadian foi'est, they now' have large busy, thriving, manufacturing centres. The chief of these German manufacturing centre; in Ontario is the busy town of Berlin in the county of Waterloo. A directory published in 1846 described Berlin as being a village of 400 people, principally Germans. Now' the town of Berlin, in place of a population of 400, has a population of 12,000 people ; but as they were in 1846 so they are in 1908. principally Germans. In that busy German town that to day prefers to be the largest town rather than the smallest and youngest city in Canada, you will find a greater variety of manufacturing industries than in any other tow'n of similar size in Canada. They manufacture every thing from a button to a piano, a traction engine or a threshing machine. A peculiar 217
thing about these German manufacturing industries is that they were not established by the aid or assistance of large municipal grants. They were not established by men who went into these German manufacturing towns w'ith large capital, but are rather the outgrowth of the business of men who began in a very small way. As an instance of that, I may say that there is to-day in Berlin a large and successful boot and shoe factory, and the man who to-day controls that successful boot and shoe manufacturing business began his career as a boot and shoe manufacturer in Berlin by making slippers by hand, aud the market for his slippers was found by his good wife who sold them on the streets of the town from a basket w'hich she carried on her arm. Very close to Berlin is the other German manufacturing town of Waterloo, with a population about half that of Berlin. As an evidence of the success of the manufacturing industries of the town of Waterloo, I may say that I do not think there is any other tow'n of its size in Ontario that pays such a large annual revenue into the treasury of Canada by its excise and customs duties. In the county of Waterloo there are also the thriving manufacturing towns of Preston, Hespeler and Elmira. In my own county of Grey, we have the busy, live German manufacturing towns of Hanover, N'eustadt and Ayton. In Hanover we have the German names of Knechtel, Peppier and Messinger among our manufacturers. Our town is supported almost entirely by manufactories and they are almost altogether in the control of German citizens or men who have learned their trade and acquired their business knoweldge in the offices and factories of German Canadians. As another instance of the manner in which German manufacturing industries are built up, let me say that there stands to-day in Hanover an inconspicuous frame dwelling, one and a half storeys high, of small size, that in the beginning of his manufacturing career, was the combined residence and manufacturing establishment of Mr. Daniel Knechtel, who is now the president and chief shareholder of the Knechtel Furniture Company, one of the largest furniture manufacturing companies in Canada having a very large factory in Hanover, another in Wal-kerton and another in Southampton.
In the adjoining county of Bruce, there are the busy manufacturing towns of Ches-ley, Walkerton and Southampton. These towns have all been for years towns of more or less importance, but they have never been busy and progressive towns until in recent years German people have gone into them and established manufacturing industries. I may particularly point out the case of the town of Southampton on Lake Huron, that only a few years ago was a sleepy, quiet fishing village and summer resort; but now by manufacturing in-



dustries in the hands entirely of German people, has become a busy thriving progressive town. In connection with these comparatively small manufacturing German towns let me say they are principally engaged in the manufacture of furniture, and that the furniture manufacturing business of Canada to-day is very largely in the hands of our German people.
One reason why our German manufacturers are so successful is because of their mechanical skill, their enterprise, their economy, their thrift, and their general business ability. But there is another reason why the German manufacturer succeeds as lie does and that is because of the high character of the German workmen whom he employs. There is no better workman engaged, anywhere, than we have in our factories, where the workmen are principally Germans. Amongst them we have no trouble from unions, strikes, or lockouts, and this is largely because the German employee of to-day feels that he is likely to be the employer of to-morrow ; or if he is himself not in the immediate future an employer of la'll our, that at least his sons will be employers, rather than on the payrolls of other taskmasters. Another peculiarity of the German workmen is that the majority of them live in attractive homes of which they are themselves the owners. In connection with these attractive homes of the German workmen, you will almost always find a very neat, well cultivated, carefully tilled fruit and vegetable garden. The German in Canada does not hold quite so tenaciously, it may be, to the use of the language of his fathers as do our French Canadian friends, and yet our German people are fond of the language that is spoken in the Fatherland.
They keep up the use of their language by holding their church services in the tongue of the .old land, oftentimes when it would be quite as convenient to hold those services in English. They also perpetuate the use of the German tongue by forming local associations for the study of that language and also by establishing in various parts of Ontario and the Canadian west newspapers printed in German. Let me say that the various German settlements in Canada are being constantly added to by new arrivals from Germany. And it is astonishing, and very much to the credit of the German people, the readiness with which they acquire at least a speaking knowledge of the English language. The German, too, is fond of music and shilled in it. As an evidence of that musical talent and skill let me say, there are no church choirs anywhere in Canada that are, perhaps, equal to the rtioirs of the German churches whatever their denomination. Their bands and orchestras, too. are the best we have in the country. Any one desiring to enjoy a great musical treat cannot do better than Mr. M11,1.MIt.
attend at Berlin one of the many Sanger-fests that are held in that town. As an evidence of the musical skill of the German, let me read a short extract from the April number of the 1 Busy Man's Magazine,' published in Toronto. This is an article upon Dr. Augustus Stefan Vogt, the now famous leader of the Mendelssohn Choir of Toronto, who was born in the village of Elmira, in the county of Waterloo, and is the son of a German organ builder :
Will Dr. Augustus Stefan Vogt, the brillant leader of the famous Mendelssohn Choir, have the honour of knighthood conferred upon him when birthday honours are distributed by His Majesty on Victoria Day next? Dr. Vogt richly deserves such distinction. He has accomplished more than many a Canadian who has been decorated with a K.C.M.G., and it will not surprise his thousands of friends and admirers if he is soon known as Sir Augustus Vogt. A Canadian who realizes the value of an ideal, he is prepared to make any sacrifices for its accomplishment. All fellow countrymen are proud of him. He has done more in perfecting choral art than apy other person, and has made Canada in this respect envied of all nations.
As financiers, our German Canadian friends excel, and, as an evidence of this, I may say that the towns of Berlin and Waterloo, in the province of Ontario, are the homes of very progressive, popular and successful life insurance and fire insurance companies, the shareholders, directors and managers of which are almost exclusively German people. Let me call the attention of the House also to the fact that the German Canadian excels also as a sport and athlete. We have all heard in recent weeks of Tommy Burns, the world's champion heavy-weight pugilist, who has been chumming with Lord Alverstone in England. Tommy Burns' real name is Noah Brusso. He was born and brought up in my own riding of South Grey and in my own town of Hanover, and is the son of Frederic Brusso, who was a workman in the factory of the Kneehtel Furniture Company of that town.
Leaving the field of sport and going to the higher ground of science, the German in Canada is noted as a scientist, as is the German in his own land. And in evidence of this, it is only necessary for me to call attention to one man, Dr. Otto Klotz, who has been for many years in the employ of this government and is now at the head of its astronomical work. Our German Canadian friends, too, are adapted to public life and have taken an interest in public affairs in Canada. One of the best wardens that my own county ever had was the late Victor Lang, a German Canadian. In the provincial legislature to-day. we have Dr. Lack-mer, member for one of the ridings of Waterloo, Mr. C. M. Bowman, the popular member for North Bruce, whose father, Mr. J. E. Bowman, was at one time a member

of this House, and also Hon. Adam Beck, *who has achieved considerable notoriety and celebrity in Ontario because of the power scheme he has advocated. And, in this House, the German Canadian is well represented. We have the very popular and always industrious member for West Hamilton, Mr. Adam Zimmerman, the very popular and deservedly popular representative of South Waterloo, Mr. G. A. Clare, and also the equally popular representative of North Middlesex, Mr. Valentine Ratz, all of German descent. In the field of law. the German Canadian has held his own and taken a leading part. When I speak of the lawyers in Canada of German descent, I will mention but one, Mr. A. B. Klein, who is one of the county court judges of Bruce. Mr. Klien, who is of German descent, was one of the ablest and most popular lawyers having a country practice in Canada and is not less popular on the bench as one of our Canadian judges. And he showed his loyalty to Canada by the interest he took in the affairs of our militia, having retired from the 32nd Battalion of Bruce with the rank and title of major.
We have large German settlements in every city'in Canada. For instance, there is a large settlement of this nationality in Toronto, and in that city many of our most prominent men are of German extraction, like the Breithaupts and the Heintzmans, who are well known in the business world. There is a large German settlement in Ottawa, and also in Hamilton. There are many Germans in Montreal and also in Winnipeg. We have Germans engaged in agricultural pursuits in considerable numbers in the county of Bussell, Ont., and in part of the province of Quebec and also in Nova Scotia. In fact, there is not a province in Canada in which we have not a considerable number of German settlers.
It will be said that many of these German people came into Canada of their own accord and not as the result of any immigration policy of this government. That is true so far as eastern Canada is concerned. But we have a very large number of German settlers in western Canada who have come to that western country as a direct result of the efforts made by our immigration agencies and our Department of the Interior. The German settlers in the northwestern Canada will make, no doubt, quite as good settlers as did the Germans in the province of Ontario. Had it cost the government of Canada, not $5, or $20, but $10,000 apiece to bring to Canada some of the German people whose names I have mentioned, the investment would have been a good one and one by which we should have very largely profited.
