We have a very large nuin her of Canadian German settlers who came as a direct result, as I have said, of the work of the Department of the Interior and because of the immigration policy of the government of the day. I am very glad that the Department of the Interior has always, under the present government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, shown its appreciation of the value of immigration from Germany. And, in evidence of what the Department of the Interior of the present Liberal government has thought of German immigration and in evidence of its 'appreciation of the German settler, I want to read a sentence from a letter from Mr. Smart, then Deputy Minister of the Interior to Mr. W. T. R. Preston, dated July 18, 1900. He says : ' We are especially anxious to bring persons of German origin.' And, in another letter from Ottawa to Mr. Preston, dated August 26, 1901, Mr. Smart, then deputy minister, acting under instructions from the Minister of the Interior, said :
I will be glad if you will let me know what has been the result of the efforts of the North Atlantic Trading Company in so far as its work in Germany is concerned. I may say that after two years the department is a little disappointed in not seeing greater results from the efforts of the company in Germany and also in Scandinavia. There is no class of people that Canadians are SO' willing to welcome as German settlers, and it seems too bad that some good commencement cannot be made in connection with the people of this nationality. I may add that Mr. Landy, whom I met in Winnipeg, told me a few days ago that it was confidently expected a good many Germans would come to this country, but in order to have authentic information on the subject, I would be pleased if you would communicate with the syndicate which is doing the work.
I was pleased when the present Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) stated to me that there are no settlers that his department welcomes more heartily and considers more satisfactory than the German settlers. I trust that no legitimate effort will be spared, whatever direction that effort may take, to continue the immigration to this country of the German people. I may say that in every respect we have no better people than the German residents of Canada, they make very loyal and in every way very satisfactory Canadians. The German settler as we have him in Canada, when he looks back to the history and traditions of the land from which he came, sings with great enthusiasm that national song of which he is so proud, Die Wacht Am Rhein. And when he looks around upon his home in Canada, and which he expects to be the home of his children, he sings with equal zeal and equal fervour, and with still greater interest, and with true loyalty, ' The Maple Leaf ' and ' God Save the King.'

subtopic: THE BRITISH EMPLOYMENT AGENCY OF CANADA,
speechtext:
The question of immigration which we are

now discussing lies at the very foundation of our national prosperity and greatness, and no more important question could engage our attention. I must say that I think it is much more important than the question which we had intruded here this afternoon. Although I stand on the opposition side of the House, I desire to say right here that I have no sympathy at all with the intrusion into this debate of the question of a little bit of dredging. The character of the immigration that is coming to our country means everything to the future of our country. The subject was brought up in this House by one of the ablest men in it, a man who never speaks on any subject unless he has something of importance to say, a man who can handle a subject properly, and it is much to be regretted that the discussion was interrupted by the break that was made this afternoon. The future and greatness of the country depend on the people who inhabit it. Look at Scotland. Scotland is not a large country, but what other country in the world exercises so great an influence over the world, according to its size and its population, as Scotland? Germany is a wonderful country, and our good friend who has just spoken (Mr. Miller) has told us that the Germans are a wonderful people. They are, and they are exerting a wonderful influence all over the world. Now then what we want to do is to get people of the right kind to come to this country, and so long as they are of the right kind, the country will go on and prosper. I believe that this country will become in due time one of the great nations of the world. Cheap labour, as has been well said toy an lion, member this afternoon, is not everything. You may get in cheap labour, but that will not make the country great. The Americans got in cheap labour in their negro population, but that did not make the country great, and it has been the occasion of the great civil war and the expenditure of millions of money. In the neighbouring republic they have that labour question on their hands, and it is complicated with the race problem, which is one of the most difficult problems that any country could have to face. In the same way we look to British Columbia, and some say that the bringing in of cheap labour from Asia will be a great help to Canada. But I think we can scarcely afford to allow immigration of that sort. These people will not assimilate with our western type of civilization, they will not assimilate with Canadians, and if they did, it would only be to lower the tone of our civilization. At the same time we have nothing against the Japanese, we admire the Japanese, but we don't wish them as immigrants because we caunot assimilate with them. Now then speaking of immigration, it seems to me that too much attention has been paid to settling up the west to the neglect of eastern Canada. It seems to me that the east has been forgotten. Of course we have a great country in the west, and there is no danger but Mr. T. CHISHOLM.
that it will be filled up in time. On the one side, only four or five days journey distant, we have the teeming millions of Europe ; and on the other side, only eight or ten days journey distant, we have the hundreds of millions of Chiua and Japan ; while to the south of us we have eighty millions of people. If we have got a good country the great trouble will be to keep people out of it whom we do not want to come here. For instance, the Doukhobors are occupying land iu the west that we ought to keep for our children and our children's children. To get these people into this country our government have paid $7 a head, besides affording them assistance after they reach here. They occupy the best land in our western country; and I can say now that if they had never set foot in this country that land would now be occupied by good Canadians. On the 7th of June last year I was in the city of Prince Albert, and there were a number of Doukhobor homesteads, discarded homesteads, that the Doukhobors would not have, that were to be opened on that day. These homesteads had been held for the Doukhobors for seven years by the government. They had lived in their villages, and had made no improvements on the land for seven years, and still the homesteads were held for them. If a Canadian boy goes uj) there to get a homestead, if he is not on hand the very minute he should be, he loses his right, but the Doukhobor can hold it for seven years. One of my own Wingham boys went up there, and understanding that, according to the regulations, the first man who was on hand the next morning would get the choice of these five homesteads, he went into the office the night before and made some inquiries, and when the time came to close the office, he was requested to leave. He walked out, but he kept his hand on the door knob all night. I went up the next morning, it was raining, but still the poor fellow had his hand on the door knob. There were four or five hundred people surging around him, his hat was trampled into the mud, the rain was running off his hair, but still he stood there with his hand on the door knob. I was proud of him as a Wingham boy. The result was that he got the first homestead. Now here were 500 good Canadians ready to take these homesteads, and if the Doukhobors had never gone there those 500 Canadians would have taken up those homesteads. These homesteads were held for these Doukhobors for seven years, but a poor boy went up there last year from my riding. You know that we had a very late spring. He went up into Saskatchewan, he got into a half built hut and he took cold, inflammation of the lungs and pleurisy. His father had to go and bring him home, and he was brought to my riding. I went to the land office a little while ago to make some inquiry to see if they would hold his homestead open. He had his side opened three times and a tube put in. I was pre-

sent at one of the operations and the Liberal doctor who is attending him in Brussels sent a letter down to the department and said that the boy had still a tube in his side, and that matter was running out of his side and we asked the time to be extended until after the first of May. What was the reply that we got from the land office?- 'they are not holding homesteads open after the first of May.' This poor fellow is expected to go back and he must go or he will lose his homestead and, of course, if he goes, he may lose his life. How does it come that these Doukhobors could have homesteads held for seven years and a poor boy in my riding cannot have a homestead held for a few months although he'has a tube in his side.
The farmers of Ontario particularly are neglected under our immigration policy. They are very hard up for help. There is a famine of farm labourers in our country; everything is being done for the west and it is draining the east. We have harvest excursions at cheap rates taking away 20,000 of our young men to the west at a time when we need them most. When we get in the so-called farm help we find that the bonus system is bringing in the wrong class of settlers. They do not bring in men from the heather mills whence my own father came nor from the vine clad valley of Germany and France. They bring in men who have been brought tfp in the cities and no matter how foolish you may think a farmer to be when he goes to the city, no matter how many mistakes he may make, they are nothing to the mistakes which will be made by the city man who goes upon the farm. He is far more out of place. It is no use for a man like that to go to one of our farmers and tell him that he has been brought up on a farm in the old country. The farmer will very soon know where lie comes from. I heard a little story the other day about a man who came from Glasgow and who hired out as a farm labourer. The farmer said : Now, Sandy, there is a farmer across the road and he and I are exceedingly good friends. We have an arrangement that if he in any way spoils any of his farm implements he is to have a loan of anything that I have and if we happen to break any of our implements we can go over and get his. If that man comes over and asks for the loan of any farm implements when I am not here, you must give it to him. One day the farmer was away and the neighbour came across and said : ' Sandy, man, have you a plough ? I have broken my plough and I wish to finish my ploughing.' ' Oeh,' said Sandy, ' Ye can ha the pleu. The boss said ye cud ha onything aboot the place bit I dinna ken whaur the pleu is and I dinna ken whether I waud ken a pleu gin I saw ane, Tout there is the wagon and maybe ye can pleu wi' it till the boss comes hame.'
Then I heard another one about a man
who came out to this country who was taken out to the bush to assist a farmer to get out some logs. The farmer said to him : ' John, will you go and get a cant-hook ? John went home and soon brought back a mooly cow because he thought she could not hook because she had no horns and that therefore she must be a cant-hook. I believe that if an effort were made this difficulty would be solved if the minister would give attention to this matter and I am sure he has tried to do the best he could, but he does not understand the situation. The farmers have solved the difficulty of the cheese and bacon question, and I believe that the farm labour question might be solved by going about it in the right way. There is a great difficulty not only in regard to the scarcity of labour, but, since Automobiles have been placed upon the highways, the farmers' daughters and wives cannot go to town and to market. They cannot drive the horses because farmers' horses, being more isolated, are more easily frightened. I have seen farmers in my county with 200 acres of land who would [DOT] have to leave the farm work and drive to town on account of the automobiles. We must get into our country a class of men about whose history we know something, about whose life history we know something. A farmer must take his hired help right into the bosom of his family, to be the companion of his sons, his wife and his daug-ters. We must have the life history of such people. We cannot take every man that you pick up in Whitechapel, or Glasgow, or Dublin. These men may or may not be suitable associates for a farmer's family. We must know them and have their life histories. I propose that the province of Ontario should be divided into districts and that the farmers who wish help should be invited to assemble at some central point during the slack time in the winter. They would give in a list of the labour that they required. One man wants a man with a family because he has bought out his neighbour, he has 200 acres of land and he has acquired a nice brick house with it. There is some man away off in Europe, in Germany, or England or Ireland or Scotland living in a cottage with his family and if that man must come and occupy that house he would think that he was in a palace and the farmer, with 200 acres of land, might give him five or six acres to work for himself and his family. In this way the farmer could get the kind of help that he requires. Another man needs a boy. Each farmer would designate exactly the kind of help that lie required and all these requirements would be written down. Then the farmers assembled together wTould elect one of themselves to go to the old country, hire the help and bring it to Canada. That man would go to the old country and he would say : Here is John Jones; he has a large family and he could occupy that house and culti-

vate a piece of land in connection with it. The man who would actually engage the help in the old country would see the man who had been delegated to go over there and ascertain from him exactly the kind of help that would suit him. If the man who was delegated to do this work did not do it properly the farmers would next year elect another representative. Let the government pay the expenses of these men who would be selected to go over to the old country and engage help. It is not my place to suggest how it should be done.
There is another thing that I desire to say and that is that as a result of the way in which our tariff is regulated the manufacturers enjoy rates so much in excess of those which the farmers enjoy on their products that it is impossible to keep farm labourers on the farm. They drift into the cities because they get work and the farmers are not able to pay them high wages because their products are not protected to the same extent as the products of the manufacturers are.
I regret that many of the immigrants we are getting in this country are not such as are desirable, or as are calculated to build up and strengthen our nation. On the contrary, far too many of them are subjects of charity aud are filling our hospitals and our charitable institutions, and still worse, in some cases they are filling our jails and penitentiaries. I quote from the St. Thomas ' Evening Journal ' of the 11th of April, a good Liberal paper, the following :
Dumped in Ontario is Hon. Mr. Hanna's claim.
Toronto, April 11.-Hon. Mr. Hanna called the attention of the legislature last night to the effect of immigration in the last year or two upon the inmates of the principal institutions. He had just received a telegram from Port Arthur, as follows:
' Port William police magistrate has committed ten male Doukhobors to Central Prison ; nine females to the Mercer Reformatory. They are in jail here. We have no room for them. Fifty-three other prisoners here now. There are fifty-seven other Doukhobors at Fort William to be sent to the Central and the Mercer. They have burned their clothes and are naked.

' Sheriff.'
This was not only a matter of so many more inmates of the jails, but indicated a condition of affairs that must be dealt with, and the responsibility for which placed where it belongs.
Although 80 per cent were native born in the province, the inmates of the ayslums were 30 per cent foreign born.
During 1907 there were 1,162 patients admitted to asylums of the province of whom 316 were foreign born. During the past five years the percentage of foreigners admitted to these institutions had increased from 20 to 30 per cent, while Canadian born patients had decreased from 80 to 70 per cent, in the same period, from 1903 to 1907, the cost of main-Mr. T. CHISHOLM.
tenance of foreign born patients had increased from $21,613.20 to $51,744.30. While the foreign born of the entire adult population were only 20 per cent, the total admission to asylums from that class was 30 per cent.
The figures showed the necessity of effective methods to prevent the dumping on the province of undesirables by friends, and others aided by charitable associations with no other object than to get rid of the responsibility of providing for them. Taking into consideration the probable length of life of these patients, the cost of maintaining those admitted in 1907 alone amount to $1,487,058.80 without including any proportion for capital expenditure.
Of the estimated total population of the province, over 16 years of age, 1,209,308 were Canadians, and 291,675 were foreigners, or 20 per cent of the whole. At the same time, of the commitments to jail, 38 per cent were of foreign birth, and the cost of providing for them amounted to $21,724.65.
Now, that is quite a large sum of money for the province of Ontario to be mulcted in by reason of this undesirable immigration. We should take care that the immigrants who are brought into this country are physically and morally fit to build up our country, and that they are not such as will deteriorate the character of the people with whom they mingle.
The lion, member for South Grey (Mr. Miller) spoke very kindly and very correctly about our German people, and I may be pardoned for following his example and saying a few words about them myself. The German settlers in this country have in every case made model citizens. In southwest Ontario, in Wellington, in Grey, in Bruce, in Huron, in Perth, in Oxford, and in Waterloo we have large German communities, and in these districts the farms are not only clean and well kept, but they are thoroughly and effectively tilled. The homes of the German Canadians are comfortable and commodious and the people honest, moral, respectable and in many cases wealthy. The Germans very easily assimilate with us Canadians because they are practically of our own race. We know that the Saxons of England came originally from Germany, and as a German would say : * Hie Deutche spreehe ist die mutter der Engleschen '-the German language is the mother of the English language. The grammar and construction of the German and English languages are so much alike that even old persons who know the one soon learn the other, which in my opinion accounts in a great measure for the ease with which our German settlers have been able to adapt themselves to the language and customs of this country. Our German settlers are not only industrious and frugal and law-abiding, but in every case they are thoroughly loyal to our King and our country. It appears to be no trouble to them to yield allegiance to the uncle of their emperor, especially when they know that his father, the late lamented Prince Albert, was

a German and that his mother, the good Queen Victoria, was a descendant of the House of Brunswick and of German George
I.	Things are made still more easy for them in this respect when they know that many of the United Empire Loyalists who made great sacrifices when they came to Canada from the United States at the close of the revolutionary war were of Dutch or German origin.
It does not need any bonusing to induce German immigrants to come to this country, because the German people are so thrifty that they always have money to meet their own wants. In my opinion, Sir, we should encourage German immigrants to come to Canada. We Should not only give the German people the glad hand, but we should' strive in some friendly way to remove from' our tariff that odious surtax which the Canadian government is levying against goods coming from the fatherland. I believe that tlie German people/ resent this tax and feel it very strange that their country should be singled out by us for such treatment. I notice here by a report of the Trade and Commerce Department that, while we have trade commissioners in Australia, China, Japan, Corea, France and Mexico, in the German empire, that great manufacturing and food consuming country, there is not a single trade commissioner. Our German friends are scarcely to blame if they feel that the Canadian government is not treating their country with that consideration which I believe it deserves from us.
Now, let me say a few words about the North Atlantic Trading Company, and in that connection I want to refer to the statement frequently made that the Prime Minister offered to give to the leader of the opposition the names of the members of the North Atlantic Trading Company. Let me quote from ' Hansard,' 1906, page 4472, what the Prime Minister said in reference to that:
But, sir, I have in my hands at this moment the names of those gentlemen with whom Mr. Preston, Mr. Smart and the government dealt in 1890. and I am willing confidentially to put those papers
No, no.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am willing eonfidentiallv to put those papers into the hands of the hon. leader of the opposition or of any hon. gentleman he will select.
What names were they ? The names of the gentleman with whom Mr. Preston, Mr. Smart and the government dealt in 1899. According to what I see here, the North Atlantic Trading Company was not in existence at that time, so that it could not have possibly been the members of that company whose names were to be given. Now I quote from a letter contained in the report of the Public Accounts Committee of 1906. written by Lord Strathcona to Mr. Smart, in which letter he says :
Inclosed with this letter you will find a copy of the certificate of registration of the North Atlantic Trading Company, Limited, dated at Greffe, Guernsey, the 11th day of June, 1905, together with a copy of the memorandum and articles of association of the same company, dated the 3rd June, 1905.
Now, how can any person make out that an effort was made to give the names of the members of the North Atlantic Trading Company five years before such a company existed ? Another point is this : I notice in ' Hansard ' of the 2nd of April of the present year that a member stated :
Lord Strathcona sent a man by the name of Charles A. Allen to Amsterdam to get these names. He felt that there was great demand in the public mind of Canada to know those names, and so he sent a special messenger over there for the purpose. And this is what he sent back to Lord Strathcona, dated June 5, 1906:
Just received letter from company, as follows : begins, very utmost we are able to do is to allow Mr. Preston to show names to Premier, Hon. Mr. Fielding, and if absolutely necessary also to only one Liberal and only one Conservative member of confidential committee, on condition that they each give a sworn declaration in writing never to mention names either verbally or in any other way and on condition that Premier takes full responsibility that these sworn declarations are kept, as disclosing names would result in some prominent members committing suicide.
Now, suppose our leader had been given those names-not, mind you, the names of the members of the North Atlantic Trading Company, but those of the gentlemen with whom these other gentlemen had dealt five or six years before-lie would have been sworn to secrecy. He dare not tell us that he had been trapped and misled, and we would have all been sitting here like boobies behind him, knowing nothing about it. I deny that the names of the members of the North Atlantic Trading Company were ever offered to the leader of the opposition, If they were, I do not understand the English language as I read it in ' Hansard '. Another thing : These men mentioned as having done business with Mr. Smart and Mr. Preston and the government in 1899, Mr. Smart himself, in his evidence, stated positively were only in business a few months. Therefore they were out of business for five years before the North Atlantic Trading Company came into existence at all; so that I either misunderstand the English language very much or there is some great mistake.	.

This Bill was not reported as amended, but it was reported as amalgamated with another Bill. Then I take up the Order Paper of March 19, and I find a government notice of motion appearing in this way :

I am sorry to take up the time of the House at this stage of the session, but I shall be as brief as possible. I am sorry also that the government did not see fit to consent to a discussion of the question without any reservation. On the 13th of this month, I put the following questions to the government :
1.	Is the government informed that chapters 2 and 25 of the statutes of the province of Saskatchewan, 1907, intituled, respectively, ' An Act for raising money on the credit of general revenue fund of Saskatchewan/ and
' An Act to provide for the organization and maintenance of secondary educational institutions/ contain provisions contrary to the educational clause of the law of Autonomy for the province of Saskatchewan, 1907?
2.	Does the government know that the delay for the disavowal of these laws expires the 22nd April next?
3.	Will the government disallow these statutes ?
To this the hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) replied as follows :
To question 1, no ; to question 2, yes ; to question 3, no.
I do not think that the Minister of Justice, in the whole course of his political career, was ever so clear or so brief. If I analyse these replies, I find that the government, in the first place, did not know whether these statutes were illegal or not, a'nd, in the second place, would not in either event disallow them. These statutes might be ultra vires or iutra vires, the province of Saskatchewan might have the right to pass them or not, this government would not take the trouble to inform itself and bad no intention of disallowing them.
They did not care.

That is what it amounts to practically. We have had the right hon. the first Minister of Justice telling us that these statutes had been passed a considerable time ago and bad never been brought to the attention of parliament and that consequently there was no urgency. Well, I am not the Minister of Justice-and at times I am sorry for the minority in the House and the country- but the moment the matter was brought to my notice 1 took the trouble to look up the statutes and find out whether they were

illegal or not. It seems to me rather strange that when a member of the Catholic minority, which comprises about 41 per cent of the total population of the Dominion, puts a question concerning the most sacred interests of that minority and even the rights of this parliament, which passed the law giving the province of Saskatchewan its autonomy, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) does not take the trouble to consider whether the statutes passed by that province are in contravention of that autonomy law and consequently should be disallowed. But on the other hand, if a province in the west thinks fit by statute to exclude from its own limits Asiatic immigration and determines to remain a white man's country, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) has no hesitation in disallowing any such law without waiting for any one to put him a question regarding it in parliament. More than that, the correspondence brought down with reference to the Japanese treaty shows that the government promised the Japanese consul that they would disallow the laws of British Columbia even before they were passed, when they had simply been mentioned in the speech from the Throne. Thus, the situation is that it has come to pass that 40 per cent of the Canadian nation are less in the estimation of the government than a few Japanese yellow citizens who are coming to this country against the will of a whole province.
Were these statutes ultra vires? Of course it is not my place to answer and I shall not attempt to give a definite answer; it would be for tile Minister of Justice to state whether they were or not. He did not think it expedient to answer the question or necessary to examine the statutes; he was prepared to disallow them without even knowing what they contained. He will find that in this case a report has been made to the government of Saskatchewan more than six months ago and it appears that he reported to that government without even knowing what was contained in the statutes. As I have said I do not know, and I would not express a legal opinion as to whether these statutes are or are not illegal. I do know that when the statutes were passed and certain taxes were raised in Saskatchewan, a certain portion of the population, the Roman Catholic taxpayers, refused to pay the taxes imposed under chapter 2 and chapter 25 of the statutes of Saskatchewan. Cases were entered before the courts. The courts did not decide the cases, I think the election of the Attorney General of Saskatchewan took place before the eases were concluded and they were not pushed to a conclusion, somebody paying the fine which was asked from the Catholic taxpayers. Whether the fine was paid by the taxpayers or by friends of the government or by friends of the opposition I do not know and shall not say.

It is certain that, judging from what lias taken place, the minority in Saskatchewan felt that these statutes were infringing on the rights granted to them by the constitution of 1907. If we look at the debate of 1905 on the Autonomy Bill of the Northwest in this House we will find at page 5984, May 15, 1905, the then Minister of Justice (Sir Charles Fitzpatrick) described the privileges left to the minority in the Northwest in this way:
1.	Right of separation-by the ordinance- common to Protestants and Roman Catholics alike;
2.	Half-hour religious instruction-by ordinance-to Protestants and Roman Catholics alike; common to public and separate schools.
He then goes on to describe the rights which are left to the separate schools and says :
4.	Right to elect trustees, who choose the teacher-by ordinance; common to all schools.
It may be objected that the statutes passed by the Saskatchewan legislature concern especially secondary and not primary schools; but I have carefully examined the British North America Act and the statutes of interpretation and find nothing making a difference between schools for primary and for secondary education. By chapter 2 of tile statutes it is provided that the population may be taxed for permanent public improvements authorized by the legislature, after the first day of September, 1905, and by chapter 25 of the statutes of Saskatchewan, we find among these improvements, high schools. The law at first sight appears to permit the high schools to he established without any separation and we see nothing there granting separation to the minority if it wishes it in a public district. You will see also that they have the right to choose all text books, which is contrary to the law of the Dominion passed in 1907. They have also the right to choose trustees and it is enacted that the population may be taxed for the maintenance of their high schools, even if they want to have a separate school of some other kind, and that no municipality can exempt them from those taxes.
Therefore I shall not say that the statutes are unconstitutional, but I may say that they have a strong flavour of being unconstitutional and contrary to the educational clause of the Act passed by this parliament in 1907. The least we should expect from the Minister of Justice was that before stating that he would not disallow these statutes he would have looked into them, would have had a report made upon them and have had the opinion of his officers as to their constitutionalitv. He said before the House that he would not disallow them even without looking at them; so it has come to this that in this country the Catholic minority is considered by the Department
of Justice and this federal government to be less important than the yellow allies who come from the extreme orient. If this is the spirit which is to be maintained in our confederation, I may say that our confederation has seen its best days. It is time that the rights of the minority should be a little more respected and also that when there is some doubt about the rights of the minority or when those rights are placed in jeopardy, the Minister of Justice who is the natural guardian of the rights of minorities should take the trouble to glance over the country and see whether or not the laws of any province are against the rights of the minority, I care not if it is the Catholic minority of the other provinces, or the Protestant minority of the province of Quebec. A thorough examination of these statutes would be only common courtesy on the part of the government towards 41 per cent of the population of Canada. But it is more than that; it is a matter of the future prosperity of our country, because while it may not be the opinion of the entire province of Quebec now, it is the opinion of the entire youth of that province, of the men who are in the colleges and universities and who will come out from them to-morrow or the day after to-morrow. If the confederation is to go on in this way with a superior race and au inferior race, a superior religion and an inferior religion, confederation has seen its best days. The youth of our province are loyal to our confederation but they want it to be remembered in this parliament and in the country that they are a part of the confederation in the terms of equal partnership.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is, Mr. Speaker, upon the minutes, upon ' Hansard,' upon the records there, in answer to a question put by my hon. friend from Nanaimo (Mr. Smith), that in the course of the last ten or twelve years there have been no less than five statutes of the province of British Columbia disallowed, but I am answering to my hon. friend that there has been no disallowance of the statute to which he refers, a statute passed by the legislature of British Columbia within the last few months. On the contrary, that statute was the subject of proceedings in the courts of British Columbia and within the course of a few weeks after it had been assented to was held by the courts of British Columbia to be ultra vires the legislature which had passed it. Under these circumstances the illustration which my hon. friend has selected as the means of showing that there has not been, in his judgment, due attention paid to the interests of the highly important minority for which he purports to speak is, I think, an unfortunate illustration and is certainly one that has no application in so far as i am able to see.
My hon. friend accuses me, and I regret that he should think that there was any cause for the accusation, of some feeling, if I understood him correctly, of illiberality towards that ancient faith to which he gives adherence. Let me remind him that it is only a few days ago, that, across the floor of this House, as I saw next day by ' Hansard,' although I did not hear it at the time, I was accused, as if it were a reproach, that I too had been called a Roman Catholic. I think, under these circumstances, my hon. friend might have spared me the attack which he has made upon me personally and in respect to which I certainly am not aware that I have given to him or to any one the slightest cause.

G- H. BERGERON (Beauharnois). Mr. Speaker, I never thought that the position taken by some of us with regard to the Autonomy Bill a couple of years ago would be vindicated so soon. When the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier) brought down the measure to grant autonomy to the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan there was, in the first instance, incorporated in that measure clause 16 which was in accordance with what we thought to be the constitution of the Northwest Territories as embodied in the statute of 1875, and which gave to the minority of these provinces entire autonomy and the rights and privileges to which they were entitled. But, for reasons best known to himself and which were disclosed to this



House by the retirement of one minister and by the protest of another the right hon. gentleman brought down clause 16, No. 2, which was vague and which could produce no other result than that which we have before us now. There were some other hon. gentlemen who, taking a different position from the one that the right hon. gentleman took, or who did not entirely share his opinion, said that it was better to leave these new provinces free to do whatever they desired to do in the future. They were willing to grant these provinces autonomy, having entire confidence in the judgment which they should exercise in time to come. We, myself and others, who were of my opinion, and who were afraid to leave this question in the hands of the new generations coming into the west, expressed the opinion that it was dangerous and stuck more than ever to clause 16, No. 1, which was a repetition of the statute of 1875. Now, we have proof that the position which we took was the correct one. These things are done with a great deal of cuteness. This is the opening of the door to what will happen later on. The hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) knows very well that it is not a question as to whether it is legal or not. It is a question whether the legislatures of these provinces are acting in the spirit in which this parliament granted autonomy to them. Did we mean to say that the minority in these provinces should be entirely at the mercy of the majority? Did we mean to say that the minority in these provinces should have no power, no rights and no privileges? If we did the law passed by the legislature of Saskatchewan is legal, but it is not according to the spirit of the Autonomy Bill as expressed at the time by the majority in this House. Now, the ministers or the government who do act in that way have a very cunning way of going about it. When my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) and myself happened to be in the west the Liberal organs in the province of Quebec. which are not at all in partnership with truth, said that we had gone to Prince Albert for the sake of influencing the election at a time when the Attorney General of Saskatchewan was seeking election in that part of the province, I being a French Canadian and a Roman Catholic. It was known to those who wanted to know the truth, that there was nothing in that statement. It had been decided weeks and weeks before it was known that there was to be an election that we should have a meeting at Prince Albert on Saturday night. In the meantime the election was announced. The election was on the very same day we were to have our meeting and our friends, without our knowledge, decided that it would be better to have the meeting the night before so as not to interfere with the election taking place next day. Instead of holding a meeting at Prince Mr. BERGERON.
Albert on Saturday night we held the Prince Albert meeting on Friday night, and held a meeting at Rosthern on Saturday night. And, Sir, the man who at that time was defending what my hon. friend from iMont-magny condemns to-day-and which I think is an act of infamy and a lack of good faith on the part of the Saskatchewan government towards the minority of that province-the man the Saskatchewan government had to defend that measure was a Roman Catholic and a French Canadian. Had we wanted to take any part in that election we could have done so, but we chose not to mention a word about the local election for we were there to discuss federal affairs and we spoke about nothing else but federal affairs. The election of Mr. Turgeon took place the next day. I saw a good many French Canadians on the evening of the meeting who were in favour of Mr. Turgeon because he was a Roman, Catholic and a French Canadian. Men I knew intimately said to me : How can we vote against a man of our race and our religion ; it is true he is championing what we are opposed to; we do not believe in Prime Minister Scott forcing the Roman Catholics of this province to contribute towards the support of schools to which we shall not be allowed to send our children, but how can we vote against one of ourselves, a Roman Catholic and a French Canadian? I neither answered yes nor no to that because had I spoken my own mind I certainly would have said something that would not please them. And, Sir, this is but the commencement of what is going to happen in Saskatchewan. When this government granted autonomy to the Northwest provinces they knew that thirty years before the minority in these provinces had been promised justice, and promised that they would have respected their rights and privileges in the matter of education. But to-day we have the Minister of Justice approving of a provincial law which will force the minority to pay taxes for schools to which they will not send their children.
Is that what the right hon. Prime Minister had in his mind when he changed the first clause, No. 16, for the second clause, No. 16. That was what was probably in the mind of the member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) and in the mind of the Minister of Finance, but surely the Prime Minister did not con- . template that. And when the delegate who represents the highest authority of the church accepted the second clause 16 was he told that before a year the government of Saskatchewan was going to give the lie to all the promises which had been made to him, and the minority would be forced to contribute towards the building of schools which their children would not be allowed to attend?

Are we to understand from the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ber-

geron) that the amended clause No. 16 had to be submitted to the delegate of Rome before it could be passed by the Canadian government?

I will tell my hon. friend this, and with his usual intelligence he can draw his own conclusions ; I can tell him that when it was decided to substitute the present clause 16 for the original clause 16 it was explained to the delegate. My hon. friend (Mr. Hughes) can draw all the conclusions he wants from that. My hon. friend from Montmagny (Mr. Lavergne) appears to be surprised at all this but I can tell him that I am not a bit surprised. The party which prevented the minority in Manitoba from having their legal rights and privileges could not be expected to give justice to the provinces of the west. It is a most extraordinary thing that when the Manitoba Remedial Bill was before parliament the right hon. gentleman and all his followers from Quebec except seven of them, voted to prevent the Manitoba minority from getting their rights-I am not speaking about privileges now but their legal constitutional rights. And when the question was before the Manitoba legislature and when Mr. Roblin, the present premier of Manitoba, voted against the member for Lisgar (Mr. Greenway) who was then Prime Minister, and the member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) and Mr. Joseph Martin who were taking away from the Manitoba minority their rights and privileges as Roman Catholics and abolishing the use of the French language; when Mr. Robliu told these men that they were stealing from the Manitoba Catholics to act in such a way; when Mr. Roblin, a Protestant, took that course, nearly all the Roman Catholics in the legislature were against him and supported Mr. Greenway. It was a most extraordinary state of things and I direct the attention of my hon. friend from Montmagny to it. It was history repeating itself. It was like the settlement of the New Brunswick school question, when men were fighting there for their very existence and when high dignitaries of the church were accepting the half measure of Mr. Mackenzie. I will tell my hon. friend (Mr. Armand Lavergne) more than that:	In Manitoba today, where the Prime Minister of that province, a Conservative, is trying to be as kind as he can to the minority without transgressing the law, does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lavergne) know that it is Roman Catholics of Winnipeg who go over to the Manitoba ' Free Press ' and say :	Why
don't you write against Roblin because he is transgressing the law and allowing the Roman Catholics more privileges than they should have? It is French Canadians and Roman Catholics who are acting like that today. It is a most extraordinary state of things and l direct the attention of my 218*
hon. friend from Montmagny to it. The hon. gentleman is astonished but he will see a great deal more than that probably before very long. I want to say one word more. I want to tell the right hon. gentleman that this kind of thing has gone on for some time and that it may go on for some time longer but it will not go on for ever. Just fancy what occurred in this House in 1895 and 1896 in connection with the Manitoba Remedial Bill when a majority of Protestants and Orangemen in this parliament were voting to give their rights to the Catholic minority in Manitoba, and when the Roman Catholics in this House were voting against that measure. That kind of thing cannot last very long. A time will come when these people will discover the insincerity of those men who go to them and say : We are your friends, we think like you, don't you think we will do more for you than will the people over there who are Protestants and Orangemen. A time will come when there will be a stop put to that, and then I fear for the result. I am very glad that my hon. friend from Montmagny has brought this question before the House, i It is a matter to which the attention of the public should be hailed, but the hon. gentleman will find that he will not get much thanks from certain quarters.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is not the first time in this House or out of it that I have seen a Roman Catholic trying to be more Catholic than the Pope, and we have just had an instance of that from my hon. friend from Beauharnois. It is not the first time he has raised discussions of tills kind, and that he has availed of every convenient opportunity to say something calculated to spread the very sentiments which he attributes to others. The hon. gentleman tells us that he was in Prince Albert during a certain election and for a certain purpose, and that a meeting which-he was to address along with the leader of the opposition and which was to come off on the day of the election at which Mr. Turgeon was running as attorney general for the province, was postponed ; not, mind you, till the day after that election but to the day before the election. Of course, the meeting could not take place on the very day of the election, and so it was transferred to the day before election, because it might interfere with polling, which would have been completed two hours before the meeting was held, and so it was transferred to the day before the elections. It could not be postponed till the day after the election, and so in order not to arouse those Roman Catholic prejudicies which he deprecates, or those Protestant prejudicies which he also deprecates, he had his meeting put off till the day before the election. If my hon. friend thinks this is not too thin, he is very much mistaken. He

says that co-religionists of his and of mine told him that they could not vote against Mr. Turgeon because he was a Roman Catholic, but they deprecated the legislation now under review. I take his word, but will my hon. friend permit me to tell him that if there were Roman Catholics in Prince Albert who entertained such sentiments as he now attributes to them, which he says were expressed by them to him, how is it that they proffered their complaint to him who could not do anything in the matter, while the government never heard a word of complaint from them ? My hon. friend says this legislation is a tyrannical invasion of tire very rights which have been conferred by this parliament on the minority. That is his complaint. I have to say this to my hon. friend, that from the day this legislation was passed to the present time there has never come from the province of Saskatchewan to this government a single word of complaint against it. With ail due deference to the great confidence which the minority repose in my hon. friend, I venture to believe that if they had been so oppressed as he says they were by that legislation, they would have thought proper to proffer that complaint, not to him, but to us. We are asked to disallow this legislation. If there were any substantial minority in the province of Saskatchewan to find fault with" that legislation, I suppose they would have done what was done by the minority in Manitoba in 1891, in 1892, in 1893, in 1891, in 1893, when the party supported by my hon. friend was in office. That minority complained to the government and asked for disallowance. The minority in the province of Manitoba had a grievance, and they brought that grievance before the parties who could remedy it. But the minority in Saskatchewan have not asked for the disallowance of this legislation. Under these circumstances I think that these men who went to my hon. friend and shed a tear on his bosom were very poorly advised. They could have done better than that on their own behalf if they had a grievance, a thing of which I have my own doubts. But my hon. friend tells us that this is the result of the measure we gave to the minority in 1905. My hon. friend remembers the legislation that we passed at that time. He knows that it was passed with his concurrence to a certain extent, but not with the concurrence of those who sit beside him. He knows that such questions are always involved in a great deal of difficulty. He knows that the Manitoba question, of which he spoke a few moments ago, was for five years before the government which he supported, and that they never dared in that time to come to a conclusion upon it, and he knows that when they undertook to give the minority a remedy, it was an illusory remedy. He knows that it is impossible to legislate on questions of this kind without arousing the prejudices, the hon-Sir WILFRID IAIIRIER
est prejudices, of either one section or the other. We did the best we could under the circumstances. We thought we gave the minority the legislation to which they were entitled. If I could have done more I would have done it, but I know this, that little as my hon. friend says we did, the minority in the province of Saskatchewan were duly thankful, and no one knows it better than the representatives of that province who sit in this House. Now, it is charged that the legislature of Saskatchewan has already violated the disposition of the statute which we then phased. If such be the feeling of the minority, which I do not believe, what would have taken place ? Before we could proceed on the lines my hon. friend suggests, we would have to consider this question :	Is this
legislation legal or illegal ? Is it an invasion of the rights of the minority or is it not ? Is it a violation of the dispositions contained in the Act of Saskatchewan or is it not ? Upon this question we have a division of authority. My hon. friend from Montmagny, who has looked into the question, says he cannot tell us whether the law is legal or illegal, whether it is intra vires or ultra vires of the legislature of Saskatchewan. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice, who is an authority on these questions, tells us that he has looked into this matter and he cannot find that the legislation is an invasion of the rights of the minority, and under such circumstances he would not advise disallowance. My hon. friend from Beauharnois (Mr. Bergeron), who is more of a champion of the rights of the minority in these later days than he was in former day, tells us that we should disallow the Act, though the Minister of Justice expresses the opinion that there is no violation of the law. I would expect that the members from the province of Quebec would be chary, and very chary, about advising the government to disallow any Act as to the validity of which there may be even a doubt. We have taken the position, in the province of Quebec and in the province of Ontario, that disallowance is a power to be exercised very sparingly, and unless it can be shown that the Act is absolutely illegal, it should be left to the courts to determine, because the subject is too sacred a one to be lightly treated.
Mr. Speaker, may I be allowed to say a word.

speechtext: With the indulgence of the House.
Spoke.
I ask only witli the permission of the House, but I shall have another chance of doing it, and I will do it better.

If the hon. Minister of Justice had answered my ques-

tion, which was put as plainly in French as I could make it, and had made only one-half the statement he has made this afternoon, probably this debate would not have taken place. What we might have expected from the Minister of justice was that he would have said that the government were informed that the statutes were legal, and the debate would have ended there ; or that the government were informed that the statutes were illegal and that he would look into the matter. It would have been less curt and less brutal to the minority. The minister knows that I am making no personal attack against him. I have simply taken his answer as he gave it, and it is not the first time he has answered my questions in that way. So long as the curtness of his replies merely reflected on my own personality, or indicated lack of personal regard for myself, I paid no heed to that fact, but when interests more important than my personal feelings are involved,
I think it my duty to protest. The hon. minister has accused me of mis-statement when I said that this government had shown no scruple in disallowing statutes regarding immigration passed by the province of British Columbia, and he added that it was not the government but the courts that had disallowed the British Columbia statutes. Well, on the very same day I find this question put by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Ralph Smith):
What number of provincial Acts in all the provinces have been disallowed by the Dominion government since January, 1904, to January, 1908, and in what provinces respectively ?
To this question the Minister of Justice replied :
Five; all Acts of British Columbia.
Two of these statutes were to regulate immigration into British Columbia, and these two statutes, with two others following relating to other matters, were re-enactments of statutes which had been previous-1 ly disallowed and were disallowed again for the same reasons. The minister must admit therefore that I made no mis-statement of fact, and it is evident this government has been more anxious to disallow provincial statutes passed by a province which wanted to exclude undesirable immigration than disallow statutes which take away the rights of the minority. I would just say a word in reply to my hon. friend from Beauharnois (Mr. Bergeron). I know that in this parliament we need not expect that any statute passed .by any province will be disallowed out of respect for the rights of the minority. We have seen no such disallowance in the past, I care not under what government, and I do not expect any change in the future. I know therefore that my protest is useless. And as I am not Minister of Justice, I know that my opinion is not worth mentioning, but that opinion nevertheless is that these
statutes of the province of Saskatchewan have a strong flavour of illegality, and if not disallowed, the government of that province will be able to tax the minority for schools in which they do not believe and make them pay for schools to which they will not send their children. That is likely to be the result of the autonomy law which was passed in 1907. It seemed to me that that law did protect the minority in that respect but it may not. I was in favour of clause 16, not as it was drafted by the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton), but as it was drafted by the then Minister of Justice (Sir Charles Fitzpatrick). Unfortunately however when the hon. member for Brandon resigned from the government on that question, the government took fright and allowed him to redraft the clause. I stood with six other members of this House in favour of the clause as first drawn, but the law as it now stands is an accomplished fact and we cannot undo it. My words therefore are useless, but nevertheless I thought it my duty to take the stand I have done, and I hope I can leave my case in safety in the hands of the English speaking majority of this House and country.
