Bill (No. 147) to repeal the Canned Goods Act.-Mr. Fisher-read the second time and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,

This is an old statute, passed twenty years ago, which has never been put into effect. It applies to all canned goods, whether sold in the province or not, whereas the Act we passed last year only applies to foreign and interprovincial trade. When we passed the Act of last year, we decided that it would be better to leave the local trade in the hands of the provincial authorities. As last year's Act deals with the matter, there is no reason why the previous Act should remain in our statutes.
But suppose the local authorities do not do their duty, you will expose the whole province to the danger of having canned goods sold, which are injurious to health.

That point was thoroughly discussed last year, and parliament in its wisdom decided that it would be better for the Dominion not to undertake to deal with purely local trade. My hon. friend seems to intimate that we ought to hold the power to act in case the provincial or municipal authorities will not do so.
Yes.

I am not disposed to agree with my hon. friend .because if we hold the power the municipal or provincial authorities may take that as a reason for not

themselves acting ; whereas if we relieve ourselves of that duty, then the municipal am] provincial authorities will have to act. It is almost impossible for a department of this government to deal with these purely local affairs and it is contrary to the general spirit of our constitution. There is no doubt as to the authority of municipal and provincial authorities to deal with these matters of public health and sanitary affairs, while eminent authorities have expressed doubt as to our power to do so. Unless it is absolutely necessary for us to undertake that work, I believe it will be better to leave it in the entire control of those as to whose authority there is no doubt. If we retain the power here to deal with these matters it affords the local and provincial authorities an excuse for their remissness, whereas if we have not the power it is clearly incumbent upon them to take action and the public will hold them responsible if they are remiss.
Have the provinces the organization and legislation necessary to carry on the work ?

They have the machinery in their health officers, market inspectors, &c. I cannot at the moment quote the exact scope of the provincial statutest but they can, at any time, add to their statutes whatever provisions are required. The provisions of the Act concerning export and interprovincial trade are covered by the Canned Goods Act of last year and therefore there is no necessity for the existence of this Act, especially as the penalties imposed in it are much less than those under the Act of last year and some people maintain that they should be prosecuted under this Act and not under the Act of last year.

Why, for instance, is it necessary to repeal the section of this old statute requiring that every package of canned goods for local consumption must, be stamped with the name and address of the packer ?
I have explained to my hon. friend (Mr. Bergeron) the reasons for doing this, that it was thought better to allow these matters of purely local trade to be left to the local authorities.
After this Act is passed, exports will be subject to inspection ?

By the Act of last session.
ill1. J. D. REID. According to the Act of last year there was an inspection for interprovincial trade. Now under this Act is that inspection abandoned for local trade or interprovincial trade?
No.

For instance, goods manufactured in the province of Quebec Mr. FISHER.
and sold to a Montreal wholesale merchant, can they be distributed into other provinces?
Subject to the Act of last session.
As I understand it, if they are manufactured in that particular province they would not be subject to inspection?
They are subject to inspection if they go out of the province.
Therefore, local trade throughout the Dominion is practically without inspection?
So far as we are concerned, yes.

So far as the Dominion government is concerned. I do not see how the provincial governments can carry an inspection into force. For instance, to-day a person can ship an animal from the province of Ontario to the. province of Quebec without inspection, and that animal may be diseased. Even if it is a dead animal they can ship it without inspection. For instance, any person in my own county can purchase dead hogs and ship them to Montreal without any inspection whatever.
No, by the Act of last session that has been forbidden up to the present time. If it is not shipped to a packing house which has been declared to be under the operation of that law. it is forbidden.
I do not see anything in the other Act with regard to false marking the quantity or weight of the package.
Section 17, subsection 3.
This all applies to exportations.
The whole Act applies to exported articles.
Then the other would apply either to products for home consumption or to exports.
If the hon. gentleman will read the Act 134, he will find that clause 3 says ' every package of canned goods, &c., in Canada for consumption therein.' It does not apply to exports.

Then it would apply to a product used for home consumption but not exported. Then if I understand it, chapter 27 does not provide any remedy for false marking the quantity of goods in any package when they are to be used for home consumption. That ought to be provided for also.
I have already explained that so far as the local consumption is concerned, that would come within the purview of provincial or municipal authorities to deal with.
Don't you do it with regard to butter and cheese? We passed a law here some years ago concerning markings on cheese.

It seems to me the proposal of the minister is a departure from the policy which has been in force in this country for the last twenty years. This Act was obviously passed for the purpose of protecting public health, among other things. You find it in the revised statutes immediately following the statute wThich forbids adulteration. You might as well say that the Act respecting adulteration should only apply to articles for export. The minister shakes his head, but that does not settle the matter by any means. Now, why is it that the parliament of Canada, having jurisdiction over public health, should by this statute permit any person throughout the country, so far as this parliament can permit, to put up packages on which the date nr the weight, or the quantity may be falsely stated? What particular inconvenience or detriment was the country suffering from the enforcement of this Act for the past twenty years?
It has never been enforced.	'
That might be a verv good reason for enforcing it, but it is not a very good reason for repealing it.
I have explained it.

The minister has explained it. but he has not explained it very satisfactorily to my mind. He says that this is a matter that might be dealt with by the provinces and that it had better be dealt with by the provincial or municipal authorities under provincial laws.
For local purposes.

For local purposes. Is there any particular reason why this parliament, having jurisdiction over public health, should not enforce the provisions of this Act all over Canada? What is the particular reason against it?
I am not quite sure that this parliament has jurisdiction over public health. That is a moot question.
Well, if it had no jurisdiction over the subject dealt with by this statute it has surely no jurisdiction as to the adulteration of food.
Yes.
What provision of the British North America Act would support the statute in regard to adulteration of food and would not support this?

I cannot say offhand that there is any particular section defining it. but I can only reiterate the argument which was made here last year when the Act
was passed that it was unwise for us to undertake local business which was clearly within the purview of the provincial or municipal authorities and which might not be within our powers. I can only say that it is possible that it is not within our powers. It may be within our powers. I am not altogether sure upon that point. There is a question as to whether it is within our powers whereas there is no question ns to its being within the local powers. I therefore thought it was better not to undertake to enter upon a work that is clearly and definitely local and in regard to whch possibly we might find ourselves without due authority, especially when, as I consider, it is better not to have a mixed authority in regard to any subject. It is better where a subject is clearly and definitely within the purview of one authority that the doubtful authority should not enter into that field.
What brings it definitely within provincial authority?

There is no question about the provincial authorities being able to deal with market inspection, meat inspection and things of that kind in connection with the sale of foods. We all know perfectly well that every considerable municipality provides for the protection of the public health, that municipal authorities, under the provincial laws, have local health boards everywhere. There is a law in the various provinces giving authority to municipalities to provide for the inspection of foods sold within their respective limits.
But they have no power to analyse.
They can analyse for the purpose of enforcing the law.
They certainly have no staff for that purpose. The Department of Inland Revenue makes an analysis of food in connection noth the enforcement of the Adulteration of Foods Act.

I know that in Montreal there is an analyst who is employed by the board of health of that city and whose special business it is to analyse foods sold there. He is regularly employed, I am inclined to think, on salary, but if not on salary, on fees. I used to know a gentleman who was engaged in that work. Dr. Girdwood was employed for years for that purpose. I know there is an analyst in the city of Toronto, although I cannot give his name.

That might apply to large cities, but it does not applv to rural districts generally. Under the Inspection of Foods Act, which was passed years ago, the country was divided into districts, and each district had its analyst to whom samples of food might be sent for analysis. The local authorities do not provide for the

analysis of food as far as I know. We have here the weights and measures branch of the Department of Inland Revenue, so that the question of weights and measures must be controlled by us and the inspection must be made by the federal authorities. The Department of Inland Revenue make an analysis of food under the Adulteration of Foods Act to ascertain whether they are adulterated or not. The work in that respect is not duplicated by the provinces in so far as I know. It has always heretofore been understood that the adulteration of food was attended to by the Inland Revenue Department, that it looked after the adulteration of molasses, honey, butter and everything of that kind, and if you drop it here I am quite sure the provinces are not likely to take it up. They have not the machinery that we have to do it, and they are not likely to do it to the extent that the interest of the people requires.
I have not been able to find any instance of the enforcement of this Act during the twenty years it has been on the statute-book. This matter has been attended to by the provinces.

How does this question arise at this time? We passed the law of last year dealing with the subject and I would like to know whether there have been any protests or representations from any of the local governments. This statute, as I understand it, has been in force for twenty years, and unless there have been some protests from some of the local governments it seems rather peculiar that this question should now arise at all.

The way in which the question arose was that when we were undertaking to enforce the new Act there was some question as to whether the penalties provided by this Act or the penalties under the new Act of last year should apply. A question was raised as to the legality of the prosecution under the new Act. As we did not see that the old Act was of any benefit we thought it better to repeal it.
The question arose as to the legality of the new Act?
Not as to the legality- I should not say that-but as to which Act the prosecution ought to be taken under.

Suppose that you had the Act under which you were attempting to prosecute, would you not lay the complaint under that statute? I would think that you would lay it under the statute that you were undertaking to enforce.

In my opinion the very reasons given by the minister for repealing this Act would be the very best reasons for repealing, or improving the Act of last session and making it apply to the Mr. SPROULE.
whole trade. Last session I had the temerity to say that the Bill ought to apply to the food that Canadians eat as well as to the food that is shipped out of the country for other people to eat. I have been confirmed in that opinion after having conversed with my constituents and with people in various parts of the country since then and I am bound to warn the minister here, in so far as my humble opinion may be regarded as any warning, that if it is a wise thing, notwithstanding what he says about mixed jurisdictions, for this government to interfere, I think it should interfere in regard to all food and not limit it to the food consumed by a certain class of people. While my hon. friend's inspectors, under the. Act of last year are doing their work, while they are seeing that these marks are upon packages of food which are intended for the export trade .and while they are condemning food that they find not up to the standard for export, w-hy should this Act not provide that the condemned food shall not be eaten by Canadians ? What province is going to create a civil war because the Dominion government should undertake to protect the lives and the health of the people of that province ? I believe the Dominion government should do all within its power to guarantee the purity of the food we eat. but, if the Minister of Agriculture is going to say that food for export shall be pure and shall be condemned if it is not pure, why should he be afraid of oflleuding any province by saying that the food which is eaten locally shall also be pure? I have not even a remote idea that any province would raise a question of provincial rights under such circumstances as that. If the Act is not applicable to the conditions it is intended to remedy it ought to be repealed, but if by repealing it you are going to remove the only protection we have to the lives and health of Canadians, then I would certainly be against its repeal. In my opinion the provisions of this measure should apply to the province in which the goods are produced as well as to other provinces or to foreign countries.

It is a new thing for the Minister of Agriculture to be so anxious about provincial rights, and I am father surprised at his anxiety in this case. 'This is a most important measure and this parliament should do all it can to improve the food products of this country. The minister has not yet been able to show that any provincial government has complained because the federal government is applying this law to all the provinces, and until there is such a complaint I think we should assume that wre have power to take measures for the protection of the health and the lives of our people. Under existing circumstances hogs can be shipped for export

to Montreal and if an animal is found diseased his export is prevented, but it can be disposed of locally and given as fool to the working people of that city. In the same way the unhealthy organs of an animal are taken out and while the meat would not be allowed to be exported, it can be shipped to Montreal, Toronto and other centres and disposed of there. The Minister of Agriculture knows that in repealing this law he is taking a retrograde step, and I am surprised he should propose to parliament any such measure. The bon. gentleman tells us that a judge cannot tell under which Act he is to impose a" penalty, but if there is any doubt as to the jurisdiction of the court it would be a sensible thing for the minister to propose an amendment to the law which would make it plain.

While the government seems to have one policy with regard to canned food they have an entirely different policy with regard to drugs, because Bill 146, which has been Introduced by the Minister of Inland Revenue, contains provisions of exactly the same character as those which the present Bill proposes to repeal. Section 4 of the Inland Revenue Bill says:
All proprietary or patent medicines shall be put up in packages and bottles and every one of them intended for sale or distribution in Canada shall have ulaced upon it in conspicuous characters forming an inseparable part of the general label the name and number under which the medicine is registered and also the manufacturer's name and address.
Section 7 says:
No proprietary or patent medicine can be manufactured, imported, exposed, sold or offered for sale when it contains any drug which is included under schedule A of this Act and the name of which is not conspicuously printed on the label.
I cannot see any distinction in principle between the provisions now proposed to be repealed and the provisions In chapter 134, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1900. The minister says there is some doubt as to our power to legislate as to public health. Wherein Is the power contained which enables us to legislate with regard to the adulteration of food ; wherein is the power to be found which enables us to legislate respecting proprietary and patent medicines?

I will explain, in answer to the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) I may say, that last session we fully discussed the application of the Bill not only to local but to export matters. I want to take straight issue with my hon. friend (Mr. Lancaster) upon o.ne point. I am sorry he is not in the House, he said what he had to say and then goes away evidently not taking enough interest in the discussion to follow it up.
He may have a reason far leaving the chamber.

He may be back. I do not think it is the duty of this parliament to supplement or implement the duties of another legislature. I grant that if it is the duty of this parliament to look after the public health, we ought to perform that duty ; but I do not think this parliament is called on to do or ought to do what it is the duty of the local legislatures to do ; and if the local legislatures are remiss in the performance of their duties, that is not a reason why this parliament should step in and perform those duties. I take direct issue with the hon. gentleman on that point. This parliament would be committing a wrong if it overstepped the bounds of its duty and did what the local legislatures ought to do and are remiss in doing. The local legislatures are simply shirking the question, and the people should hold them to their duty and not call upon another legislature to do that which is no , part of its duty. Last session it was clear- " ly understood and discussed, and I think unanimously decided by parliament, that as the provincial legislatures, through their municipal Acts and their health Acts, had full power to deal with these subjects so far as they related to trade within the province, this parliament would not legislate upon them in that respect.
X would like to ask the minister if he holds that this parliament has not the power to pass such legislation ?
No, I do not hold it. I have said, however, that a doubt has been raised on that point.
Who has raised it ?
A number of lawyers.
Has the opinion of the Minister of Justice been sought on this matter ?
The Minister of Justice said he was not prepared to say positively that we had not the power, but he said that there was a doubt as to our power.
If there is a doubt about it, it seems to me that there is a similar doubt about the Adulteration Act.

I do not think so, because that Act applies to commerce all over the country, both that Act and the Act respecting proprietary medicines. These relate to subjects of general commerce in the country, which are not subject to local restrictions or police regulations. '
The minister is entirely mistaken, as I will show him in a moment.

I would like to point out what I think is the difference. The restrictions in the Adulteration of Foods Act

and the Patent Medicines Act are not confined to any particular locality, but apply to general trade in the country everywhere. The Act passed last session applies to all trade which is not within a province- to interprovincial trade and to export trade; because the provincial and local authorities could not deal with these. But the provincial and local authorities can deal with transactions which are entirely within one province or one locality, therefore it is not necessary for this parliament to deal with them, and I think it is better that we should not do so. Where the provincial legislature can deal with the inspection aud sale of food in a locality or withiu the bounds of the province, I contend that it is the duty of the provincial legislature to deal with it, aud if it is their duty, it is not wise for us to step in and do what the provincial legislature is called on by the constitution of the country to do.
The minister has absolutely convinced me that there is not the slightest ground in anything he has said for the repeal of this Act.
I was not discussing that now.

I admit that the minister has confused two things ; he has confused the jurisdiction to p>ass the Act with the expediency or the necessity of continuing it. I will deal in the first place witli the question of jurisdiction, which he has explained not to my satisfaction, but in a way absolutely contrary to the position he has taken. He justifies the jurisdiction of parliament to pass the Adulteration Act and the Act respecting Patent Medicines on the ground that these extend to trade and commerce all over Cau-ada. The Act which he is repealing does precisely the same thing, and therefore he has argued most convincingly that this parliament has absolute power to pass the Act respecting Canned Goods. Therefore his suggestion that parliament has not jurisdiction to pass it falls completely to the ground.
My hon. friend has uot understood me at all.

I think I have understood the hon. gentleman a little too well. Let us take up the other argument. Let us not confuse two things ; jurisdiction is one thing, the advisability or expediency of passing a statute is another. I find no words in the British North America Act which enables parliament to pass the Adulteration Act or the Act respecting Patent Medicines which would not also enable parliament to pass the Act respecting Canned Goods. Let us now come to the question of expediency. The minister says parliament has no duty in respect of this particular matter because it can be dealt with Mr. FISHER
better by the provinces who will enable the particular municipalities to pass by-laws regarding it. In that connection let me point out that the words in section 92 of the British North America Act ' Municipal institutions,' do uot go quite so far probably in the direction the hon. minister suggests as he may imagine. There have been pronouncements of the Privy Council on the construction of those particular works. I find, in the Adulteration of Food Act, that you may not offer milk for sale if a certain quantity of water has been added or certain constituents taken therefrom. How is it that milk is less a matter of local consumption than canned goods or why is it more the duty of parliament to legislate with regard to milk than canned goods ? I can see no distinction. If any distinction be made,' milk might be regarded as more of a local article than canned goods. So far as expediency is concerned, I can see no reason for eliminating the Act respecting canned goods from our statutes and leaving the Act respecting the adulteration of milk.

The Act of last session covers everything except the local trade and it is only a question of the previous Act remaining on the statutes for the purposes of the local trade. Under the Act of last session we are required to have inspectors wherever the goods to which that Act applies are produced in Canada and sent out from one province to another or to foreign countries.	.
What is the difference between that Act and the Adulteration Act or the Act regarding Patent Medicines?

The difference is this. The Act we passed last session regarding canned meats and canned goods requires that we should have inspectors wherever the goods to which the Act applies are produced in Canada and sent from one province to another or outside the country. The adulteration of Foods Act and the Patent medicines Act do not require a complete system of inspection. They are a good deal like the Fruit Marks Act in that respect.
Is the hon. gentleman dealing with the question of jurisdiction or expediency ?

Expediency. The matter was dealt with last session from that standpoint. If we were required to undertake a very complete inspection of all canned meat goods, for local as well as interprovincial and export trade, we would be asking something practically impossible for a department of the Dominion government to do effectively.

Leaving the Act on the statute-book does not bring about any such results.

6S82
If it remains, it is in direct conflict with the principle on which the Act of last session is intended to be administered.
I do not see how.
To this extent The clear intent of the Act of last session is that the local trade is not to be dealt with.

The result of leaving the first Act on the statute-book is simply this. So far as the articles for interprovincial trade or export are concerned, you must have inspection. So far as concerns the articles for local consumption in the province, you would still have prohibition of false labels or statements.

That Act has been on the statute-book some twenty years and has never been enforced, but when we began to enforce the new Act there seemed to be a clash or doubt, because the provisions of the new Act are different for the same kind of offence from those of the old Act. I do not think it matters very much whether it remains on the statutes or not, but it has never been enforced.
It ought to be.

It provides no machinery for its enforcement. It would have to be amended and machinery created for its enforcement, and it would be impossible, unless the Dominion inspectors are to be increased infinitely, for them to undertake to do work which is purely local.

Then what need was there for clause 10 of the Adulteration of Foods Act which provides for the appointment by the Inland Revenue Department of local inspectors to examine articles of food in any city, township, county or other municipality, after they have passed an examination showing their competence to act as inspectors, on the nomination of the municipality ? That is purely local and purely for the safety of health. The Adulteration of Foods Act defines clearly what shall be considered as adulteration. '
That is a question of adulteration, not of public health.

It is an Act respecting the adulteration of foods and other articles, it defines adulteration and provides for these inspectors all over the country. They are local inspectors, but that service is administered by the Inland Revenue Department.
That is not for public health only but for trade and commerce, because they are deceiving the public in pretending to sell something which they are not selling.

But it is for public health, because it provides for the case of articles injurious to public health: it deals
not with export trade but with public health. What does it mean by saying that vinegar shall be considered as adulterated if any mineral acid or vegetable salt having copper or lead as its base has been added thereto? That is adulteration because it is injurious to health.
Partly.
That is the reason we take it up, we do not say anything about commerce.
Oh, yes.
No, this is for public health. It is the same with regard to alcohol and milk. Milk to which water is added becomes adulterated.
That is not health.
It is for the benefit of health.
That is because you are being cheated.
If you are feeding children on milk represented to be pure which is not pure and you are destroying the health of the infant, because the milk is of less value
That is it, because it is of less value.
So with canned goods improperly dated, the consumer is getting less value.

No, it is a matter of trade and commerce.

The discussion on this Bill has included the Meat and Canned Foods Act passed last year. Before this Bill passes I wish to aslc the Minister of Agriculture if he has made any special provision for such parts of the world as the northwestern provinces.
As soon as this Bill passes I will ask the committee to take up the next Bill which deals with the Meat and Canned Foods Act. I will suggest that my hon. friend wait until that Bill comes up.

I think that if we are repealing this Act because we have not jurisdiction to deal with it in this parliament, we must repeal a great many other Acts standing in practically the same position. I understood the minister to say that one of the main reasons, if not the reason, for this Act is that a doubt had been expressed as to the jurisdiction of this parliament. and that the suggestion had been made that this was a matter which should

bo left within the exclusive control of provincial legislatures, so far as this Act that we now propose to repeal chapter 123 is concerned. I understand the minister to say that this Act had not been enforced as a matter of law, but that it was practically a dead letter. As to that I do not know : I take it that the Minister of Agriculture has ascertained that to be a fact. But assuming that to be a fact, wTe must not shut our eyes to this other fact, that as soon as we repeal this Act there will be an intimation to all parties who have found this Act embarrassing, that they are no longer controlled by it as they were before. So we may expect that tile evils that sections 3, 4, 5 and 6 were aimed at will probably prevail. I am not innocent enough to believe that the minister has not some reason for wanting to promote this legislation, and I am almost suspicious enough to believe that there are some motives for promoting this legislation that the minister has not seen fit, for reasons of state or otherwise, to divulge to the House.
I have given all my reasons.

At all events, there is this peculiarity, that we find the minister, who is an astute and clever debater, resorting to arguments which, so far as I can see and as appears to many other members on this side of the House, are not borne out by the facts before us. I commend the minister on the position he has taken, and I suppose he stands alone in the cabinet in that regard, in realizing to some extent the proper limits of provincial rights. I would be glad if other members of the government were more pressed by the desirability of keeping strictly within the limits of our own jurisdiction. I agree with the minister when he says that the failure of a provincial legislature to exercise jurisdiction is no reason why we should usurp it and attempt to legislate. I am with the minister in another respect, that I think we have too much legislation. I am bound to say that the minister who is promoting this legislation is not the least guilty of the ministers in that regard. I often think that if there is anything in which he has conspicuously erred it is iu having tried to spoon feed the farmers, and in interfering too much with private and domestic concerns, trying to legislate where no legislation is required. So in this view I am not at all sorry that he is repealing this Act, and I would be glad if he would sweep away a lot of other legislation that he has put upon the statute book recently. But this statute is an old statute of some twenty years standing, and while I agree with him that we are interfering far too much with provincial rights, yet when we have a statute in existence for some twenty years we ought to hesitate very much before repealing it. As regards the difference between Mr. LENNOX.
this statute and others, such as the Adulteration of Foods Act, I am entirely unable to follow the minister in his reasoning. The Act chapter 144 is, so far as it goes, an Act that relates to every package of canned goods that is put up for consumption in Canada, not in any particular province or locality, or by any particular class of men. Misrepresentations relate to all misrepresentations in Canada. The Act is as general and as broad as Canada itself. When I turn to the statute immediately preceding that, the Adulteration of Foods Act, I find that it is also general iu its character relating to questions of health and also relating to questions of trade and commerce. I quite agree with the minister when he says that pot only does this Adulteration of Foods Act deal wTith questions of public health, but it also deals with questions of trade and commerce, with dealings between man and man and that it aims, in addition to protecting public health, at securing honest dealing between parties. So, we have this provision in section 23 :
Milk from which the cream has been removed by skimming, or bv a separator or creamer, may be sold as skim milk, if contained in cans bearing upon their exterior the word ' skimmed ' in letters of not less than two inches in length.
Can the Minister of Agriculture point out how that provision is broader or more general in its nature than sections 3, 4, 5 and <j of the statute which be proposes to repeal ? I am not at all opposed to simplifying- legislation and I would not be sorry if we could eliminate some of the provisions of law that the minister has from time to time introduced. I am delighted to find that he is, for the time being, a convert to the principle of provincial rights. The sin of ignoring provincial rights is becoming more prevalent every day and I take this as an intimation that we will have a better state of things soon. Maybe to-night we will have a question of provincial rights before us in another form. I notice that the Adulteration of Foods Act has been held to be intra vires of this parliament in the case of the Queen vs. Stone, so that if we have the power to pass the Adulteration of Foods Act we had certainly the right to pass the other Act. We have legislation with regard to the subject of adulterating maple syrup and sugar -which contains a provision that if these articles are not pure there shall be a statement on the can or receptacle that they are adulterated or mixed. I see that the law is observed to some extent at all events and that is exactly upon the line of the statute that we propose to repeal.

I understood from the minister that one reason why he proposes to repeal this law is that there was some confusion, when prosecutions took place, as to which Act would apply, having regard to the penalties imposed. Could he give

any instance of suc-li a prosecution taking place ?
I cannot give an instance. The deputy minister drew my attention to the fact and told me that that was the case but I could not give an instance.

When you draw an indictment against an individual do you do it under a certain statute and under a certain clause of that statute? The violation of that clause must have some penalty attached to it in the statute and I cannot understand how there will be any confusion in prosecuting under such a statute as to which penalty shall apply. The penalties in the statute should be the penalties that would apply to a case taken under the statute.
I confess I cannot exactly explain what the difficulty was that arose but I know" there was such a difficulty.

The Act that the minister proposes to repeal and which deals with canned goods applies to Canada as a whole. Section 12 of the Act of 1907 provides that :
All articles prepared for food in any establishment and packed in cans or similar reT ceptacles, or in any package whatever, shall be subject to inspection during the whole course of preparation and packing; and all such packages shall be marked with-
(a)	The initials of the Christian names, the full surname, and the address, or, in the case of a firm or corporation, the firm or corporate name and address, of the packer;
(b)	A true and correct description of the contents of the package.
Now this is the provision that I suppose conflicts ;
Provided, however, that if it be established to the satisfaction of the Governor in Council that such marking would hinder the sale of any of said articles in the British or foreign markets, he may exempt such articles from the provisions of this section.
That implies that the Act has reference entirely to the export trade. Is there any reason why the minister should not embody in this Bill a clause that would cover the whole of Canada ? There is no objection, as I understand, from any of the provincial governments. It strikes me that there is some other motive than that of simply desiring to repeal the Act, that there has been some influence brought to bear on the government to secure the repeal of the Act.
Mr. FISHER, You are altogether too 'suspicious.
I have reasons to be suspicious.
No, you have not.

The Act of 1907 applies entirely to goods that are exported. If a person were brought up for violating the
law', as I understand it, no judge would convict him under this Act, because it simply applies to export goods, but a conviction could be secured if the Act which has been in existence for twenty years were retained upon the statute-book. If there has been no complaint from the provincial governments why should not that Act be allowed to stand or else amend the Act of last year in such a w7ay that it will apply to goods consumed in Canada as well as to export goods ? I want the Act to apply to the whole of Canada.

I think my hon. friend had this question pretty thoroughly explained to him this afternoon. I do not think I could explain it any more clearly. I do not know why my hon. friend does not understand it. The imputation of the hon. gentleman that there is anything behind [DOT]what I said is absolutely without foundation or justification. I have given my reasons and I want the hon. gentleman and his friends to understand that there are no other reasons in my thoughts. It is therefore not right for them to say that I am hiding ideas or reasons. My hon. friend should accept that statement, and it is true. I state frankly to the hon. gentleman that the parliament of Canada decided last year that a clause should not be inserted making this Act apply to local trade within the province.
That is because we had an Act that did apply to it.
No, it was not. The hon. gentleman did not know that Act was there.
I knew it.
It was not referred to during the whole discussion. The hon. gentleman himself I believe urged that the Act of 1907 should apply to local trade.
Why should it not?

Because parliament decided that the Act of 1907 should not apply to local trade and it is not feasible that it should apply to it. The only reason for repealing this Act is that it provides for somewhat the same offences, different penalties and different provisions from the Act of 1907 covering practically the same thing. As a matter of fact, section 134, R.S.C., has been on the statute-books for over 20 years, and it has been practically a dead letter ever since. The Act of 1907 deals with interprovincial and export trade and it is well known that the provincial authorities can deal with the trade within the provinces.

There is no reason why both these Acts should not be incorporated into one. The necessity for protecting our Canadian market was discussed last year, and the Minister of Agriculture preferred to have chapter 134 apply to local condi-

tions, and so long as we had that Act it was satisfactory, although I would like to have the whole thing included in the meat and Canned Foods Act. My idea is to protect our own Canadian people as well as foreigners, but the repeal of this Act leaves our people without protection. Even if the provincial governments have laws bearing on tlie subject, there are unorganized territories under federal jurisdiction, and if for no other reason this Act should be left on the statute-books so that they might be protected.
Is that the only reason the hon. gentleman has?
Have I not given other reasons?

So far as that particular reason is concerned, the only unorganized territories are Mackenzie, Keewatin, and as there are not going to be any canned goods put up in these territories for a number of years to come, they are protected by the Act of 1907 the moment canned goods are shipped to them from any of the provinces.

I understood the minister to say that certain* clauses of chapter 134, which it is proposed to repeal, are practically repeated in the Meat and Canned Goods Act. Section 17 of chapter 134 provides a penalty for falsely representing the weight in the package or falsely representing the date, and that applies to canned goods for home consumption as well as for export. But if chapter 134 is repealed then the corresponding provision in the other Act would only apply to export goods that are to be sent out of a province.
That is quite right.

Don't you think it is a very salutary provision to guarantee the date of canning and the quantity in the package? If you repeal chapter 134 there is no enactment to prevent false marking of goods put up for consumption within a province.
My hon. friend is quite right in saying that so far as the Dominion law is concerned, there would not be any such provision if this Act is repealed.
They have been depending on the federal law all along.

Although they have been depending on the federal law. it does not provide any machinery for the enforcement of its provisions, and the consequence is that anything that is done under it can only be done by the authority of inspectors provided by provincial Acts for provincial organizations. The Act of 1907 does provide full machinery for the enforcement of its provisions, but it does not provide macbin-Mr. J. D. t?EID.
ery for the enforcement of the provisions of chapter 134.

Clause 7 of chapter 134 provides for lodging a complaint before a justice of the peace. That is all the machinery that is required to put the law in motion and to secure the infliction of a penalty. It is the same as many other laws in that respect. Although there may never have been a conviction under the Act, I am far from reaching the conclusion that it is of no value. We know that many laws which provide penalties for doing wrong are the very things whioh prevent people from doing wrong-they fear the danger of the penalty. How can we tell how many thousands of people have been prevented from falsely marking goods by fear of the penalty provided by this law. The fact that no prosecutions have taken place under it may be only because people knowing that the law was in existence were deterred from violating it to the extent that would bring them under the ban of the law. If this law has been instrumental in preventing people committing these offencgs, though no prosecution has taken place under it, it would be valuable nevertheless.

My hon. friend perhaps did not understand what I meant when I said that there was no machinery provided for enforcing this Act. 1 grant that there is a penalty provided, but there is no machinery for inspection. It was only because the Act of 1907 provided machinery for the enforcement of that Act that anybody found that this Act was in existence, though it was absolutely ignored.

Under the provisions of this Act inspectors are not so much required, because any one dealing in the article can lodge a complaint before a justice of the peace. If this Act is repealed, I think we ought to go further and amend the Meat and Canned Foods Inspection Act, and make clause 7 of chapter 134, both as to quantity and weight and false marks, apply to goods manufactured for consumption in the country as well as to goods for export. If the minister would amend the other Acts in that respect, I do not think there would be any objection to the repeal of this Act.
No, I would not do that.
Then I do not think the hon. gentleman is justified in repealing this Act, and I do not think he would do so if pressure of some kind had not been brought to bear upon him.
Nothing of the kind. The hon. gentleman has no right to impute motives.

I am saying nothing that I have no right to say, and I will repeat it if the hon. gentleman desires. From what

I have heard I have reason to believe that some representations were made from sources that might be interested to have this Act repealed. That is the information I have ; whether it is correct or not I do not know.
I would like the hon. gentleman to state what sources they are and from whom the representations were made.

It may be from the very parties who have not disclosed their aim, and who. because of dread of the enforcement of this Act, dare not embark on the lines which they contemplate doing, and which they will be likely to do when this Act is repealed.

Why did the hon. minister not repeal this Act last session ?
Mr. FISHER, Because the matter was not then brought to my attention.
In regard to the Canned Meats and Inspection Acts passed last session, has the minister ]jad representations made to him by wholesale grocers in regard to private brands ?
As soon as this Bill is passed, I am going to take up an amendment to the other Act, when that whole question will come up.
But the hon. gentleman has had representations made to him from reputable wholesale merchants ?
Tes, and I ,intend to bring up amendments to that Act.
I would like to ask the minister if any representations have been made to him in regard to chapter 134 by any of the parties who put up canned meats or foods for the local market ?

Representations were made that the trade did not know which Act to follow in regard to the marks on the cans.
Mr. .1. D. REID. Have these representations been made by people putting up canned meats or foods ?
Yes, the people who come under the provisions of the Act.
By those engaged in the export trade or those engaged in the local trade ?
Both.
These are the people who have made representations to the minister and have asked that this Act be repealed.

They simply wanted to know what they should do-which Act they should follow. I could not see any advantage in having the two Acts, and I thought
the simplest way was to repeal this Act and leave the other in force, and thus avoid confusion.
If everything they put up that way is entirely for export, how could this interfere with it?
The two Acts provide for two different markings, and they say they do not know what Act to follow when putting labels on their goods.
Why not then have amended the old Act by simply making the markings the same?
No doubt, that would have met that particular point. But there is no object in keeping the Act on the statutes, and I thought the simplest way was to repeal it.

The Act passed last year applied only to goods manufactured for export or inter-provincial trade and not to products put up for local consumption. If you repeal the first Act, you will have no law to control the goods put up for local consumption.

The whole trouble was simply in the marking, and if the minister had simply amended the old Act so as to make the markings exactly the same for the local market as for export and inter-provincial trade, there would be no difficulty. Instead of doing that, he repeals the old Act entirely and leaves the people helpless in those provinces where there is no law now to protect them against the putting up of goods for local consumption unfit to be used. If that is the stand the minister and the government take, I make my protest, but so long as the people understand it, we have done our best.

Bill (No. 149) to amend the Meat and Canned Foods Act-Mr. Fisher-read the second time and House went into committee thereon.

In the province of Saskatchewan, a number of hogs are slaughtered and sent by the carload to Winnipeg. That has been the custom in years past, hut this year, under the regulations of the department, this export business has been knocked on the head, and the farmers have to practically ship the animals alive and take what prices they can get from what is supposed to be a combine in the Winnipeg market. Has the minister considered the possibility of providing some means by which farmers may be able to slaughter at home and have the animals inspected right on the spot and shipped in the old way? Winnipeg is the only large market they have to which they

can ship these products. I am told the regulations have been a source of considerable inconvenience and actual loss to them?

I do not remember having received any representations from the province of Saskatchewan, but the same question has come up in various parts of the country. The difficulty is one for which I have not yet found an adequate remedy. The inspection of the packing of meat is required to secure a reputation for our Canadian meat and canned meats. We know how important the export and the interprovincial trade is in bacon. Our export trade in bacon depends ou the enforcement of just such regulations as are provided by the Act of 1907. Without such inspection as is required under that Act, we would in a short time be shut out to a considerable extent, if not entirely, from the English market. We require therefore such an examination of the carcasses as will enable the veterinary officers to declare honestly that the meat packed or put into the cans is healthy. The expert veterinary authorities universally agree that they cannot judge the health of a carcass unless the organs

especially the heart, liver and lungs-are open to their inspection, so that dressed hogs, or hogs shipped without those attachments, cannot be declared honestly by the inspectors free from disease. It is very difficult, if not impossible, to provide machinery by which the trade in carcasses can be safely carried on. I do not Say that where those goods are being shipped to a factory not declared to be under the operation of certain clauses of this Act, those clauses would out apply. That meant that only factories dealing in the export trade would be brought under the operation of those clauses of the Act.
Does the Act proscribe the export from one province to another of carcasses which are not intended to be packed, but simply intended for local sale?

The Act does, but the regulations provide that it is only when the carcasses are shipped to a factory which is declared to be under the operation of those sections of the Act that the shipment is forbidden. We found great difficulty because there are more factories in what is called the export trade than we supposed before the passage of the Act, and the result is the change I am now proposing, requiring the exemption of certain factories from the operation of the Act instead of declaring certain factories to come under it. That will make the condition of affairs my hon. friend describes a little more acute, because heretofore farmers in Saskatchewan could ship dressed carcasses of hogs to a packer or to the market in Winnipeg, except to a few factories in Winnipeg declared to be under the operation of the Act. In Mr. LAKE.
future they cannot legally ship to any factory unless it lias been declared exempt from the operation of those sections. But the farmers may ship to any place that is not a factory, to the local butcher or the market without being interfered with by the operation of those sections. Section 5 of the Act of last session provided for these shipments by farmers.
They could ship out; of the province equally well under that provision?
Yes.

AIcI.KAN. In Prince Edward Island there is no factory under the Act. Farmers, knowing that, slaughtered their hogs without meeting the requirements of the Act. When the buyers came down from Montreal last fall as usual to buy hogs, they could not buy them for their factories, they had to return without purchasing, and consequently there was virtually a monopoly among the few buyers on the island, and the price of pork went down with consequent loss to the farmers. There is something wrong in the Act when such' a condition could exist under it. The minister should frame an amendment to avoid such a condition. The farmers lost money last year through its operation and the neglect of the government to inform them of the provisions of the law. In fact very little is known in the country of what the law really is. It is possible to find out from the department I suppose, but almost impossible to find out from the statute itself.

When this difficulty in the island was brought to our attention we provided that hogs there could be inspected locally and shipped. It was unfortunate that the farmers there killed their hogs before the Quebec buyers came, as killing in that way they did not comply with the regulations which would have permitted them to ship to factories under the operation of the Act. Aly hon. friend is speaking a little harshly in saying that we created a monopoly. There was no monopoly ; it happened that certain buyers were not able to buy the hogs for shipment, but others were able to buy them for the local markets.
AIcLEAN. Is that not a monopoly ?

It prevents outside competition by other buyers, but there is no monopoly in itself. The difficulty was overcome before the end of the season; we arranged to have them inspected locally and shipped. As soon as the situation was presented to us we hastened to meet the difficulty and overcame it in that way.

It is a pity that information was not more widely circulated among the farmers in order to provide against such a contingency. I am also sorry the

minister does not seem to be able to improve the conditions in Saskatchewan.
I am quite ready to do what I can.

Could not an arrangement similar to that in the island by which there might be local inspection? I do not know how many inspectors there are in Saskatchewan, but it might be possible, by giving notice to the farmers in a particular district, to arrange for them to slaughter at the one time so that inspection would be possible and the carcasses could be shipped to these factories.

My bon. friend will remember that there are two considerations in respect to Prince Edward Island which are peculiar. The first is that the buyers go to the island and buy, the formers ship only after the animals have been bought, and they, therefore, know the destination, they know that the carcasses are going to a factory which is under the operation of the Act. Then there are in the island practically only two shipping points through which trade passes to the places where factories are in operation. Consequently it is a very easy thing for us to make an arrangement for inspection at the point of shipment from the island, instead of on arrival at the factory. But my hon. friend seems to overlook the fact that it is only when the hogs are sent to a packing factory that they come under the operation of the Act. If a farmer is shipping a carload of hogs to the Winnipeg market, the Act will not operate on him at all. It will be difficult, if not impossible, to arrange to have inspectors at all the shipping points in the province of Saskatchewan so that the cargo may be inspected locally before it is shipped.
How many inspectors are there?

We only have inspectors at the factories. In the case I speak of in Prince Edward Island last fall, an extra man was sent there specially. I think the hogs were all shipped from Charlottetown, and the inspector saw them before they were shipped.

It would be a great convenience to the farmers in Saskatchewan if they could be made aware of the extraordinary position in which they are placed. It will be impossible for them to ship carcasses-[DOT]
I am not taking that position.

The organs have to be left in them if they are to be shipped to a factory. I think some provision should be made by which the carcasses may be shipped. as in the past: and further, that an intimation should be given to the farmers 210
throughout those parts of the Northwest where hogs are raised for shipment. It ought to be a comparatively simple matter to spread the information so that the farmer who exports hogs will know all the conditions he has to comply with.
My officers made a resume of the provisions of this Act, which was sent to every newspaper in Saskarcne-wan, and throughout the whole of Canada.

Will the minister explain the sections of this Act as they will affect the use of private brands? I understand some wholesale merchants who have been selling canned goods for many years, reputable merchants, work up and advertise a private brand. They object that they have to put the name of the packer on their can, and contend that their own guarantee in many cases is better than the guarantee of the packer, and that it destroys the value of their private brand when they have to put on the name of the packer. That complaint is made in certain parts of the country. I would like to know what position the minister is going to take in regard to that matter.

That point has been the subject of discussion between the wholesale merchants and the canners of Vancouver. It was brought before the minister, and he suggested when the Bill came before the House that an amendment might be moved to clause 12. Clause 12 of the Meat and Canned Foods Act reads:
The initials of the Christian name, the full surname and address, or in the case of a firm or corporation, the firm or corporate name and address of the packer.
The point the hon. gentleman brings up is this, that a wholesale firm has been buying for some years the output of a factory. They place upon the can their label, Smith, Jones & Brown. The wholesale firm buy from Robinson; Robinson does not appear at all, but Smith, Jones & Brown are a first class reputable firm, and they have sold under their brand for years. Further, in the province of British Columbia nearly all the wholesale merchants purchase the output of some small cannery that is packing salmon. They will buy from one man this year his output, say he packs 4,000 cases, and they will put their own label upon it. Next year this man may have a small pack, he may be holding his salmon for a higher price. By this Act they would not be allowed to go into the market and buy from another small canner. That is the point that was brought up by the wholesale merchants of Vancouver. They wrote to me, and I suggested an amendment which I will make to section 12.

speechtext: I had better read section 1 first.

That does not touch the point I want to refer to. I want to



ask the minister a question about that Saskatchewan matter. I understand that the farmers of Saskatchewan are in this position: The Winnipeg packers can go to them and say, We cannot give you the full price of these hogs because there is not a demand for them in the home market, and therefore for the export trade we pay you a less price. Is that the position that the Saskatchewan farmers are in now? I also want to ask the minister if the packers of this country are allowed to bring in hogs in bond from the United States, pack them and ship them out again?
That is a customs matter, but I think not. The question of bonding does not enter into this at all.

The minister knows that other manufacturing establishments have that privilege and if pork packing establishments have that privilege, it certainly would be a very serious thing for the farmers in Saskatchewan.
I do not think that any factory in Canada is a bonded warehouse under the Customs Act.

If the pork packing establishments in Winnipeg can force the farmers to take a less price than their product is worth by representing that there is an overproduction on the home market it would place the farmers of Saskatchewan in a very unfortunate position.
Mr. FISHER, I do not think the farmers are in that position.

Does the minister not think that the very fact of them being subject to inspection puts them in that position ?
Mr. FISHER, I do not think it allows any person to force the farmers in any respect.
Well, I disagree with the minister in that respect.

You repeal clauses 3 and 4 of this Act ?
Mr. FISHER, Up to the present time section 11 only applies to such factories as are declared by the minister to be under the operation of sections 3 and 4 and 6 to 10. We repeal that section and substitute this section which says that the Governor in Council may, upon application of the owner thereof, exempt any establishment from the operations of this Act. That is to say that the active operation in dealing with it is for the purpose of exemption. Before, the active operation in dealing with it was for the purpose of putting it under the Act.

A great many hogs are killed in our part of the country, they are shipped in carcasses to Toronto and sold to Park, Blackwell & Co., or Harris or any-Mr. J. D. REID.
one else. How does the individual who sells these carcasses know whether they are intended for export or not ? Do these carcasses come under this clause of the Act or do they not ?
Mr. FISHER, If they are -bought to be taken to a factory that is under the operation of the Act, of course, they do. If they are bought and not brought into such a factory they do not.
They may be bought by any wholesale butcher who sells them again.
Suppose that a wholesale butcher buys them from the farmer

No, he buys them generally from a merchant.
Mr. FISHER, Well, supposing the merchant buys from the farmer, he can do that without this Act affecting him in any way whatever, but if the merchant sells a carcass to go to a factory which is under the operation of the Act he cannot do it unless the carcass has been inspected.

A merchant, for instance, in the town in which I live, purchases a number of hogs. A buyer comes from Park, Blackwell & Co. or Harris, and he purchases them ; is it the duty of the seller to ascertain whether these carcasses are going to be shipped to that factory for export, or what disposition is to be made of them ?
No.
Surely it is not the duty of the seller and yet if they were going to a factory I take it that they would come under the operation of the Act.
Before they went into the factory they would have to be inspected and the inspector would reject them if they had not complied with the provisions of the Act.
Who would be responsible for the inspection, the buyer or the seller ?

That is something I cannot tell you ; it depends on the bargain between them. If I sell to a man who does not ask for a guarantee that the law had been complied with he is responsible. If I sell to him and say that these carcasses have been inspected and are all right to go into the factory he would hold me responsible. It is a matter of private arrangement.
If there is no understanding reached between them the seller would be exempt from any liability with regard to the inspection ?
As far as I can tell.

It seems to me that it is not absolutely clear in regard to this matter of export. The interpretation clause

says that ' export ' means out of Canada or out of the province in which the establishment is situated. I imagine that the matter of exporting from one province to the other must have got mixed up with transactions in regard to carcasses which are bought simply for the local market. I do not think that is clear. In section 5 there is a clause which apparently makes it possible for a farmer to slaughter at home for the home market only, but I understand from the minister now that it is perfectly clear that the farmer may slaughter at home for the home market and he may export into another province provided the carcass does not go to an establishment that is packing for export.
That is clear.
Is the minister quite clear in his own mind upon that point ?
Yes.

Absolutely and perfectly clear ? The reason I ask is that in the 5th section it is stated ' unless the minister otherwise orders.' What does that mean ? Have any regulations been made by the minister under the 5th section ? I have heard two different versions of the matter. It is said that hogs which are exported out of a province are liable to inspection under this 5th section, unless the minister otherwise orders. Has the minister made any order or are there any orders in council in force ?

If carcasses are sold from one province to another by a farmer who has slaughtered them, or if they are sold on the ordinary markets or sold to a dealer and they do not go to a packing house for export they are not under the operation of the Act at the present time. If they are being sold to go to a factory which Is under the operation of the Act then they have to comply with the regulations.
That is to say that the organs have to accompany the carcass or else the animals have to be shipped alive.
As a matter of fact, any person who ships hogs will have to comply with the regulations to be safe.
It he is not pretty sure it is going into local consumption.

As far as my province is concerned the regulations under this Act are not approved by anybody, because of the uncertainty of the market, the uncertainty of the inspection, and for many other reasons. I have condemnatory letters of all kinds.

The arrangements which were made at the end of the season with regard to Prince Edward Island and which we expect to be able to continue will I 2194
think remove the difficulty my hon. friend mentions.
What were these arrangements ?
In the case of Prince Edward Island the carcasses would be inspected and allowed to go forward and to be received by the factory they were shipped to.
If an inspector would inspect a carload of hogs at Saskatchewan could they go to a packing house and be afterwards exported?
Our inspectors are usually at the packing houses. If an inspector inspected carcasses in Saskatchewan which had the organs attached, and marked them as inspected they could go to the factory.
Is it necessary that the carcasses should contain all the organs when they are inspected ?
The veterinary experts inform me that any inspection without the organs attached to the carcasses is futile.
I do not see that provided for in the law.
That is a regulation.'
When animals are purchased is there an understanding between the buyer and the seller that they are to be subject to inspection before the buyer pays for them ?
That is a matter between the buyer and seller.

Suppose a carload is consigned to, say Harris, of Toronto, and they are to be paid for when delivered, but on inspection at Toronto it is found that some are diseased, could the buyer charge the loss to the seller ?
That is not a matter for the department, whose duty is simply to see that no diseased hog is taken to the factory.
Supposing no understanding existed between the buyer and the seller, the buyer could not charge the loss back to the seller ?
That would be a question for the courts to decide.
What establishments are at present under the operation of this Act ?
I am told there are nearly thirty.
These will now be exempt ?

No. Those already under the operation of the Act will remain under it and if the amendment is passed all other factories would come under the operation of the Act until an order in council exempted them.	,

On section 12,
Mr. (MACPHERSON. I beg to move that the Bill be amended by adding thereto the following section :
Paragraph (a) of section 12 is amended by adding thereto after the word ' packer ' the words:
Or of the first dealer obtaining it direct from the packer who sells or offers the same for sale. Such dealer shall upon the request of the inspector appointed under this Act give the name of the packer of such articles.
That will meet the wishes of the wholesale man who sells under his own brand the goods which he buys from the packer.

I understand this amendment to be for the purpose of allowing the first purchaser from the packer, who has made arrangements with different packing houses, to put his name on the package instead of the original packer, he being then responsible for the character of the goods. 1 know that this is an amendment which the wholesale trade of Canada generally are very much in favour of. I think it is safeguarded by the second clause which requires, iu case of a suit, that the name of the original packer shall be given to the inspector and therefore I would not object to the incorporation of this amendment in the present Bill. The object of the whole Act is to secure that the public shall be safeguarded by the name of a responsible person on the package, so that when a consumer buys the article he can know where it comes from. Originally the intention and idea of the Act was that he should know the actual packer; but representations have been made, reinforced by a considerable number of good names, that the name of the wholesaler is frequently as good a guarantee as the name of the original packer. As the law requires that in case of any suit or action arising out of an infraction of the Act the name of the original packer shall be given, which under this amendment shall be done, I think the general intent and principle of the Act is observed to a sufficient extent to justify this facility to the wholesale trade being granted.

In the month of January I asked a question in regard to an article that appeared in one of the English papers on the subject of the importation of frozen meats into England. I would like to ask the minister if this Act will affect the export trade of frozen meats in boxes during the winter mouths.

As I gathered the tenor of the article to which my hon. friend refers, the fact that we have this Act will preclude our meats being objected to in the English market, although we have not any official declaration to that effect. The Eng-Mr. FISHER.
lish are no doubt jealous of imported food stuffs, and one of our objects in passing this Act last session was to throw all possible safeguards around our trade with England in those articles. My hon. friend will notice that in the article Canada is not mentioned as a country from which dangerous food of that character might come, which I think is attributable to the fact that we have this Act.
I suppose any Act they might have would apply to all countries.

That would depend, of course, on the provisions of any such Act; but we have the assurance from the authorities in England that compliance with the provisions of this Act will be sufficient to justify them in not applying any such exclusion to Canada.
Bill reported, and amendments read the first and the second time, and agreed to.
On the question, when shall the Bill be read the third time:

With reference to the clause ignoring the manufacturers' label with the name on the can, I would ask that this Bill do not receive its third reading now, as I wish to communicate with some of the eanners in London in reference to it.
