Mr. FISHER moved second reading of Bill (No. 148) to amend the Inspection and Sale Act.
This Bill has not yet been translated into French. However, I do not object to going on with it.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.

The Inspection and Sale Act, chapter 85 of the revised statutes, is a consolidation of a large number of Acts affecting different commercial products. That Act is divided into ten parts. Part 1 does not apply to grain, but is not otherwise limited. Part 2 applies exclusively to grain, part 3 to flour and meal, part 4 to beef and pork, part 5 to leather and raw hides, part 6 to pot ashes and pearl ashes, part 7 to fish and fish oils, part 8 to dairy products, part 9 to fruit and fruit marks, and part 10 to certain staple commodities. Under the Department of Agriculture's legislation, partly since I have been in office and partly before, there were a number of special Acts passed applying to dairy products and to fruits, and it is only to those parts of the Act which apply to dairy products and fruits that this Bill relates. I may say that the Act passed by this parliament a few years

ago now forms part 9 of the Inspection and Sale Act. Part 1 of the Inspection and Sale Act does not apply to grain but is otherwise not limited in its application, and I want to exclude from it dairy products, fruits or fruit marks.

A number of the members interested in dairy products and farming generally are absent, and I think it would be better if the minister would take up some other Bill so as to give them an opportunity of discussing this one.

We might go over some of the amendments and get them passed and then let the committee rise and report progress, and get leave to sit again.
On section 2,

This section repeals certain provisions of the Inspection and Sale Act which are practically obsolete. They were taken from the old General Inspection Act and have been replaced by a special Hairy Act passed some nine or ten years ago.
On section 3-adulterated cheese,

This is to prevent any inferior curd being incorporated in the new cheese during the process of its manufacture and also to prevent the placing of any foreign substance in the cheese. There has been a. little difficulty lately through careless cheese makers incorporating sour or inferior curd in their cheese.
Is there no Act to prevent this already ?

The Justice Department say there is not. Then some foolish people have taken it into their head to put bottles and little cans into their cheese with their name or something of that kind in them. That is complained of seriously by the trade. It is a fraud because people are getting what they did not buy, and besides the quality of__ the cheese around the foreign substance is apt to deteriorate.
Mi1. SPROULE. I am afraid the bon. gentleman is not a gallant or he would hesitate before doing what may be a great injustice. I remember reading not long ago of some young lady putting in a cheese a small bottle with a paper inside it. giving her name and address, and shortly afterwards she got an offer of marriage from the lucky purchaser of the cheese. It would be strange for a bachelor to make such an amendment to the law as would prevent the possibility of this occurring in the future. I would think he would be more chivalrous than to attempt to do so. Besides he might get a wife himself in that way.
Would colouring matter be regarded as a foreign substance?
I do not think so; I think that is part of the process of making the cheese and would not come under the section.

Of course the insertion of any such thing in the cheese must be deliberate, it cannot be an accident. There has been very serious complaint on the part of those engaged in the trade and it was thought necessary to stop the practice. I do not think a magistrate would impose the extreme penalty unless there were strong reasons, and $25 is not too high a penalty if it is desired to deter people from doing such acts.
I would suggest that the minister might use some more definite form of expression which would include the cases he has mentioned but would not be broad enough to include colouring matter.

This clause was submitted to the Minister of Justice, but as the Bill has to go back into committee I shall ask the Department of Justice whether colouring matter would come under it, and . if so, we will see that it is provided against. I would not wish for a moment that colouring matter should be included under this section.
On section 5-making of regulations by Governor in Council.

These two sections were in the special Act, but in the consolidation of the statutes, in consequence of the other sections that we are now repealing having been left in, these two were omitted. It is now necessary to reinsert them to enable us to appoint inspectors and make regulations.
These referred principally to milk?
To dairy products.
Is it not rather irregular to give authority to the Governor in Council to make regulations and to impose such large penalties for contravention of them?
That has been in all the agricultural Acts.
That is not a very good reason.
And it has worked well.

We are empowering the Governor in Council to authorize penalties of $50 for infringements of regulations of which we know nothing. They may be innocent and unimportant or they may be very important, and yet we are fixing a penalty of $50 for what may be a very trifling offence. Could not the minister so frame this as to afford better protection to all parties?

The regulations must necessarily be in accordance with the provisions of the Act; you cannot make regulations contrary to the provisions of an Act. I do not think the penalty herein referred to is too high for infractions of regulations in consonance with the Act.

I do not think the provisions of the Act control the regulations to any extent. We have not the slightest idea of these regulations or what crime the government may formulate by them.
Mr. FISHER, The regulations cannot enlarge the operation of the Act. they can only be consistent with it.
When such an expression as this is used 'The Governor in Council may make such regulations as he considers necessary.'
In accordance with the Act.

I do not see that it is limited in any other way.
In order to secure the efficient enforcement and operation of this Act, and may by such regulations impose penalties not exceeding $50.
I fail to perceive that the Act limits the power to make regulations at all.
Yes, that is well understood in legislation.

The Governor in Council may make regulations for the efficient carrying out of the Act, and they have to relate to the subject matter of the Act. He makes a regulation, we will say, that certain facilities are to be afforded to the inspectors, and he may make other regulations as to other matters, some of them may be very trivial. For the non-observance of some of these regulations a penalty of $1 might be ample, and $5 might be an outrage. Now we are here making the law. and we are delegating to the Governor in Council, without knowing anything about the nature of the regulations, unlimited power to impose such penalties as they see fit up to $50, and they come into force bv Mr. SPROULE.
the mere fact of publication. The minister said a moment ago that this was merely a re-enactment of the sections that were left out when the revision was made. Perhaps he will tell us where we can find the statute as it was originally.

I think 56 Yic. chapter 37, is the original Act. My hon. friend has pointed out that infractions of the different regulations would require different penalties. Now this clause empowers the Governor in Council to make regulations and to apply penalties suitable to the gravity of the infraction. It does not say that to every offence a fine of $50 may be applied ; the Governor in Council is empowered to go as high as $50 when the offence is a serious one, but if it is a trivial one a smaller penalty would be applied. It would be impossible for the Act to fix penalties to be applied to regulations that are not in existence when the Act is passed. You have to leave it to the discretion of the Governor in Council when they make the regulations to attach a proper penalty for the infraction of a particular regulation.
Give us some idea of what the regulations are likely to be.

We have regulations fixing the duties of inspectors, but we have not found occasion to make any regulations for offences. The penalties for offences provided in the Act itself apparently have been found insufficient. We have not had a great deal to do to enforce this Act, the Act is well known, and the dairymen have been living up to it pretty thoroughly. Once in a while we have had some serious cases, and we have dealt with them and imposed a penalty, but I think in every case where the offences were serious, the penalties provided for under a special clause of the Act were found sufficient.

The minister says they have found no need for regulations up to the present, then why propose to amend the Act ?
Mr. FISHER, Because the need may arise at any moment. But we are not amending the Act, we are reinstating clauses that were in the Dairy Act which were taken out of it when the consolidation of the statutes was made last year ; because there were some old clauses which seemed to apply to the Dairy Act as well as to other parts of the Inspection Act.
The revisers could not have done their duty properly.
It was supposed that the general provisions under this Sale and Inspection Act would cover it, but that has not been found satisfactory.

The minister stated that the dairymen had been living up to the Act. It would seem almost a waste of time to

make enactments when there is no need of them.
Mr. FISHER, My hon. friend has misunderstood me or has not grasped the situation. There are clauses in the Act providing for certain offences and penalties. We have enforced these clauses without any difficulty. Only the other day in Quebec we had a man fined $300 and not long ago we had a Montreal man fined $200 and costs under this Act. There have been occasions when, if we had been fully convinced that we had the authority to proceed, we might have proceeded, hut since the revised statutes have been in force we have not had that assurance; consequently, we have hesitated to proceed, and we want to be in a position to enforce the Act should occasion arise.

That is a different explanation now. If authority is needed it should be provided.
On section 6-' Culls ' define'd.
Mi1. FISHER. We found it necessary to define culls.
Is this an entirely new definition ?

Entirely new. It is the best we could work out.
On section 7, false marking.

The only difference here from the original Act is that we put in the words * no culls.' If my hon. friend looks at the last part of the clause he will see that it provides that No. 2 quality shall contain ' not less than eighty per cent free from worm holes and such other defects as cause material waste.' We found that people were interpreting that to mean that the other twenty per cent might be pure culls. That was not the idea of the Act and now we say that this quality includes no culls.
On section 8, penalties respecting marking.
Mr. FISHER, This section increases the penalties under the Fruit Marks Act. We have found that the penalties were so small that people engaged in the trade seemed practically to ignore them. We took all the trouble and expense of prosecuting and upon securing the conviction of a man who shipped 100 or 1,000 barrels might be fined $3 or $4. We have had 168 convictions during the last season and I remember seeing not long ago the list of penalties imposed. Hardly any of them exceeded $10 and it seemed perfectly ridiculous.
You raise the minimum ?
We raise the minimum and maximum and make the penalties so severe that the people will be deterred from breaking the Act.
In a case where a man sells a certain kind of apple and then ships other than the kind or quality sold a penalty should be provided.
That is the intention of the Act.
I know, and the law has been broken.

Yes, we have taken out prosecutions to try and put a stop to that. It is false marking. But if a man takes an order for one kind of apple, ships another and marks the barrels with the name of what is in them we cannot deal with that.
Of course, he is breaking his contract.
Yes, but that is not a matter that we can deal with. It is only when he breaks the law that we can deal with him.
Yes.

Before leaving section 7 I desire to point out to the minister that it defines No. 2 quality as having not less than 80 per cent free from worm holes. My impression is that No. 1 quality must have 90 or 95 . per cent free from worm holes.	-
Ninety per cent.

I notice you are not amending that clause. Consequently the same difficulty that the minister referred to before might occur with regard to culls ; the balance of the barrel might be made up with culls as well as in the case of No. 2 quality, and I was wondering why the minister had not amended that section as well as 321.

We have not found such infractions in the case of No. 1. I suppose they might possibly occur and I would not object to amending the section by putting in the same words. It hardly seemed worth while for the packer to put in 10 per cent of culls in No. 1 quality, but when it came to 20 per cent he would do so.
Ten per cent is a good profit.

I do not see any objection to putting that into No 1. I will consider that before the Bill is finally taken out of committee.
On section 9, penalty for tampering with marks.

Section 329 provides a penalty for defacing or changing the marks on a closed package. It is a deliberate fraud and we wish to increase the penalty. The penalty under the original section was $40 tine and we are making it $100 for the first offence and $200 for each subsequent of-

fence. That seems to he a very deliberate crime and I think it ought to be severely punished.
On section 10, penalties respecting apples and berries.

Some time ago I called the attention of the Minister of Agriculture to some of his inspectors in Nova Scotia whom it was thought were not in a position to deal fairly with the public because of their interference in municipal politics. The minister then did not seem to pay much attention to the matter but I would now ask him if he has decided to appoint inspectors under this Act who are not mixed up in public affairs. It was thought these inspectors could not be impartial owing to their environment and the minister was asked if he did not think it wise that such inspectors should refrain from taking part in such contests. Even supposing these men were doing their duty fairly it is in my opinion not desirable that the action they take in the direction I have indicated should lead to suspicion that they might treat those who support them with greater partiality than those who do not support them.

I would say quite frankly to my hon. friend that if a complaint were made and proven that any inspector in consequence of any action of his in a municipal contest was guilty of discrimination, I would not hesitate at all to dismiss such an inspector. If an inspector made use of his position, by reason of personal spite in connection with ally-contest, whether municipal, political or personal, to discriminate between individuals I would look upon such an one as unworthy to be an inspector. But I do not think I would be justified in taking action on the mere supposition that an inspector might possibly do a thing of that kind. The particular inspector in this case is not engaged by the year, he only acts as such for six or seven months in the year and at the time of the municipal contest I am not sure that he was engaged as inspector.
My information is that he was.

That may be, but at all events he is not a permanent officer on salary. I know of no complaint which has ever been made about him. The correspondence referred to by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) did not say that he had been guilty but simply that he might possibly be guilty. I do not think it would be fair for me to say to that gentleman that he should not take any part in municipal affairs because for a portion of the year he is inspector under the Act. While it is possible that a man might do something wrong under certain circumstances, I think my hon. friend will agree with me that just be-

cause of such a possibility it would be harsh and unfair on my part to interfere with him. If it were shown he had acted unfairly or had discriminated it would certainly be my duty to remove him from the opportunity of making such discrimination. Since I spoke last on the matter in the House I have no indication that this inspector has done anything unjust or unfair and if he had I think the information would have reached me by this time. I therefore think I was quite right in not taking any steps to remove him.

Does not the minister think it is desirable that in such a case eveu the possibility of suspicion should be removed from the public mind. Suppose a man who is engaged as a public weigher should himself be a purchaser of cattle and that he was called on to weigh his own cattle along with those of others, would there not be a feeling in the public mind that there was danger of his acting with partiality towards himself? I have a letter before me written to Mr. A. L. Davidson, of Nova Scotia, which says :
I have to acknowledge receipt of your let-t0r of October 22, and note what you say in regard to Mr Freeman Fitch and his duties under the Fruit Marks Act. Your statements require careful consideration which I shall certainly give them. I cannot say, however, speaking from memory and without investigation, that there is any law or rule in the public service that debars members from taking part in municipal affairs. I will see what the practice is in regard to such things and will act accordingly.
I do not know whether the minister has since communicated with this gentleman, but the letter upon which that was based is as follows :
I beg leave to call your attention to the following: Freeman Fitch, of Clarence, in the county of Annapolis, is at present employed by your department as inspector of fruit under the provisions of the Fruit Marks Act.
As such inspector his duties are to inspect apples packed by growers and dealers thereof and to ascertain if they are packed in accordance with the provisions of the said Act.
If, as such inspector, he finds apples fraudulently packed he is required to mark the package in which such apples are contained with the words ' falsely marked/ It is also a part of his duty to prosecute parties for violating the provisions of the said Act.
From the quasi.judicial nature of the office of inspector it is possible for the occupant of the said office, to discriminate between those toward whom he is friendly disposed and those toward whom he is unfriendly disposed.
The ratepayers of pollinc district No. 3, in the county of Annapolis, are nearly all engaged in the pursuit of raising apples for sale, and it is a part of the duty of the said Freeman Fitch as said fruit inspector to inspect the apples as packed by the different ratepayers of the said polling district No. 3, in the said county of Annapolis.
690!)

The said Freeman Fitch is at present a candidate for the office of municipal councillor to represent the said polling; district No. 3 in the municipal council of the municipality of the countv of Annapolis. The election for the said office will he held upon the 19th day of November, 1907. when the ratepayers of the said polling district will elect their councillor by ballot.
As a candidate at such election the said F reeman Fitch is peculiarly open to the temptation of showing favouritism as an inspector to those of the said ratepayers of polling district No. 3 as may support the said Freeman Fitch at the said election and discrimination against such of said ratepayers as'do not support him at said election. If elected as a councillor the said Freeman Fitch will be peculiarly tempted to refrain from enforcing the law against his supporters for the fear of estranging their support, and his usefulness as an inspector will in the nature of things be seriously impaired.
The time spent by the said Freeman Fitch in canvassing the said polling district as a candidate as aforesaid, coming as it does at the season of the year when his official duties are the most pressing, cannot hut interfere with the proper discharge of his duties as an inspector as aforesaid- as will also his duties as a councillor should he be elected to that office.
All of which facts are respectfully submitted.
This is dated October 22, about the time the fruit is being put up, and therefore I take it that he was engaged in inspecting then.
Yes, I think he was in that case.

It is apparent that he is running for municipal councillor at the very time his inspection must be done, and that he must of necessity have friends on one side and those who are not his friends on the other side, and he is inspecting for both alike. Would there not be an impression left in the minds of those carrying on a vigorous contest against him that they would hardly get hot justice, or at best more than very cold justice, whereas those canvassing and working for him would be more likely to get fair play ? Does the minister not think it would be a proper thing to ask his inspectors to refrain from running for such offices or to appoint others to these positions ?

I think it is quite necessary that the people should feel that they are getting fair play ; but I have had no representations except that one letter to show that there was any feeling in regard to this gentleman. I have had no complaint that the inspector has shown any partiality or discrimination of any kind whatever, and I do not think it would be fair to judge him on the suspicion of one correspondent that he might possibly act unfairly. As to public officials taking part in municipal affairs, there is no law or rule against it, and I think it is a matter of judgment how
far it should be allowed. I do not think public officials should take part in municipal affairs to an extent that would interfere with their official duties ; and if it could be shown that Mr. Fitch was not attending properly to his duties as an inspector because he was at the same time a municipal councillor, I would have no hesitation in saying to him that the two things were incompatible. But that is not suggested in this letter. The only suggestion is that if he happens to be a candidate for the municipal council, it is possible that he will exercise Ms powers as an inspector in favour of those who vote for him and against those who vote against him. Under these circumstances, I do not think it would be proper for me to say" that Mr. Fitch should not be an Inspector.
You think he could at the same time carry on an election and properly attend to his duties as an inspector ?
It might be a little hard to do it.
The minister does not see any objection to his official doing the two things at the same time ?
If the one interfered with the other, there would be.

It is plain to me that it is sufficient to destroy that confidence in the public mind which ought to exist, and in my judgment it would justify the minister in notifying his inspectors that they could not be regarded as eligible for that position if they were at the same time running for election either as municipal councillors or in any other capacity that would practically divide the public Into two portions, one of whom would be friendly and the other unfriendly. It is not human nature for people to feel that they are likely to get fair play under such circumstances, and to my mind it is a good deal to have the people satisfied that they are getting fair play, whether they do or not.

I again repeat that there is nothing whatever to indicate that anybody has the feeling expressed in that letter. This gentleman says they may have that feeling. He does not say that anybody has been hurt or feels that way.
If they had no suspicion would they write the letter ?
Only one man wrote the letter.
The whole community is made up of units and one man has an equal right to another and an equal claim to have an abuse remedied.
If only one man has a suspicion and writes a letter, I am not to take it for granted that he represents the whole community.

But you take it for granted that he misrepresents the facts and is not worthy of consideration because he is only one man. But this one man gives the circumstances which justify suspicion and cause public dissatisfaction, and the minister in his reply said that he would give the matter careful consideration. Has he given it any consideration?

Yes, and I have explained the result of my consideration. I have said that I did not consider the statement of one individual that certain improper things might happen, which he does not say have happened, or that certain people might have a suspicion, which he does not say they have-I did not consider such vague statements required any action on my part.
Why then did this man write the letter he did instead of making a direct charge?
Why did he not make a direct charge?
A good many know of wrong doing, but do not make direct charges ?
Then I do not bother about them. If a man has not the courage to make a direct charge, I do not take any account of his suspicions.
The bon. gentleman had better tell the apple raisers of that county that that is the way he uses the farmers.
That is how I use that man.
I would suggest the substitution of some other word for the word ' foreign.' I would suggest the word ' nonedible.'

I would not like to see an oyster in the middle of a cheese.
Progress reported.
Bill (No. 119) to encourage the construction of dry docks-Mr. Fielding-read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This Bill is founded on a resolution which was fully discussed and explained some time ago, and which I think commended itself to the general consideration of the House. This amendment is destined to adapt the machinery of the Act, which was put on the statute-book some years ago, to some difficulties which have been met in its administration. Under this general legislation a dry dock had been constructed at Halifax and another at Col-liugwood and an agreement was entered into for the construction of one at Vancouver. The latter, however, has not yet Mr. FISHER.
been constructed. The essential difference between the present law and the amendment touches two points. The limitation of the amount in the law is 3 per cent on $3,000,000, but in view of the increased size of steamers and the need of larger docks, it is proposed to increase the amount to $1,500,000, which, at 3 per cent, represents $45,000. The second point of importance is with respect to the method of payments. Under the Act payments are to be made for twenty years, subject to the condition that the dock shall be at all times kept in successful operation. Capitalists, however, take exception to that. They say that the men who advance the money might reasonably ask for a definite fixed assurance of payment and the government should provide other means for insuring the operation of the dock. The proposal now submitted provides that the twenty years' payment of the subsidy shall be fixed and definite and that, in the event of the company failing to operate the dock, the government shall take possession of it.
Is it intended to grant an additional subsidy to the Collingwood dry dock?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, that dock was constructed under the present Act and that transaction is closed. Of course the dock might be enlarged, but we have no such proposal before us.

Would this cover the case of the enlargement of a dry dock and how would the basis be arrived at in the case of enlargement? Take the Collingwood dry dock. Suppose the company should sjiend an additional sum in order to enlarge it, on what would you base your additional subsidy?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If they propose to enlarge the dock, they would be entitled to an additional subsidy, but would have to come under the condition with respect to non-operation. Under the existing contract they are only entitled to a subsidy so long as the dock continues in operation. Under the new Act, the government would have the right to take over the dock. Should they extend the dock, they would come under the new Act both for the extension and the jiortion already built. You could not separate the two.
If for instance, the Collingwood Company desired to enlarge their dock and applied for an additional subsidy under this would the government then take over that dock ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Only in the event of failure to operate.
Suppose that after enlarging they proposed to operate the same as before, on what basis would you then grant an additional subsidy ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They would have to receive an additional subsidy under the terms of this Act. They would get a subsidy for twenty years on the additional amount and that would be a fixed and definite subsidy under the provisions of this Act. In order to avail themselves of that subsidy, they would be obliged to give the government the right to take over not the new work alone but the whole dock, because there could not be any distinction between the two.
But if they desired to continue to own the dock ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then under the present law we do not interfere with them. Even if tlie government took it over they would not own it but would only operate it temporarily.
Would you base the additional subsidy on the cost of the extension or upon the valuation of your engineer of the works, including the site ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The cosc would have to have reference entirely to the proposed new work. The work of the past is disposed of. I understand the company to have received all the subsidy to which they are entitled. If they proposed additional work then only the cost of the additional work would be considered,
And that would be upon the basis of the valuation of the government's own engineer ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, the engineer would have to examine and report in order to fix the subsidy.
On section 2-interpretation,

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I beg to move to amend this section by adding the words :
And ' dry dock' includes floating dock.
I do not think this is absolutely necessary but it is well to remove possible doubts. Marine docks are now being constructed largely under the system of floating docks, and we want to make it clear that if it is thought well to build a floating dock it will be included under the Act. It has been so interpreted now, but we want to make it clear beyond all doubt.
On section 3-basis of subsidy.
There seems to be no time limit. Suppose you make annual payments-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is twenty years, the same as the old Act.
What do they receive for the Collingwood dry dock per annum ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The figures were given in a previous discussion.
I think it is $15,000 a year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall be pleased to get the figures before the Bill is disposed of.
It does not seem necessary for the parties who are enlarging to show any data as to the cost, it is all left to the judgment of the engineer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Necessarily the engineer will have to receive the representations made by the company, with their plans, &c.; this would have to be submitted to the examination and inquiry of the engineer. I fancy it would require the co-operation of the company and the engineer.
The actual cost and an estimate are different things.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The actual cost could only be determined when the work is completed ; but in order to fix the cost for subsidy purposes it is necessary to come as near to it as possible in advance and that is the provision of the Bill.
Would that be changed in the light of experience ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, the engineer in his report would have to be careful not to place the estimate too high, because you give a guarantee to the financial people of a certain amount at certain times. Difficulty arises from the necessity of fixing the subsidy in advance.

That would be the case if a company is investing money but with a few individuals building it on the strength of preliminary arrangements made with the government on the basisi of a valuation with a condition that they be paid three per cent on the cost of it, then after the completion of the dock the actual cost could be obtained from data furnished during the construction and the payment could be made on that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The very essence of this is that you shall be able to give financial people absolute certainty of so much money at certain times. If the government were to allow that payment to be fixed on an excessive valuation that would be improper; that would realize the danger which my hon. friend suggests. We would have to see that the report of the engineer was carefully made, and did not value the property in excess of its real value.

This does not seem to go on the same principle as the last Act. Reading subsection 2 of section 4, the basis of the subsidy would appear to be as the1 minister suggests, that the chief engineer of the department shall make a careful estimate, before the work is executed, as to the probable expense, and upon that the government shall base a subsidy that shall be final. That would appear to 1 be in accordance with the wording of the

section. But I know as a matter of fact tiiat under the old Act, after the work had been executed the government sent an engineer to value the work, and by the valuation of the engineer and by the examination of the accounts, the government ascertained what was the actual cost. I do not know whether there is any reason for changing the system. Take the case of Collingwood. After all the work was executed, Mr. Coste, I think it was, examined the work and determined that a certain amount must necessarily have been expended. Also certain accountants went into the matter and went over the books and papers so far as they could be obtained for the purpose of ascertaining where the money had been actually expended. I think that was in accordance with the old Act. Is there any reason for departing from that principle? Is not that a better principle than this merely preliminary estimate before the work is executed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I rather think that the old system was the better one. But the difficulty has been that it .leaves an element of uncertainty as to the payment of the subsidy. Although that did not avail against the Collingwood dock, it has been found to avail against other schemes of docks. The Collingwood people were willing to construct a dock under these terms. There was some discussion last year over the Collingwood dock. I am not familiar with the details, but I know that the essence of the old arrangement was that the cost was determined by a report of the engineer at the time of completion, and on that the subsidy was paid. Now it has been found that financial people who have been asked to assist another dock scheme, particularly the one at St. John, N.B., people who were disposed to put money into it, said, Well, we are financial people but we are not dock operators, and we do not want to be called upon to take the risk of this dock being operated to the satisfaction of the government; we think the government should make some arrangement for the operation of the dock. It is to meet that difficulty that this change has been made. Therefore we propose to have a report made by the engineer at the beginning, and in view of the facts suggested by hon. gentlemen opposite, we shall satisfy ourselves that the report is a very conservative report, and thereupon a valuation shall be fixed. Then we shall say to the financial people, We have satisfied ourselves that this dock will cost say a million dollars, and we will agree to give you 3 per cent upon that million dollars for twenty years, and we undertake by another method to look after the operation of the dock. It is to meet that condition that the change was made.
On section 0,

I think the minister has made the time limit rather short when the purpose is to get new docks. I Mr. LENNOX.
can understand that docks already in operation would take advantage of the time for enlarging them, but is there a sufficient inducement for capital to take hold of a new dock in a guarantee- of twenty year bonds at 3 per cent? Unless the minister may have some information I have not got, I think it will be difficult to find capitalists willing to build docks with such a limited guarantee as twenty years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should not like to make the conditions too hard, because the object is to secure the construction of docks at appropriate places. On the other hand, I would not like to make the conditions so easy that people would be tempted to go into the enterprise as a pure speculation. It is well that people should look at the matter carefully, and be content with a moderate guarantee such as the government gives them, and look for a balance out of the operation of the dock itself. The subsidy originally allowed was only 2 per cent, we increased that some years ago to 3 per cent. A twenty-year subsidy of 3 per cent is a fairly strong inducement for people to put money into an enterprise where there is a commercial basis for it. They would have to look for the development of trade for their compensation over and above this twenty years. But unless there is that condition of trade which gives promise of some revenue to the dock, then it is not desirable that the dock should be constructed. We do not want to make it so easy for docks to be constructed that the construction shall be undertaken at numerous places where there is not really business for them.

And especially in view of the fact that the tendency of money is always downwards. Three per cent is not a bad interest on money, it is all the interest that banks will allow. Three per cent for twenty years would indemnify a company for going into the enterprise.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think it is a fair inducement.
On section 13,-The Dry Docks Subsidies Act. chapter 116 of the Revised Statutes, 1906, is repealed.
If you repeal the Act how do you deal with those docks that are now in existence ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would think that the agreement that we have made, for example, with the Collingwood dock under the Act existing at the time would continue. But. if there is any doubt about the matter I would be glad to take the hon. gentleman's suggestion into consideration. We have no desire to prevent payment to existing docks. If my hon. friend really thinks that it is open to doubt I will let the Bill stand in committee. It is one of those questions with regard to which we should make assurance doubly sure and I should be very

glad to let the Bill stand and ask the Department of Justice to look into it.
The agreement depends upon the statute and usually in repealing a statute you substitute something In its place.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am obliged to my bon. friend for the suggestion and I will have it considered.

It does not seem to me that clause 9 provides that you should be paid for any outlay besides operating expenses and maintenance. Suppose you have an initial outlay of $10,000 or $20,000 to put a dock in condition after you take it over ; then you can only pay for the advances which have been made out of operating expenses and maintenance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Read the last portion of section 9. It says that the government shall apply the balance first in repayment of the advances made under the next preceding section and secondly in payment of accrued interest on bonds. But the working expenses must be the first charge. In order to have the cow give milk, the cow must live. You must have working expenses in the first place and anything over and above that is applied to two things, first, to the payment of government advances and. next, to the payment of interest on bonds, if there are any outstanding.
Progress reported.
Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.
What business will be taken up to-morrow ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will proceed with the adjourned debate on the motion for Supply and the amendment of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk).

I wish before the House adjourns to call attention to one fact. It seems to be unusual that the government should go on with any other work when a motion of want of confidence is still undisposed of. I think it is unheard of in the British parliament that any minister should attempt to carry on any work except to dispose of a motion of want of confidence so as to show parliament and the country that the government retained the confidence of the majority of the members of the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That only shows what a very obliging and accommodating government we have in Canada. When we proposed on the last sitting day to take up to-day the adjourned debate, the whip of the Conservative party, and who at that time was leading the opposition, asked the government as a special consideration not to
proceed with the debate to-day because a number of hon. members on that side of the House could not find it convenient to be here and he asked that we should proceed with the Bills and let the debate stand over until to-morrow. I hope we did not create any violent convulsion to the constitution, and if we have done so it has been on account of our desire to accommodate hon. gentlemen opposite.
It is in keeping with the government's management of the House generally.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We had better not be so obliging.	-

Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 11.20 p.m.
. HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Wednesday, April 22, 1908.
